--- THE TWO MEN OF COLOGNE. BY Emma C. DOWD. A long time ago there lived in Cologne, Otto Von Hiller and Rupert Van Tone; And Otto wrote tablets, But Rupert made tahles— " The very beat tables that every were known!" So said every sensible frau in Cologne. "Friend Rupert," said Otto Von Hiller, one day, "Come. tell me the wonderful reason, I pray, Why men call you clever, When, really, you never Professed to have very much learning von keow, And I—well, in truth, I've enough for a show. "I'm master of Latin, I'm famous in Greek, Beth /trench and Italian I fluently speak; I could talk by the year Of our nation's career; Yet, some one has said—to his shame be it knowe— That lam the stupidest man in Cologne!" Said Rupert Van Tone, "If you'll promise to try it, I'll tell you the se.sret—l've learned to keep quiet." "But I've so much to say !" "'Twont spoil in a day; Who lets ha tongus run like a vibrating lever Stands very small chance of being called clever;' But led " so much to say," this Otto Von Ruler; 'Twas now to the judge, and now to the miller; He'd appear without warning, And stay all the morning. Till his hearers would sigh as he left, "What a drone! He is truly the stupidest man in Cologne."

Bat Rupert Van Tone worked on at his trade; He listened and thought, but his words be well weighed, Till at two score and twenty He'd money in plenty; And through summer and winter his mansion was knows As the home of the cleverest man in Col)gne. —St. Nicholas.

A LAMENT. We severed in Autumn early, Ere the earth was torn by the plough; The wheat and the oats and the barley, Are ripe for the harvest now. We sunder'd one misty morning, Ere the hills were dimmed by the rain; 'Through the flowers those hills adorning, Thou comest not back again. My heart is heavy and weary With the weight of a weary soul; The midday glare groweth dreary, And dreary the midnight scroll; The corn-stalks sigh for the sickle 'Neath the load of their golden grain; I sigh for a mate more fickle— Toots comsat not lie again. The warm sun riseth and setteth, The night bringeth moist'ning dew; But the soul that longeth, forgetteth The warmth and the moisture too. In the hot sun rising and setting There is !lough. save feverish pain; There are tears in the night dew's wetting,— Thou comest not back again. Thy voice in mine ear still mingles With the voices of whisp'ring trees; Thy kiss on my cheek still tingles At the kiss of the summer breeze; While dreams of the past are thronging For substance of shaded in vain. I am waiting, watching, and longing— Thou comest not back again. Waiting and watching ever, Longing and lingering yet, Leaves rustle and corn•stalks quiver, Winds murmur and waters fret; No ansyer they bring, no greeting, No speech save that sad refrain, No voice save an echo repeating— "lie conaeth not back again." -...-ADA7/1 LINDSAY GORDON, an Australian Poet.

Is the False Prophet to be trusted when he gives us any information as to the "Dark Races?"—Punch. The following notice recently appeared in a shop window of a tailor at Coek :—" Wanted, two apprentices, who will be treated as one of the family." NATURALLY—Prince Bismarck declines to "play the Postman to his enemies." He doubtless considers that he is tie Pillar of ths State, notits Post.—Punch. A rollickome. frolicsome, rare old cock As ever did nothing was our dog Jock; A gleescnne, fit-asome, affe3tionate beast, _ As slow at a fight as swift at a feast; A wit among dogs, when his life 'gan One couldn't but see the old wag in his tail, When his ears grew long and his eyes grew dim, And his course a bark could not strengthen him. Never more now shall our knees be press'd By his deur old chops in his slobbery rest, Nor our mirth be stirr'd at his solemn looks As wise, and as dull, as divinity books. Our old friend's dead, but we all well know He's gone to the kennels where the good dogs go, Where the cooks be not, but the beef-bones be, And his old head never need turn,„,for a flea. —From "Some Literary Recollections,' in the Cornhill Magazine for March. Cram LIFE.—Clib life is undoubtedly a luxury—a luxury so great that the female mind cannot imagine the; amount of equivalent a man receives in return for his eight or ten or eleven guineas a year. In a club you have twenty or thirty servants to wait upon you, yet you are not worried with the management of them. You move about a species of palace, with the feelings of a proprietor. You have at your disposal an accumulation of periodical literature that a duke or a prince of the realm could not enjoy in his own home. You lunch very sumptuously for half a crown, or lest. Your choice of meats at dinner is as great as a monarch's table could afford, and the wines you drink and pay for could not be bought outside for the same money. In most of the clubs von are able to place before your friend a repast which satisfies and flatters him much more than would any hospitality you could show him at home. What a pleasure to step from the hard and crowded pavement into a building carppted with thick material that luxuriously eprings under your feet like turf; a place in which each ttendant is as aefsrential as if you were in the peerage; a place wealthy in all its fittings, and, so to speak, redolent of good living; a place in which there are rooms—for those who wish them—where silence reigns as completely as in Trappist cells; a place where a rubber of whist before dinner or a game of billiards after dinner cartbe enjoyed with men whom you can trust; a place where the burnt. offerings of the smoker can be made in Oriental comfort; a place where you ca; receive letters and write as many as you choose, subject to no interruptions. Truly, the bache lor is tempted more and more to think, as he grows older, that the pleasures of domesticity would need to be very great indeed to counterbalance the comforts of the club. Sxonms ov Sugrvwrorts.—lt has been well remarked by one of the ancient sages that " the association with fools brings prosperity to no man;" in proof of which the fol- lowing Hindoo story may be cited :—A foolish fellow travelled with a shopkeeper, and when it became dark the blockhead laid himself down in the road to sleep, but the shopkeeper wisely crept into a hollow tree. By and bye some thieves came along the road, one of whom stumbling , against the fool's legs, exclaimed—" What's this—a log of wood?" "Go away, go away," cried the noodle; "is there a knot well tied, containing four annas, in the loins of a plank in our house?" The thieves then seized him, and took away his annas, and as they were moving off, one of them called out to him, "Is this money good?" The simpleton said—" Ha! ha! is it of my money you speak in that way, and want to know whether it is good or bad? See, there is a shopkeeper in that tree, show it to him." There. upon they robbed the shopkeeper of two hundred pagodas, and went their way rejoicing.— It is well known that fools or simpletons are prone to follow instructions rather too literally. Thus, in the " KathA Sarit Sagara" (" Ocean of the Rivers of Narrative"), probably the largest ex- tant collection of ancient Hindoo tales in Sanskrit. we are told of a merchant who said to his servant, "Take care if the door of my shop; I am going home for a short time." When the master was gone the foolish fellow took up the shop door on his shoulder and went off to see an actor perform. As he was returning his master met him and gave him a scolding, but the noodle simply answered, "I have taken care of the door as you told me." Now, compare this with the following tran-lation of a Sci- 'lm story:—" Giusa's mother wanted to go to mass, and she said to him, Giusa, if you want to go out draw the door after you;' but instead of shutting the door, Guisa took it to church." Equally profound blockheads were those "ser- vants who kept the rain off the trunks." The camel of a merchant gave way under tts load on a journey. He said to his servants—" I will go and boy another camel to carry half of this camel's load, and clothes." " ou d a remain here, and take partioular care that, if it eToo naystr, , the rain does not are v full ia o:: we: the leather of these trunks .which With these words the mer..ba, left the of the camel and went off. Suddenly a elsoanidca.m; the side ;:uurp, and . began to discharge rain. Then the fools d—. Y ter told us to take care that the rain did not totichntalZ leather of these trunks ;" and after they had made this sage reflection they dragged the clothes out of the trunks and wrapped them round the leather. The consequence was that the rain spoiled the clothes. On the master's return he exclaimed in a rage—" You rascals! Talk of water! Why, the whole stock of clothes is spoiled by the rain." But they answered him—" You told us to keep the rain off the trunks; what fault have we committed ?" "I told you," said he, "that if the leather got wet the clothes would be spoiled ; I told you so in order to save the clothes, not the leather." "Thus," moralises the narrator, Somadera, "fools with un- discerning hearts turn things upside down."—Leeds Mer- cury.

, It was announced in Dublin on Wednesday that is entirely free from foot-and-mouth disease. Dr. Arthur Leard suggests the use of charcoal for flatu- lence in horses, and also as a remedy for that frequent fatal distention of the first stomach from carbonic acid which occurs in cows after certain food such as clover and potatoes. A Montgomeryshire correspondent writes :—" A large Shropshire ewe, the property of Captain Adams, of Peny- lan, had eight lambs born on the 4th of March. The first lamb is alive and doing well; the other seven were well' formed, but were dead when produced. I have had a great deal of experience among sheep, and 1 never heard of a simi- lar occurrence." Hoxoun TO A FARMER.—On Thursday night, Mr. James Gifford, who has been farmer for many yesrs atiorhonskie, near Wigtown, but is leaving for another farm in the south of England, was entertained to a dinner at the Galloway Arms Hotel, and presented with a silver salver, suitably in- scribed, value £25, and 100 sovereigns, as a mark of esileem by his brother farmers and others. Mr. Lawrence Drew, the well known agriculturist and breeder of Clydesdales. at Merryton, near Hamilton, a few days ago. Mr. Drew, who was in his 56th year, suc- cumbed to an attack of diarrhoea, following upon erysipelas, which he contracted, it is believed, by exposing himself while suffering from illness at the Glasgow Stallion Show. Mr. Drew was the chosen- tenant-farmer candidate for the Parliamentary representation of South Lanarkshire. LIVER-ROT IN DUMFRIESSHIRE.—In severaLalistricts of Damfriesshire a considerable mortality among ewes is re- ported from liver-rot. On the hill farms it is more severe, and a good many deaths have occurred. The disease has also extended to the low grounds, and several horses have been affected with it. •It is due mainly to the damp ' weather. Farmers are anxiously looking for dry weather, so that the disease may be checked, as it is spreading to an alarming extent. l Burma FACTORIES IN DERBYSHIRE —Lord Scarsdale proposes to establish in the village of Kedleston, near Derby, a "scientific dairy," similar to that so successfully founded by the late Lord Vernon at Sudbury. There will be ma- chinery for separating cream from the milk, and the chief product of the dairy will be butter. A building is in course of construction, adjoining the deer park. Kedleston being in the centre of an important dairying district, the new fac- tory will be a great boon to the farmers. CHESTER Housa FAlR.—Wednesday's fair at Cheater was not so large as usual, dealers reserving their stock for the Lincoln fair. Best Irish carriage horses and hunters were Inot shown in anything like the numbers exhibited at pre- vious fairs. Scarcely any good cart horses were on offer, but a few very good cart horses changed hands. Ordinary cart horses made £4O to £5O. Large animals, suitable for town work, realised £55 to £75. The demand for all sorts was slack, and buyers were not at all numerous. It is ex- pected that the holding of cattle fairs will shortly be re- sumed, the county being almost free from foot and month disease. THE AGRICULTURAL POPULATION OF FRANCE.—The new Bulletin of the Minister of Agriculture, No. 1 for 1884, is just issued. The agricultural population is thus made up: Proprietors working their own land F,rmers and metayers Smal farmers working for others .... Presley,, char° sal burners, Au. Families and domestics of the above 11.713,793 Total 18,249,209 1 According to the returns, 49 per cent,, or nearly half the population of France obtain their livelihood by the culti- vation of the soil. About 24 per cent. follow industrial pursuits; 10 per cent, are engaged in commence • 7 per cent. live upon their private income; 4 per. cent4elong to the liberal professions; rather over 2 per cent. tii-seafaring oc- cupations; 1i to the public forces, while of 24 per cent, the professions are unknown or nil. Of the 49 per cent, who live by the cultivation of the soil, about one third are actual workers, the remainder consisting of members of the family and domestics. LIVE STOCK AND CATTLE DISEASE STATISTICS.—SOMe statistical tables relating to home an I foreign animals and ' returns relating to foot and mouth disease have just been issued by the agricultural department of the Privy Council. A table compiled from the agricultural returns shows the number of cattle, sheep, and pigs in England, Wales, and Scotland on the 4th or sth of June in each of the years 1879, 1880, 1881, 1882, and 1883:— Cattle. Sheep. Pigs. 1879 ...... ...... 5,858,358 1880 1881 1882 1883 Average Another table gives the results of contagious or infectious diseases la Great Britain for the same five years. This shows that 416,145 animals were affected with foot and month disease in 1883, against 37,950 in 1882, 183,046 in 1881, 32,378 in 1880, and 15,947 in 1879. Pleuro-pnen- monia attacked only 931, as compared with 1,200 in 1882, 1,797 in 1881, 2,681 in 1880, and 4,296 in 1879. Of the other diseases, swine fever was the most widely prevalent in 1883, 11,225 animals having been attacked, against 14,763 In the previous year, 7,994 in 1881, 9,865 in 1880, and 17,074 in 1879. Sheep scab, since 1879, when there were 54,607 cases, his kept at a little over or under 30,000, the number of animals affected in 1883 being 34,571. Only 705 horses were attacked by glanders last year, whereas 1,346 were attacked in 1880, and nearly as many in 1881. Farcy has not fluctuated greatly, the cases having num- bered 481 in 1879, 764 in 1880, and 534 in 1883. Details relating to the prevalence of these diseases in the various counties are given in separate tables. POTATOES: VARIETIES—MANURES.—Sixty-One varieties of potatoes were planted in drills at Glasnevin, on March 3, 1883. Farmyard manure was applied at the rate of 20 tons per statute acre, and the sets were placed one foot apart in drills n feet wide. The tubers were dug on Sept. 24, and sorted and weighed on Oct. 4, the sorting being into the three qualities of marketable, small, and diseased. The heaviest total yield was from the' Red Emperor variety, which gave slightly over 14 tons per acre. Next in order come the Red Fluke, Reading Hero, and Red-skinned Flour Ball, which yielded between 12 and 13 tons each. These are followed by the Vicar of Laleham, yielding nearly 12 tars, and the International and Walker's Regents, giving over 11 tons. The lowest yield of all, not quite three tons per acre, came from a variety which seems not very happily named the Fillb asket. The largest yield of marketable tubers, 11 tons, was given by the Red Emperor, the Vicar of Laleharn, Red-skinned Flour Ball, and Red Fluke following next in order. The smallest marketable yield, four-fifths of a ton, was from the unfortunate Fillbasket, and another variety, which rejoices, not very appropriately, in the name of First and Beet. From experiments made at the Munster Agricultural and Dairy School, Cork, Mr. Andrew Smyth reports that the largest crops (stated below in hundred- weights per acre) were given, viz.:— . 25 tons dung and 4 cwt. bone meal 50 tons dung alone 272 25 tons dung and 2 cart. sulphate of ammonia. 26B} 25 tons dung and 4 cwt. kainit 265 25 tons dung and 2 cwt. nitrate of soda 247 2 tons dung and 2 cwt. kainit 2411 The best results at Cork with artificials alone were :- 4 cwt. kaioit and 2 cwt. nitrate of soda l5l 4 owl. kainft and 2 cwt. sulphate of ammonia l5O 4 cwt. kainit alone 1331 2 cwt. kalnit alone ll7 Of the special manures used singly, kainit gave by far the largest increase ; nitrate of soda, which stands next, gave about half as much increase at four times the cost. THE DYNAMITE EXPERIMENTS AT UNDERLEY.—In refer- ence to our paragraph respecting dynamite experiments on the Underley Hall Estate, given a week ago, we have received from Mr. Punchard, the agent of Earl Bective, the following letter, which will be read with interest. The particulars of the experiments were communicated to us by a correspondent who had visited the wood in which the explosive had been used, and his impression as to the effi- ciency of dynamite was not at all favourable. We are pleased to give the authoritative statement below : Underlay Estates Office, Kirkby Lonsdale, 20th Match, 1884 —To the Editor of the Preston Guarchan.—Blr.—l have to-day read the paragraph In your paper of 15th Inst., relative to the experiments with dynamite at Underley, which states that the exPeriments did not fulfil my expectation. I should be glad if you would correct this statement. I was perfectly satisfiefl with the results (as the enclosed copy of my letter to the fief) from whom I obtained the dynamite will show). The trials were most successful in all cases, except with the butts that had been propped up vertically when the trees were sawn off. These latter, owing to the softness of the wood, did not offer enough resistance to secure the full effects of the explosive. The work was got through much quicker and easier than I anticipated, and is merely dropped for the present because all the ground that was wanted for this present season's planting has been cleared, and the men cannot be spared to go on with the remainder just now.—Yours truly, F. PUNCEARD. [Copy] —Underley Estates Office, Kirkby Luadale, 10th March, 1884.—T0 Messrs. Kitchen and Co.. Agents for Nobel's Dynamite. Gentlemen,—l have much pleasure in reporting the very satisfactory results of mar experiments in the use of Nobsre dynamite for blowing up the butts of trees. For the fixed butts the explosive was most effectual, large butts being blown to pieces and the parts hurled into the air by a charge of about it hs of a lb. There can be no more effectual or expedi- tions manner of doing the work. The butts which had been blown over by the wind and had been let back again on to the solid ground (which formed a resistancato the explosive) were equally effectually dealt with, though they were not blasted into so small pieces as In the case of the fixed ones. The trial with the butts which had been blown over and had been propped up vertically, was not so satisfactory, the timber being soft (spruce, Boots fir, ,to.) and not offering sufficient resistance , to secure the full effects of the explosive. I am, however, more than satisfied with the experiment. and most confess that with the fixed butts the results far exceeded my expectation. One hnndred and six butts were blown up in threads's, with 100Ibs. of dynamite.—Yours truly, F. PuNcaann, Agent for Earl of Bective. sales of pure-bred Shorthorn cattle for the year 1883. As compared with the result of the Shorthorn herd sales in 1882, this statement shows an increase on the mean average of £9 Os. sd. per head of the animals sold, an increase of One in the number of sales, and a decrease of seven in the number of animals sold ; last year's statement showing an average of £34 17s. 7d. on 1,588 animals in 35 sales. The highest price realised in any herd sale of Shorthorns during 1883 was 1,505g5. for a four year old Airdrie Duchess cow, Duchess of Leicester, in a draft sde from the herd of Mr. liolford in Dorsetshire ; and the highest price paid for a bull was 900 gs , which was given by Lord Fitzhardinge for a two year old red bull, Duke of Leicester 3rd, at the same sale, the average of which was £2OO 6s. 7d.-on 38 animals— the highest average of the year. In 1882 the highest price given for any single animal was £766 10s., paid by the Duke of Devonshire for the imported cow Airdrie Duchess 9th, at the sale of the herd of the late Mr. Stone, and the highest average realised of any herd sale was £B3 63. 7d. on a selec- tion from that of Mr. B. St. John Ackers. An analysis of the list of herd gales given above shows that 704 of the animals sold in 17 of the sales averaged under £3O; and that 1,219 of the animals sold in 29 of the sales averaged under the mean average of £43 18s. Taking the single animals which made the highest figures in the sales over 100 gs, it will be found that nine animals averaged nearly £423 each; and takidg the two sales which averaged in their entirety over 100 gs it will be seen that the 172 animals included therein realised £14,743 Is.. out of a total of £69,410 15s. If, therefore, these 172 animals be reckoned separately, as they may very justly be, and if the top figures realised at other sales in which the average exceeded £lOO be also taken separately, without any farther reference to exceptional prices, the result shows in round Sores that 172 animals averaged nearly £B6 each in two sales; that seven animals in other seven sales averaged about £328; and that the re- maining 1,402 animals, or about 90 per cent, of the whole number sold, averaged a little over £37. THE CATTLE DISEASES BILL. —The Times says of this bill, which the House met to read a second time on Tues- day, a purpose that was frustrated by the Irish members "The arguments for and against restrictions upon importa- tion of cattle are tolerably familiar to our readers, and the speeches of Tuesday will not materially alter the conclu- sion at which moderate and practical men have arrived. That conclusion we take to be that cattle disease, like the , infectious diseases that attack ourselves, is a real and serious evil which we are bound to use all reasonable means to abate, but that, on the other hand, it is not to be allowed to fill up the whole field of our vision and derange all the ordi- nary business of life. Sensible men take reasonable care to avoid dietetic and hygienic errors, but when a doctor carries his regulations to each a point that the mere avoidance of death threatens to become the sole occupation of life, they rebel and declare that they prefer to take their chance. If once we get cattle disease on the brain, there is simply no end to the vexatious regulations we shall be compelled to adopt. We might reach total prohibition of all imports whatever before we had excluded every possible source of infection. It is wiser to assume at once that there will always be some foot-and-mouth disease, just as there will always be some smallpox and some scarlet fever, contenting ourselves with catting off all obvious and palpable risks. Sir Lyon Playfair, who treated the whole question with moderation and impartiality, is of opinion that foot-and- mouth disease has been acclimatised, and that we may ex- pect periodic il outbreaks without infection from abroad. Since 1839, he says, there have been ten outbreaks, the average period being four years. Mr. Chaplin engaged on behalf of the farmers that they would submit to any restric- tive measures, however severe, if complete security were given against importation of disease. We do not think they would, and we are certain that the consumers could not afford to alloy them. Farmers may, however, do better by steadily endeavouring to discover whether there is no error in diet or regimen predisposing their cattle to this disease, and in the meantime by assisting the vigorous en- forcement of the existing regulations to effect isolation of infected animals. Their advocates are not well advised in favouring the dead meat trade, since that cats at the very root of stock breeding and stock fattening. Live animals cannot be landed in good condition from a Tong voyage, but they are landed in excellent condition for the fattening pro- cess, which is found to pay the farmer very well. Mr. Barclay stated that his Scotch constituents have found title out, and are very anxious that store cattle should be Im- ported as freely as is compatible with reasonable precau- tions against disease. Cattle from the Canadian and United States North-West brought by certain routes are as free from risk as cattle can possibly be, and they are not at all difficult to convert into prime Scotch beef. The preference given to store beasts from the North-West is stimulating the United States to take vigorous measures for stamping out disease. A bill is now before the Legislature giving ex- , tensive powers and the Senate has passed a resolution appro- priating $50,000 for the work, which will, of course, be car- ried out in concert with the different State authorities. It is surely infinitely better for all parties that the States and Canada should compete in supplying our farmers with sound beasts to fatten on our home pastures than that we should peremptorily exclude everything because disease is raging in Kansas. • The farmers have only to look at the matter coolly, as the more shrewd among them have already done to their great private advantage, in order to see that the bill as originally drawn gives them every reasonable protection, together with valuable facilities for making money, which encouragement of the dead meat trade would take away."

LADY HOLLAND.—Once Lady Holland turned to a poet who was dining at her table, and said, "I hear, Mr. that you are publishing a volume of poems; can't you sup- press it?" And even Moore, who was writing a Life of Sheridan in the happy hope that he was doing full justice to a remarkably good subject, was crushed by her ladyship's placid remark, "This will be but a dull book of your's, this Sheridan, I fear." He must, however, have had one mo- j ment of sweet revenge when Leila Rookh was published, and this lady, who presided over the most literary society in London, made such a mistake as to say, "I don't intend to read your Larry O'Rourke, Moore. I hate Irish things I" It was hard to be restrained by intimacy with the family from making the story public. I believe it never has been made public—it is usually told as if she had only said, "I hate Eastern things," but this is the true version. Holland House is a treasare-house of books, pictures, miniatures, MSS., autographs, and all kinds of memorials of the lute- , resting people associated with the place. It is, however, so , difficult to get an order to see it that most people have either to be content with the glimps, they obtain from the public way on the east side, or to go to the Crystal Palace, if they wish to study some of the details of the facade nearer. It is still a delightful residence, though the park is a mere vestige of its former self, and the new streets, new square, and railway stations, foreseen and dreaded by Macaulay, have already begun to "displace those turrets and gardens which are associated with the courtly magnifi- cence of Rich, with the love's of Ormond, with the counsels of Cromwell, with the death of Addison." The last ten or fifteen years have seen the park dwindle down to a mere shred, and have silenced the gun which nightly warned the neighbourhood thst eleven o'clock had struck. This was a custom said to have been introduced by Lord Holland far the better information of burglars, who might like to know that he kept an armed watchman to patrol the grounds. From the Art Journal for March. SICILIAN SUPERSTITIONS.—Ia•the farmhouse called La Scala, in-the Placa, the farmer found that the rats had eaten all the inside of his cheeses, leaving only the rind. He told one of his labourers of this, saying he mast carry off his cheeses to Bronte. The man, whose clothes had also been gnawed, replied, "Leave it to me; I will see about it." He then sharpened a nail to a point, like a needle, and stuck it in the floor where the rats passed, saving, "May the rat which gnawed my drawers fall on this and kill himself." The farmer and he watched until they saw the rats come and walk past the nail unhurt. At last one rat ran upon it and was killed. From that time no rat came near the place. This man had the power of charming away pain when horses, were suffering from colic. He was refused absolution by the priest after confession, .and not allowed to receive the Sacrament. There was_also a "Monaco di Casa," who lived in Linguaglossa, who had these supernatural powers. She was consulted by those who had been robbed. After listening to their story she thought for a few minutes, and then told them where the stolen goods were to be found. One of the Maniacs men went to her when the driving bets of the engine were stolen, An old robber who died in Bronte, four years ago, at the age of ICA had the same reputation; and a poor, sick, scrofulous boy, bedridden for the last twelve years, is also one of the " white witch" tribe. He knows the name of and cure for all diseases; where sto- len ' _.__

Len things are hidden; where money is to be found buried under stones' and the like; and he has predicted his own death, which is to take place in two years from this d ite.— Sicilian fishermen are very superstitious. Knowing this, a party of thirteen young men, from a village on the coast, went one moonlight night down to the shore where some fishermen were lying half asleep, waiting till it was time to draw in their nets. Going into a cave they undressed them- selves to their shirts and drawers, tied handkerchiefs round their elbows and ankles, and noiselessly approaching the fishermen over the sands, joined hands ins circle and danced round without uttering a sound, separating every now and then to perform a grotesque yes seul. This went on for some time in profound silence. At last one of the fisher. men was roused, and rubbing his eyes, he called out in a voice shaking with fear," Cola! Cola! magari ! i magari!" . .

visible to the naked eye.—Mr. W. J. Ridd described some lunar mists he had observed, which he said seemed to prove the existence of an atmosphere, and something of the char- acter of a watery vapour. Partial obscuration might, how- ever, sometimes be caused by clouds of dust arising from landslips, of which there were many examples, and which were, no doubt, the effect of extreme changes of tempera. perature, such as the moon is subject to.—Captain W. Noble, P.R.A.S., gave an account of the late transit of the fourth satellite of Jupiter. Its shadow on the planet was singularly dark, whilst the satellite itself was not visible. Mr. &pin said that the work of photographing star.charts was proceeding favourably. In some of the pictures there were stars down to the 11th magnitude. Several plates were passed round for examination, including one of a mile cluster near alpha Persei, and another of Preesepe, showing the planet Mars. .The secretary announced that the Rev. S. J. Perry, F.R.S., 6rc., of Stonyhurst Observatory, had promised to deliver an address on the 21st April on " Sun- spots : Their Birth and Changes." The lecture will be illustrated by limelight photographs.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

ONIONS.—For these a piece of ground, the richest in the garden, should be prepared. It a piece was not trenched and manured last autumn, we should select the portion that has been occupied by celery. In the latter case the ground is not only as a rule well manured, but it is sweet and friable. Whether the raised bed or the flat method of sow- ing be selected, the first proceeding should be to level the ground. Autumn-trenched ground will exhibit some irre- gularities, particularly that on which celery has been grown. ' Having secured a general rough level, commence at one end, and dig and fork the whole to a uniform depth. If there is more soil than is desired to preserve the required , level, some can be laid aside, as it may be wanted before the : end is reached; if not, it is easily disposed of by distribut- ing it over the whole. The ground must now be left till ' it is so dry on the surface that it will not adhere to the feet. On heavy land the bed system is. perhaps the most suitable. A 4ft. bed will admit six rows at Bin, distant, allowing the , tame distance on the outer sides. It is of no great comae- ; queues to a couple of inches what the distance may be, because the thickness of the crop can be regulated when the plants are thinned. For instance, if they are Bin. dis- tant, the bulbs may touch each other in the row when fully developed. To mark the outline of the beds, the line should be stretched on each side, and if the ground is trod on the outer side of the line, which should be done by keep- ing the feet close together and moving them alternately a few inches at a time, and then in the opposite direction, this will indicate the.path on each side, which may be one foot wide. The line may then be stretched 6in, from either side, and with the back of a small iron rake mark the rows, which should be used with a slight pinching action so as to form a shallow channel to receive the seed. The beds should have a slight beating with the back of the spade before the drills are made, and every pat must be of equal force, or the surface will be proportionately uneven. To cover the seeds, simply draw the back of the rake across the beds and beat them, if anything, harder than before. To give the beds a finished appearance, the line should again be laid longways, and the sides trimmed even and the paths or alleys raked. When dealing with light or moderately heavy land, we do not hesitate to give it a treading, length- wise and transverse, with the same motion of the feet as previously described. Then rake over and draw the drills. Every eighth row, leave a space of 15in. for the sake of having room to place the basket when weeding and thin- ning the crop. The following are the best sorts for sowing this time of the year :—Brown Globe, one of the most use- ful and best keeping varieties; Bedfordshire Champion, fine shape and an excellent keeper; Nuneham Park, an im rove- ment on the White Spanish. Troughton's Lancashire Prize- taker is similar to this, but grows much larger, and for this reason, as well as its fine shape, it has carried off several prizes. Tits FRONT GARDEN.—The pruning of Standard and Dwarf Roses may be proceeded with now. The cottagers' rose trees, after pruning, look as if they had been gnawed and mangled by some animal. This is owing to the heed- less and reckless manner in which the knife has been applied. When the knife is to be used it should be placed near a bud, and on the top side. If it is used higher or lower there is always so much dead wood, which is an eyesore till cut off, All weakly shoots, and more especially those in the middle, should be cutaway first, and reduced till they are from 4in. to flin, apart on the outside, with two or three occupying the centre. If the whole of the shoots are now shortened within Bin. to 3in, from the base, and in such a manner as to assume a semi-globular form, it will be a fair specimen of the Standard Rose. The bud selected should be on the under side of the shoot, or lateral ones. Those on the top side woull have a tendency to grow upright, and they are those which the inexperienced invariably cut above, con- sequently it is impossible to maintain the symmetry of Standard Rose trees. Dwarfs do not show this 111, treatment so much, because they throw shoots up occasionally from the bane, and even annually where on their own roots. When pruned as bushes they may be left a little longer than the Standards. Excepting newly-planted ones, or those in their second year, we only reduce the length of the shoots one- fourth, and the portion left we peg with wire or wooden hooka within Bin. or Bin. off the ground, and, where we can, quite close. These shoots, if strong, will flower the whole of their length, and serve the purpose of covering a great portion of the ground that would be otherwise bare. Moss Roses are always best when treated in this way ; beyond moving the oil wood and cutting the weak points, no prun- ing is required. THE Wnenow.---The Pelargonium: This popular window plant receives treatment at the hands of the cottager that is Inconsistent with its requirement. From a desire to give it a liberal and generous treatment, with the view of securing a good show of bloom, the plants are frequently potted not many weeks before they come in flower. This, instead of improving the quality and increasing the quantity of their infloresence, has an opposite tendency, and the plants have a superabundance of leaves at the expense of flowers. The Pelargonium, like many other plants, flower best when the pots they are in are packed full of roots. We would, there- fore, advise that they should not be potted after this date, for it: is necessary for them to be in their flowering pots three or four months before the flowering season, which usually continues from May to the end of July. Late potting also iaterferes with the plant's season of rest, which should be in August or September. The plants persist in growing at that season, instead of going to rest, and the wood shrinks and assumes a dirty yellow colour, instead of maintaining its solidity and a brownish hue not unlike the shell of a filbert nut. If the plants are at present inclined to run up, the points of be shoots may be taken out, which will induce them to bravh out and be more floriferous.

The annual literary prize of 25,000 f., instituted by the King of the Belgians, will for 1885 be granted to the author of the best work on the means of popularising the study of geography, and developing it in the different educational establishments. Foreigners may compete equally with Bel- gians. The works of the competitors must be sent to the Minister of the Interior before the Ist of Jarmary, 1885. A BUDDHIST PRIEST AT OXFORD.—The degree of MA., hanoris causti, was conferred upon Bunyio Nanjio, a Japanese student, on Tuesday, in a convocation held at Oxford. he Public Orator gave a sketch of the career of Banyio Nanjio, who, being a Buddhist priest, had come to England to pro- secute the study of the language and manuscripts of his Sacred Books, and had been for some time resident at Ox- ford for this purpose. There he availed himself of the as- sistance and guidance of Professor Max Muller. INTERESTING HISTORICAL DISCOVERY.—In making Some excavations in ground formerly attached to the Manor House at Chelsea, built by Henry VIII. as a residence for his daughter, the Princess Elizabeth, the workmen came upon probably the only portion existing of a historically- known subterranean communication leading northwards from the three great houses—Manor House, Winchester Palace, and Shrewsbury House—in the direction of Ken- sington. The great leaden ducts constructed by Henry VIII. to supply Winchester Palace and the King's New Manor House with water from a conduit built by him in the grounds at Kensington, had already been found, and re- moved as obstacles to building. Remains of the ancieat crucible works for gold refining and the Chelsea china works, both in crose proximity, had also been dug up, but this curious passage Was not known to have any existing re- mains. About 30 teat of it in good preservation and care- fully arched have now been uncovered. THE REHSRKSBLE SUNSETS.—At a recent meeting of the French Academy of Sciences M. Angot drew attention to the fact that in 1831 a series of striking twilights was ob- served extending over a considerable part of the year, and M. Tissander the well-known aeronaut, now points out that during the first days of July in 1831 there was a volcanic eruption in the Sicilian Sea, between the coasts of Sciacea and the islan-I of Patitellaria. A new island (Julia), which subsequently disappeared, rose from the bosom of the sea together with an upshot of ashes and cinders. M. Constant Prevost was sent by the Academy of Sciences to study the new formation. Prince Pignatelli assured him that during the early days of the eruption, the 10th and 11th of July, a 86ry column arose from the crater "like a bouquet of arti- ficial fire." At the beginning of Augustan immense column of dust rose and emitted a bright light. On the sth of August "an impalpable dust carried by the winds fell in abundance." The eruption lasted several months, and the coloured sunsets of 1831 began ab mt the beginning of August, goon after the commencement of the volcanic effects. The peculiar twilights were remarked at Odessa, Rome, Madrid, and in Germany—that is to say, over a considerable

area. WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIA- . TION. FREE TRADE V. FAIR TRADE. Last evening Mr. Joseph Howes, of the National Reform Union, delivered a lecture under tbe auspices of the above association, at the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, on the subject—" Free Trade v. Fair Trade; Jr the Fallacies of Protection exposed," which was intended as a reply to a speech delivered some time age, at Warrington, by Mr. Ecroyd, M.P. There was a crowded audience, and great enthusiasm was manifested, the remarks of the lecturer being loudly applauded. Councillor Frederick Monks, J.P., presided, and was supported by Councillors W. Pierpoint, F. Dixon, and J. Brown, and Messrs. F. A. Roberts, J. Winser, E. J. Guest, W.Burn, H. Whitharn, J. Bonnet], T. Birchall, H. Roberts (sec), rice Jtc. The CHAIRMAN said that the subjeot of the evening's lecture Was one which he thought would prove exceedingly interesting. Some of them were old enough to remember the time when labour was much worse paid for than it was at the present day, and when there was a great deal less of it, and who were old enough to remember the agitation that took place for the abolition of the Corn Laws and the freedom of trade. He thought that they were now inclined to take too much for granted in this way—that the younger men who Were growing up, and who knew nothing whatever of the hard times that were then in existence, accepted as gospel truth the staternetes of their forefathers, and he was glad that this question had been taken up in a yerykernest man- ner, and that it Was now about to be discussed so that ' every intelligent man in the room would have a betta grasp and appreciation of the real questiou at issue. He was very much inclined to think that they dwelt too much upon the manufacturing industries of ...the country, to the ex- clusion and neglect of the agricultural interest. He was one of those who believed that a great bulk of the wealth of every country came out of the land—(hear, hear)—and that no country could afford to neglect its agriculture, or could permanently maintain a state of prosperity, where the land laws were antagonistic to the free development of the land, and therefore, he thought, that the time was coming when they would have to look the question fairly and fully in the face as t how far the restrictions of the land were really and truly the cause of the depression of which they felt co much. He thought that they shoold impress upon the constituencies that the largest industry of ithis country was the agricultural industry, and they might 'depend upon it that so long as the agricultu- ral industry was in a depressed and impoverished condition, they would not have such a state of prosperity as many of them would like to see on this question of the land; he believed Mr. Cobden once made the remark that "great as was the benefit which had arisen to this country from the freedom of trade, greater would be the benefits to this country that would arise by the freedom of restrictions on land." He (the chairman) thought that there was a great truth in that, but what they had to deal more particularly with that night was what he called the fallacy of Fair Trade which was put forth by their Con- servative friends with a view to getting votes at the next election. There was just one thing that he wished to refer to, and that Was that the Conservative party had %Rhea° posed as the patriotic piety. He thought that they would all be agreed that in regard to the Conservative party being the patriotic party that that was all sheer nonsense, and that they were the non-patrietic party. He thought that the way in which the Opposition had conducted itself in the Home of Commens was a disgrace te any party—(applause) —teed they might depend upon it that it was doing more injury to the interests of the House of Commons and the true welfare of the country than they, or most people, would imagine. If they allowed the House of Commons to drift into a state of anarchy, and allowed the Govern- ment to be baited as the present Cievernimant bad been they might depend upon it that the best men of the country would not give their services. It was not unlikely that with that sort of incompetence they would then see the management of the country drift into the hands of what the Americans called "carpet baggers," and he was satisfied that when the true patriotic spirit had fled—the spirit in which the interests of the country were held above those of party—as soon as that spirit had fled from the House of Commons, the decay of the institution of which they were so proud would have begun, And that would .be a bad day for the country. He then latroductad the lecturer Mr. HOWES, who was warmly received, said that it would seem singular that it should be necessary in the latter part of the 19th century to discuss the advisability of Free Trade for England. If there was one point in the Liberal pro- gramme stronger than another on this question, and if there was anyone question which Englishmen generally con- sidered had been decided and disposed of, it was the question that they were asked by their opponents to once more re- fute. As they were always willing to satisfy their op- ponents whenever they could, they had no objection to once more :dating their very strong arguments as against the extremely weak position their opponents took up. He recognised that the Tories were in a fix, and had been ever since the last general election. That election was a severe blow to them, and they might naturally expect that they would try every point in the compass to endeavour to make a resting-place if they possibly could, so that they would not be again so ignominiously defeated at the next general election. After the last general election the Tories had to rally themselves, and shortly after their appointment of Lord Salisbury as chief, they made two very startling dis- coveries. Their Tory friends were good at diicoveries. They frequently made them, but they did not seem to bring very much profit or reward. The Tories discovered that trade was bad I The Liberals had discovered that sometime before the last general election, but the Tories would never allow that there Was anything like bad trade until they dis- covered it after the election. Then they discovered, or pre- tended to, that they had found out the Cause of bad trade, and that it Was to be found in the wicked conduct of the wicked foreigner, who kept putting wicked tariffs on the goods that were sent to him. There was a peculiarity about this discovery. From 1868 to 1874 this country enjoyed an amount of prosperity that it had never known before or since. (Applause.) Trade extended and prosperity in- creased by leaps and bounds. From 1874 to 1880 a dif- ferent state of things existed. Things began to wane. They get bad in 1877, they were dreadfully worse in 1878 and 1879, and people were on the brink of starvation every- where in 1880. From 1868 to 1874 they had a Liberal Governmept, during the time that all the prosperity existed, and from 1874 to 1880 they had a Tory Government, during the time that all the misery existed. Their opponents said that that was not the fault of the Tory Government. Well perhaps not, it was only a singu- lar coincidence that always, occurred in the same way. (Laughter.) He wanted to direct their attention to the bearing of these facts upon the second discovery that bad trade had been caused by foreign tariffs. From 1868 to 1874, when trade was bad, and from 1874 to 1880, when it was good, they had precisely the same tariffs, which simply meant, if anything, that under the Liberal Government foreign tariffs produced good trade, and under the Tory Government bad trade: On these discoveries being made the next step was to form an organisation in London with a view to educating the coun- try upon the lines of the discoveries they had made, and telling to the people of England that all the misery, bad trade, and poverty had resulted from the imposition of tariffs. There was a time when Tories fought for protection, and now they wished to go back to the good old time; but they were ashamed of their old motto,-and now they dare not let it get out that they were in favour of protection. So their old friend protection teed been dug up again, dressed inlresh clothes, labelled "Fair Trade,' and sent tottering through the ceuntry. (Laughter.) But the workingmen recognised him the moment they saw him—(increased laughter)—so that the organisation which was brought into existence with a great flourish had almost died out. They were told that England had been importing more goods than were exported, buying more goods than were sold from the country, and that the natural reset of that would be bank- ruptcy, the same as would befall a shopkeeper who carried on business en the same lines. But it did not, he said, always follow that when a man got more than he purchased he must go to ruin. (Laughter.) There was one great fallacy underlying the whole thing—a fallacy that their opponents must have seen, though perhaps theyedid not think it worth while to notice it to the public. This was the fallacy. If their (the Tories) argument was good at all, or to make it any worth, they would have to carry on aW their trading op rations on the ready mosey system. They would have to part with their money for every article purchased from the foreigner. Say they commenced trading operations on those principles in January and went on until December, paying ready money for everything. All the coins they had in circulation would only last them three months, and then they would have to set to work to melt up their trinkets, which would last them a little over one month longer. Before six months was over they would have pitted with all the coins, gold and silver and metal, and they would then have to stop doing aey trade at all. Still they went on trading, and did not part with their coins and metals. How was that ? Trade was carried on by a system of exchange, and owing to the fact that England had the maritime supremacy ef the world, they took tollage or freightage on the transactions carried on. He would give there the facts of the exports and ifn- ports. Certainly, if they had been buying more than they sold, and if that would lead them to bankruptcy,lhey would have been there long ago, From 1876 to 1880 the imports exceeded the exports to the extent of £622,000000. They got £822.000,000 worth of goods more than they had parted with during that period. But there was something else to consider. They had been importing and exporting bullion during the same time, and their imports had exceeded their exports in this respect also. They had imported £147 000,000 worth of bullion and exported 144,000,000, so that they had £3,000,000 more than they exported. Instead of parting with their money to get the goads, they had got the goods and the money too. (Applause.) That was going to bankruptcy ! (Laughter.) If so, they had better keep on going to bankruptcy. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Gladstone, speaking at Leeds, advised the Fair Trade or Tory party, when speaking upon this ques- tion, to talk generallv, because when men dealt with generali- ties it was impossible to refute them, but if they unfortuna- tely went into detail, that moment they would be wrecked, because then it Was known at once what they meant. The Fair trade pirty had taken this advice, and always dealt with generalities. He had a paper containing a report of an extraordinary speeeh delivered in Warrington by Mr. Ec- royd. That epeech was generalities from beginning to end, and there was iret one single detail that could be laid hold of. Mr. Fcroyd spoke of the wicked foreigner, but did not say whom he referred to ; sugeested that England should put on tariffs, but did not say what tariffs or to what amount. So long as the Tories just spoke of wicked foreigners, tariffs, mid Fair Trade, they Were perfectly safe,

div.head: BELT V. LAWES.
div.p: BELT V. LAWES.

The following has been issued for publication :—" To R. Belt, E:q ,6, Williamastreet, Lowndes Square. Yourself v. Lewes. Dear sir,—We have instructed the sheriff to issue execution for the damages, £5,000, upon the goods of Mr. C. B. Lawes, at his private residence, No. 16, Michael's Grove, Brompton, and at his studio in Chelsea Bridge-road, and we believe he is now in possession at bith places. Mr. Lewis called and saw us this morning, and made one offer which he says is "absolutely final," and will not be re- newed at any time. It is as follows: To pay a sum of £5,000 within 48 hours to settle this action and Rankin's action and all costs connected therewith. If this offer is declined Mr. Lewis has instructions to file Mr. Lawes's pe- tition in bankruptcy on Monday, and proceed with the ap- peal to the House of Lords. Mr. Lewis requested we would inform you of the fact that Mr. C. B. Lewes will not be en- titled to any property whatever on his father's death, and that if the present offer be refused Sir John Lewes will not leave him a shilling. Please let us have your answer per- , sonally or by letter not later that 10 o'clock on Monday, morning.—We remain, dear sir, yours faithfully, C. 0. 1 HUMPHREYS and Sons, Giltspur Chambers, Ho!. born Viadnct, London, 8.C., March 22, 18S4" "To Messrs. C. 0. Humphreys and Sons.—Dear sir,—l have to acknowledge your communication of the 32nd inst. I have given the proposal made to you by Mr. Lewis, as ex- plained in your letter, my most careful consideration. I should much regret that either yourself or the couasel whose Invaluable aid I fully recognise were to lose one shilling by me; but there are other considerations of an equally im- portant character which I cannot neglect or overlook. The sum offered is little more than sufficient to cover the balance of the expenses are recently represented to me by you as having been incurred on my behalf; little, if any, surplus would then remain for those generous friends who have assisted me, and without whom my professional and social career would have been completely destroyed; My own means are wholly exhausted, and I can only look forward to repay by the future earnings of my profes- sion the large sums that have been lent to me, and by which I have been enabled to clear my name from the foul calumnies which have been cast upon me. I feel that it would be a great iojnstice and a poor return for the kindness that has been shown to me to permit one sec- tion of my friends to have their claims satisfied at the ex- pense and to the exclusion of the other, and I therefore deliberately decide to absolutely refuse Mr. Lewis's pro- posal. If my creditors elect to force me into bankruptcy, it will only be one more knot in the lash of persecution to which I have been subjected. But, be it as it may', the first business of my life will be to repay at the earliest p os Bible moment every shilling which I owe to those friends who have so nobly sustained me. As I have your permis- sion to make public Mr. Lewis's proposal, I shall publish your letter and iny reply.—Yours faithfully, itICHARD BELT.—March 23, 1884." Mr. Lawes, the defendant in the case of Belt v. Lawes, who stands cast in damages to the amount of £5,000, has filed a petition in bankruptcy, and the costs of the case thus far amount to £26,000.

An old Indian relates that he once asked the station- master at Delhi whether the twelve o'clock train from Cal- cutta was in. " Which ?" was his reply, "to-days or yea- terdav's ? They are both due but yesterday's isnt" in yet.' " Pcrsca" ON THE MERCHANT SHIPPING BlLL.—Punclt says—" ' Vested Interests' stigmatise Mr. Chamberlain's Shipping Bill as 'reckless.' "No, but I have attended three balls already." "Why, how delight- ful, weally. Where were they at?" "At the pawn- broker's," sadly sighed Mr. Panier. POINTER JOCl{."—The only poem I every got paid for was a humorous one, which I had the pleasure to see the other day in an American collection of "anonymous and dead authors." It was written upon a great friend of my boyhood, a pointer called Jock:— A qessor lecturing on "English indwariee " aclass - . .

but the moment they went into detail the Liberals could get the returns of the exports and imports and refute their arguments. He hoped that that evening their opponentS would show them what they meant, so that they could see if there was a shred of argument that could be put forward in favour of the suggested theory of Fair Trade. Their opponents claimed to be Free Traders. A change had come over the scene. The Tory party that were once in favour of protection de- clared that they were free traders, but said that they wanted to see free trade universal and fair. So did the Liberate. But how did they propose to do it? The Tories said "Why, you see foreigners putting tariffs on goods we want to send, we must put tariffs on goods they want to send." What did that mean? As a principle free trade must either be good or bed. The Tories said it was good. Then let them get as much of it as they possibly could. Why did Tories' want to put on tariffs. They said that it was to make the wicked foreigner go in for free trade. Their friends said, Let us punish the foreigner." He said "Tee, by all means, but do not punish yourselves." Could they do the one without the other. The foreigner manufactured goods which he wanted to send to England, and which people in England wanted to purchase. Weat did they pt pose to do? Put a tariff on? Then the English peoPle bought them dear instead of cheap. Applause.) Sir Stafford Northcote, in referring to this question, said that "be had never stood up in favour of protection. It was true that there were men in the Conservative party who, with great energy and ability and considerable courage, had argued the question from a protective point of view. Bo did not share their opinions, but he did say this, that they would probably know the difference between an article of faith and a pious opinion. He was not aware that anyone had put forward this doctrine except as a pious opinion." They did not put their faith in it as a principle, but merely enunciated it as a pious opinion. Sir Stafford Northcots said that it was a pious opinion, but he did not share it. it was pious he ought to share it. (Laughter.) Bat who was the man who put this doctrine forth strongly at that time? It was James Lowther, and fancy Janos Lowther having pious opinions. (Applause and laughter.) Be might be ahle to give some informetion as to what was So win the next Derby, and then fancy the position of the Tory leader, leaving James Lowther to run away with all the piety and leave none for the leader& The Tory party recognised that a return to protection was impossible, for so firmly convinced were the great body of the people of the country that it would bring nothing but misery and death that they would not allow a Government to exist three months which dared to return to protection. He then re- ferred to the condition of the country when under protete tion, when the people broke out into revolution and proces- sinned the streets, bearing banners on which the worde " Bread Cr blood " were inscribed. The Tories would have them go back by degrees and protect some particular trade, but why so ? for if protection waagood for one it was good for the others. The Liberals proposed that the navigation laws should be repealed, but the Tories said that would destroy England's maritime supremacy, at a time when she had got no such supremacy. Before the navigation JaWilt were repealed the Americans had four-fiftht of the carrying trade between England and tnat country, and now America had one-fifth and England four-fifths. ( Applause.) Eng' land had now 52 per cent. of all the carrying trade of the world, more than all the other nations put together. Ia 1879, which was reckoned the worst and most demand, the population of England was 35,000,600, and the trade represented 612 000,000 of money. CI( rmany, with all i's advantages of tariffs, and with a pormia- time of 40 000,000, only had a trade to the extent of £371,000,000 that year. The United States, with a MA' lation of 50,000,000, only had a trade of £239,00000' France, with a population of 36 000,000, only had a trade of £313,000,000; and Russia, with apopwatioti a 80,000,060 s only had £183,00000@. So that in England's worst year her trade, without tariffs, rated according to population, far excelled the other great nations. Proceeding, the lecturer referred to the large expenditure involved in connection with the customs, which, he said, instead of preventing smuggling looked very much like smuggling. What was it all for? Pat on a few more tariffs, create a few more Go• vernment establishments, and make more offices for the younger eons of the aristocracy; but if England became wise ehe would make the landowners keep their own chijde ran. (Applause.) The fair traders thought fleet they had got a foothold in Warrington. They said that the trade 4 was suffering owing to their particular manufactured goedo being sent from a foreign country, and that the wiredrawer' of Warrington suffered because Germany cent wire to our colonies cheaper than they could. That was the fact, but beef would the Tories propose to remedy it? By putting a . tariff on the wire that Germany sent, so that the people in the colonies might no longer bay more cheap wire.• Thus the colonies would have to pay all the extra cost that the tariff entailed, for the producers would not work fdr nothing. They 11A a great deal of evidence to eliew the! tariff had nothing at all to do with the chewable& ee gentleman well known in the locality of Warrington gave evidence in London a short time ago, and he pointed out conclusively that the present state of things was caused not • my the tariff, but by the great difference in the prices of W., riage in Germany arid England. Whet they would have to pay here for carriage was about 17s 6.1 per ton, and in Ger- many it was 8s per ton, so th et there was a difference of get in carriage alone. How could they deal with that ? By. co napelliug the German railway authorities to pay more? Could they do that? Timers was another way, by compelling the English railway authorities to bring down their demand. Could they do that? It was simply to be considered as a question of carriage and not of tariff. He then adduced figures to demonstrate that England sent more manufactured goods to foreign countries than she received from them, and urged that tariffs would restrict the trade of the country, and thus reduce the position of the working classes to one of misery and destitution. Be also urged that the land should be opened out for cultivation, 30 that the country could supply products that had now to be imported. The purchasing power of the country required increasing. If they put their surplus labour on the land and created a home trade, they would hear nothing of tariffs; but if they had the tariffs reeeter. mended by the Tories they would have more customhouses, and more situations and pensions c the younger sons of the aristocracy. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN drew attention to the enormous develop- ment of the trade between England and India that bad occurred since India became a free trade country. Ho then moved a vote of thanks to the Lecturer, which was passed. Mr. Samuel Bowly, the veteran anti-slavery advocate and temperance reformer, died at Gloucester on Sunday night from heart disease. Mr. Bowly had reached his eighty- secmd year. The Birmingham Daily Post understands that the total amount of the £lO mortgages issued by the Corporation as a means of investment for the savings of artisans and others, has now reached £25,000; a great success in so short a time, as the issue was not commenced until the beginning of this year.

THE GOVERNMENT AND THE IMPORTATION OF FOREIGN CATTLE.—On Mond Ay a very numerous representative de- putation, beaded by Mr. W. E. Forster, waited upon Lord Carlingford and Mr. Dodsoit to urge the consumers' view with reference to the bill now before P..rliament in connection with the importation of live cattle from countries where disease is said to exist. The corporations of twenty- three of the largest cities and towns were directly repre- sented, together with the members of trades councils, boards of guardians, chambers of commerce, local boards, and other elective bodies familiar with popular sen- timents and desires. Mr. Forster said those present were anxious in the interest of consumers that the bill should not be allowed to pass in its present eh ipe. Phey were prepared, as a temporary meesure, to submit to the restric- tions originally proposed by the Government, but they cold not assent to those since added by the House of Lords. The Mayor of Salford (Alderman Makirrson r referred to the enormous truffle in live animals carried on in their market, and said he apprehended the migration of all that business, with a consequent "jump-up" in prices, to Lon- don and other places if the bill passed as at prestnt drafted. —Mr. Mark Price, the Mayor of . le, ds, and Mr. Arnold, M.P., also urged the necessity of restoring the measure to its original shape.—Lord Carlingfold, in reply, said the Go- vernment recognised the gravity of this question. He held the deputation qurte justified in their present proceedings or in any other course for the purpose of securing the defeat of the Lords' amendments. The deputation bad spoken in moderate terms, and if equal consideiatiun were shown by those representing the agricultural interest, he if,w no reason for conflict between consumers and home producers. in cases where reasonable apprehension of danger existed, the Government were prepared to stop importation, and that they were empowered to do by the old Act of Parliament. Holding that view, they looked upon the proposed restric- tions as unnecessary and mischievoas, and intended to re- store the Bill to its original form. They wOuld he no party to an uncalled-for exclusion of the food of ths people in a case where they were convinced that agricultural interests did not require greater restrictions than the Government had already proposed to the Legislature.—His lordship was awarded a cordial vote of thanke, Mr. Forster undertaking on the part of those bodies represented that the Govcirnmenr should he strongly supported in the 'coarse indicated by Lord Ctrlingtord.

The action brought by Mrs. Weldon against the London aaity Chronicle, for an alleged libel, was brought to a con- clusion, on Monday, by a verdict for the defendant. Mt. Charles Robert Newman, brother of Cardinal New- Wan, died at Tenhy on Saturday evening aged eighty-two. Mr. Newman hart lived in Tenby for more than thirty Years. In the Court of Qiieen's Bench, on Tuesday, judgment was given in favour of the Corporation of Oyer Damen in their dispute with the county authorities as to the liability Sr the maintenance of certain main roada passing through the borough. At Ipswich, on Monday, a coroner's jury -returned a ver- dict of wilful murder against Elizabeth Turner, 61 years •14, for drowning her grandchild, aged five months, by lin- Wiersing it in a pail of water, on Sunday morning, while the ' Parents were at church. The prisoner, who afterwards gave herself up to the police, was some years ago confined in a lunatic asylum. It was decided, on Monday, at a meeting of manufac- turers, merchants, woolstaolers, and others oonnected with the staple trade of Rochthile, to take the initiatory steps Or erecting a commodious Exchange in that town. A large amount ef business in Rochdale appears at presi.nt to be transacted chiefly in the open street, and sonia incon- venience is stated to result from this practice. Boosey, the publishers. The book in- cluded over 100 songs which are usually sold at 2s..each ; but Townsend, who bad purchased a number of copies in America, was retailing the complete volumes at 4s. 6d. OPERATIONS IN THE SO UDA :COMPLSTION OF Acrire Opsamo:qx—lutorin.i.,A ha. been rteeived in London that General Graham LAS tele- graphed to Sir E. Baring that he considers his active opera- tions are now complete. He says :--!‘ I can at once dis- pense with the services of regiments from India." A London correspondent says :—Tne inttlligence from the Soudan shows that the campaign on the Red Sea littoral is at an end. It bas been a brilliant one, for though our enemies were uncivilised, they fought with great bravery and steadiness, and OR more than one occasion had the advantage of vastly superior numbers. They had to contend; however, with a foe at least equally brave, and furnished, moreover, with the latest appliances of scientific warfare. Hence it is no great matter for surprise if they now see the futility of matching themselves in pitched battle against British troops, and if Oman finds his promises of magical defences of no avail to check the head- long flight of his followers. His forces have now been effectually dispersed. They no longer threaten Snakim, and the original object of the expedition having been there- fore attained, the British ' forces will now probably return at once, with the exception, perhaps, of small contingents left to garrison Saakim and Massowah. In official circles the news has been received with great satisfaction. The work of dispersing Osman Digna and his adherents has been thoroughly done without any further bloodshed. Moreover, the close of the campaign is con- sidered especially opportune, since in the climate of the Soudan military operations dating the next few months would be almost an impossibility. Our troops had, indeed, already begun •to suffer severely from the intense heat and drought, and a prolongation of the campaign would cer- tainly have entailed much aickness, if not death, among. soldiers exposed in marching order to a tropical sou The Queen received the news at Windsor Castle in the afternoon, and was deeply gratified. Her Majesty immedi- ately telegraphed to General Graham, congratulating him on his victory. The Cabinet Ministers in London were in- formedof the dispersal of Osanan's force through the medium of the Central News agency, whose special correspondent was the first to send news of the advance of the British troops, as well as the result of their move- ments. Mr. Gladstone was also notified of the fact at his temporary residence at Coombe. It is believed among military authorities that General Gra- ham's victory will relieve the - lure upon Gordon Pasha. • -

' The One Free Press of Vienna intimates that Russia intends to propose the abrogation of the last fragment of the Treaty of Paris—namely, the convention by which the neutrality el the Dardanelles and the Bosphorus WAS secured. ..Tie Austrian j mrualist believes that the arrange- ment was proposed to Prince Bismarck at Friedrichsruhe by M. de Giers. It could not be carried out except at a con- vention of the Powers

A LONG RESPITH.—A telegram from Wilmingham, Dela- ware, in a New York paper, says :—" The Governor hm reepited Louis F. List until the second Friday of Merck,. 1940. The culprit was to have been banged next Frid ry for the murder of George B. Taylor. in Septa nber, 1883. It was generally conceded that his offence was no mo a than one of murder in the second degree, and as the Governor had no power to commute the sentence, he has granted the respite of over 50 years, this amounting in fact to imprison- ment for life." .

, The Vienna police have just detected, in time to prevent them, two fresh plots to murder. In one instance a woman, the wife of a locksmith, offered a bribe to a female friend if she "'mild assist her in poisoning her husband. She was be. trayed t.y her friend and immediately taken into custody. The other case was that of a would.be matricide— t man who, with an accomplice, hal pl tuned the murder of his own mother, an old woman of seventy-three, with whom he had always lived on good terms, in order to rob her of her small property. The police got wind of the scheme, happily, in time to frustrate its execution. Tun DYNAMITE PARTY IN Amenrce.—The New Fork Herald is reported to be alone among the Press of that city in demanding that if the existing laws are not etrong enough to put down the dynamite party "the Legislature should come to the rescue of public decency." The Herald offers very cold comfort to the Fenians and their sympathisers who are reported to be gathering on the frontiers of the Dominion with a view to invade Manitoba "at a fitting moment." It seems that a meeting was recently held in Fargo, Dakota territory, at which reports were received from a number of " leagues " as to the feasibility of invading Manitoba. Stores of arms, it was said, had been collected, and the Fenians were merely waiting for the re- ports of the delegates who had been sent into Manitoba. Moral and material aid would also be forthcoming from the cities in the Eastern States, " when there should be a call from over the line." The Herald has the following °beer. rations on the proepects of the "party of action :"—" It is to be hoped that the blizzard-cursed inhabitants of Mani. teb t will not have a Fenian invasion added to their climatic woes, but if the malignant refuse of the Irish people must overflow somewhere, there is no other conve• nient locality in which they could be more easily and effectively got rid of. The farmers of Manitoba have worked hard for whatever they own, so they are quite com— petent to transform into corpses any gang of marauders, with no matter what political pretext, that maydescend upon them on robbery and murder intent. Should the ruffians who are said to be gathering in Dakota succeed in crossing the border they may not at first experience armed resistance, but all the same they will die miserably, for ramsloops are scarce in Manitoba and corner loafers freeze to death."
