GOVERNMENT POLICY lee TIM SOIIDAN.— rho Marquis of HA/W[191770N stated that in regard to the policy of the Go. vernment in the Soudan there was a strong desire to com- municate it fully to the House as soon as they were in a positron to do so, but until they had further information as to the cause end extent of the telegraph interruption be- tween Cairo-and Khartoum it woukl not be possible to say wheu the Government would be able to make a further statement on the subject. He hoped they should be able to do so some time before the Easter holidays. Whether that statement would be a complete one wuaa question which it was not in his power to answer. Almost al; the information received by the Government from Gvneral Gordon had appeared in- the -newspapers, and was down. to the 13th inst.

MERSEY DOCES.—The Mersey Docks and Harbour Board Bill was oonsidered and ordered for third reeding. THE FILiNCHISE BILL—The Marquis of' Hierenergvoie formally moved the seamed reading of the Franchise Bill. —Lord JOHN Matitenne moved as an amendment that the House declined to proetied further with a measure having for its object the addition of two million voters teethe elec- toral body until it had before it the entire scheme contem- plated by the Government for the amendment of the repre- sentation of the people. The noble Lord described the bill as more complicated and far-reaching than anv mentors of Parliamentary reforrnwhish had ever been submitted to Parliament, and said it was in the vastness of the chac-ges now proposed that he saw the real reason why the GOVen. ment were deermined to conceal their policy with respect to redistribution.—Mr. lorne Bateinv, who Was received with loud cheers, said he believed the bill to be a great bill drawn with statesman-like sagacity and %Mom ani throughout the country doting the last few months there had been a more unanimous expression of opinion in favour of the ex- tension of the franchise to householders in counties than we had had on any political question for many years. It would, bring about a general content and sympathy between the duff-rent portions of the constituent body. Referring to Ireland the right hen. gentleman said the objectors to the bill were those who wished to proceed in the management of leeland entirely upon the old lines. He aeked if there was anything in the political history of this country that was so painful and shameful a failure as the government of Ireland? Where they, then, to go on the old lines, or were I they to try some new line? He was for a new line. They could rule the Irish, as they had done for centuries, as a conquered people, or they could rule them as a portion of a great and free nation. If the old lines were to be worked on, and if Ireland was by no means to be tranquilised and united to this country, he could only wish that she could be unmoored from her fastenings in the deep and moved three thousand tniles to the west. Would it not be better to treat Ireland with full justice in regard to the question of repre- sentation? What was desired in the bill with regard' to Ireland was, to purchase tranquility by no special sacrifice from England, but by means that would win the people from disloyalty, conspiracy, mad rebellion to a happy union with that free nation in whose name and by whose authority they were met in that House. There were two paths open, one union by force and on the old lines, and the other union with justice, and he believed that the latter would, at no remote period bring abmt prosperity and peace. The debate was continued by Colonel Dawnay, Mr. Northcote, Hr. Bax•er, Mr. C. Ross Mr. Leetham Mr. J. Collings, and Mr. J. Lowther. The latter observed that the Prime Minister had described the classes as "capable citizens" which the right hon. gentle- man the member far Birmingham had described as 'the residuum."—Mr. BRIGHT: Never. (Liberal cheers.)—Mr. Lowman: I can quote the words. (Seizing a volume on the table.)—Mr. Goner: Ills not in Hansard. (Laughter.) —Mr. LOWTHER : Well,! heard the speech. (Laughter and Opposition cheers.)—Mr. BRIGHT: I argued that there was a residuum in every class, and that in the poorest class there are people ignorant and abject, to whom it would be no good to give a vote, and whose vote would be no good to the State. But I never applied the word to the working classes. (Liberal cheers.) I said there was a residuum in every class. I have known a residuum in this House. (Loud laughter and cheers.)—The Marquis of HARTINOTON said the two grounds upon which the measure was objected to were its incompleteness and its extension to Ireland, un- acoompanied by any measure of redietributi m. He ad- mitted that the completion of our representative system was one great subject of which the franchise was only a part, and that Parliamentary reform would not be complete until measures bad been passed which dealt not only with the franchise but also with the redistribution of electoral power, in the first place as regarded the three kingdoms, and in the next ' place as regarded the various areas included in them. But there was only one way in which all the branches of that great question could be dealt with in one session, and that was some admiseion on the part of the Reuse generally that the time had come for the extension of the borough fran- chise to the counties, and an equally general adinieeion that the great and glaring anomalies existing in the distribution of political power should be redressed. But there was no indication on the part of the Opposition of a tendency to any such general agreement If that Bill passed they would have to face the question of redistribution next year. The Government considered it impossible to carry through one session a complete measure, and it was their duty not to sacrifice that which they thou4ht an essential object in , the vain endeavour to do that which might itself be desir- able but which Was not possible. He had no desire to see introduced into our electoral arrangements either mathema- tical exactness or any attempt at perfection, but there were ! certain anomalies that ought to be removed. Undue im- portance was attached to a possible reduction in the number of representatives for Ireland. The exclusion of Ireland from the measure would perpetuate and in.ensifv almost the only real grievance to which Irish members ceuld now point—the irregularity of political rights as between the three kingdorne.—The debate was adjourned, on the motion of Mr. Repots. AFFAIRS IN THE SOCDAN.—The Marquis of HatcrukrroN informed Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett that General Gordon had, as was stated in the papers defeated a body of Arabs who were besieging Halfiveh. While ready too answer questions on matters of fact and prepared to give information received from General Gordon, reasons political and military required him to withold any declaration of Government intentions On the order of the day for the third reading of the Con- solidated Fund Bill, Lord R CHURCHILL moved that it was inexpedient to assent to the third reading of this bill before receiving further information as to the military operations in the Eastern Soudan, the position of General Gordon at Khartoum, and the policy of the Government in Egypt proper. The noble Lord contended that in view of the re- cent action of the Brinish troops and the present position of affairs in the Soudan the House had a right to persist in its demand for full ieformation as to the intentions and objects sf the Government. The whole country was asking what the Government were going to do to relieve General Gordon. The Government had taken the surest and most certain coarse to bring about the failure of General Gordon's mis- sion. He wished to know which of the two policies the Government meant to adopt—rescue or retirement—end whether anything had been done to deal with the embarass- rnents of Egypt, on which the whole question turned. His object was to stimulate public attention. Ile knew the present Government had the greatest contempt for the House of Commons, but there was a power which Lad some influence with the Governmvnt. and that was the power of public opinion —Lord E. FITZHAURICR said the whole ob- ject of the noble lord's speech seemed to be to make it known that he belonged to no party and'was superior to all parties, and the business of the Hones bad been interfered with in order that the country should listen to that ,ieclara- lion. It was evident that public attention out of doors was being directed to the proceedings of the neble lord and his ' friends ia interfering with the business of the Government, and the indignation of the country was being excited. He had to state in answer to the inquiry about the reported movement of General Grahams troops that it was thought desirable that the General should disperse the small force that had again gathered around Osman Digma, and that operation would have a very important re- sult, for it was believed that when that force' had been dis- persed there would be no great difficulty in opening up the road between Suakin' and Berber by means of the friendly Sheiks and tribes, and that would have an important effect en the position of !netters at Khartoum.—Mr. Cowart said he was at first disposed to condemn the speech of Lord R. TITH CUSTODY OF IIYFANTS.-ofl the motion for the secon I reading of the Infants Bill, Mr.. BRIEF pointed oat that the existing law was oppressive and unjust to mothers, and contend,d that since wives were not allowed their eqial rights of property with hush Inds, they ought to hive equal ;rights In tbe custody of their children. Ther bi I I proposed to negative the old presumption of the courts of law that the control of the children wee absdintely with the father, and would give the courts discretion, having regard to the interests of the children and the rights of the parents as tieing equal to one auother.—Mr. limn moved the rejection of the.hill, as it would bring into every hourehold where disputes existed between father and mother an endless I cause of quarred—The Loan lADVOCATE, on behalf of the Government, assented to the second reading, not because it was a complete measure, but because it would afford an opportunity of dealing with the defects of the present law.— After considerable discussion the second reading was car- ried by 208 to 73. LEASEHOLDRRS ENFIVOIC HIS RH ENT.—Lgrd R. CHUR- CHILL withdrew his Leaseholders Enfranchisement Bill, and leave was given to Mr.. Dodds to bring in a bill to 'amend the law relating to the rating of waterworks under- takings belonging. to local authorities.

div.head: IRELANP.
div.p: IRELANP.

The Dublin polineoicting on information, last evening made a seizure of two rill s and a box of ammunition at the works of the Dublin and Kingstown Railway, Grand Canal- street. One man was arrested. The results of the poor law elections show that the Nationalists have in many places been badly beaten. In Ballinglass all the successful candidates are loyalists, and in Parsonstown and Tullamere also the Nationalists have not even a seat, though great efforts have been made through- out the country to oust all those guardians whe are not fol- lowers of Mr. Parnell.

A Canon of the Roman Catholic Church is the first per- of any note to adopt Mr. Parnell's advice to the Irish people not to pay the "blood tax." The Hey. Canon O'Donnell, parish priest of Don, was summoned at the New Pallas Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, for .£1 is. Id. county cess, and he admitted his liability except in respect of the sum of 5d , the portion of the malicious injury com- pensation tax levied upon him. This tax, be said, was un- just in principle, and his being assessed to it conveyed the imputation that he sympathised with crime. The case was adjourned on a point of form. Mr. Henry George is to be invited by members of the Irish National League to deliver an address in Dublin in explanation of his land scheme. Speaking in that city, on Monday night, Mr. Michael Davitt said be himself went a long way towards Mr. George's theory ; still, notwithstand- ing his difference with the majority of the members of the League on the land question, he recognised that there must be unity of organisation if the national cause was ever to achieve anything by orgaeisation, and individuals must be prepared to make sacrifices If unity of action was to be maintained );1 the national ranks. Some sensation was caused in the Killarney district on Sunday by the arrest of several young men under the Crimes Act. The aff Lir, however, appears to be somewhat ludicrous. One Eugene Tanguey was recently liberated from custody after apprehension on a charge of complicity in the murder of Sullivan, an assistant bailiff of Mr. Her- bert's. A number of friends assembled oa Sunday to offer congratulations upon his release, and among these was Mr. Geoffrey O'Donoghue, son of The O'Dongobue, M.P. While returning home from MA99 they attracted the attention of the constabulary on account of the military precision of their march, and they were arrested. The re- sult of the investigation on Tuesday was that the prisoners were released.

COMPENSATION FOR OUTRAGE IN IRELAND.—It appears from a Parliamentary return, issued on Thuredav, that un- der the Prevention of Crime (Ireland) Act, £22,450 had been awarded by the Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland up to the 30th June, 1883, to the personal representatives of persons killed, and £20,185 to persons injured. During three years ending on the same day, grand juries in Ireland had under the Peace Preservation (Ireland) Act, 1875, awarded £7.240 to the representatives of persons killed and £2 480 to per- sons injured. The Lord-Lieutenant dealt w;th the cases of 33 persons and the grand juries with 11 persons killed, The highest awards were £4,000 to the executors of Mr. J. Young, J.P., murdered in the county of Roscommon; £3,000 to Mr. Denis J. Field, who was attacked in Dublin; and £3,000 to the renresentatives of Lord Mounttnorres, murdered in the county of Galway. THE VITRIOL THROWING CASE —At Arklovr Petty See. sions, ou Thnrsday, Miss Lilly Tyndall was charged with throwiog a bottle of vitriol ,ver Mr. Toomy, solicitor. Mr. Gyll, chemist, was also charged with counselling Miss Tyn- dall to commit the act. Miss Tyndall, whom he said was his affianced wife, had told him that two attempts had been made to assault her, aud that she was afraid to travel alone, and he thereupon, he says, give her sulphuric acid to en- able her to defend herself. At the opening of the proceed- ings it was stated that that morning Mies Tyndall -and Mr. Gyll had been married, and they appeared in court as hus- band and wife, accompanied by a large number of friends. Lord Wicklow presided, and there was a full bench. The charge against Mime Tyndall or Mrs. Gyll was first taken up. The lady is good-looking, and was dressed in black. filas is about 23. Her husband seemed to regard the matter as a grave one. Mr. Toomey sat on another bench opposite them. He is an unmarried man of about 40. The right side of his face is discoloured and one eye half closed. His neck was covered in bandages—The proceedings were ad- journed. THE MAYO MURDER CONSPIRACY.—The trial was com- menced at Cork Assizes on Tuesday of six men charged with being concerned in conspiracies to murder various un- popular persons in county Mays. The jury before whom the men were indicted at the winter Assizes failed to arrive at a verdict. The principal prisoner is a man named Patrick William Nally, who is alleged to have planned some of the outrages committed while resident in this country. One of the ohief witnesses is an " informer" named Coleman, who while a sworn member of the secret and criminal society was giving information to the police. On Wednesday, Patrick M'Evilly, of Manchester, was called to depose to the prisoner Nally's operations in furtherance of the plots at the time he was engaged "in the provision way" in Manchester. Nally, he said, was, in the habit of receiving parcels containing revolvers and sending them to Ireland;where they were intended to "do good work during the winter." Vlie witness said he ones heard arrangements being made for sending a man over to Ireland to shoot a person who had taken a farm formerly held by Nally's father. Evidence was given on Thursday in the interest of the prisoners. A very remark able feature in the defence was that a priest was called to gate that from his "general character and reput Mon " the informer Coleman, who had been one of hie parishioners, WAS not worthy of credit en his oath.

At Bi-Past a tailor's daughter has obtained a verdict, with £2lO damages, againet a publican, named MiConville, for breach of promise of marriage. lieplying to an influential deputation at the War Office, on Wednesday, who opposed the abolition of the Scotch regimental feather bonnet. Lord Hartington said the Govern- ment had resolved. in deference to the strong feeling exist- ing on the subject in Scotland, 1p deice no change this year with regard to the bonnet, deferring arty decision until next year. At Stratford (Essex), on Wednesday, John Minns, 64, I general dealer, was cluarged with stealing one pennyworth of ceke from the Wesleyan Chapel at East Ham, the trus- tees of which felt compelled to prosecute, as much of their coke had lately been stolen. The prisoner, who denied the offence, and who had already been a week in jail, was sen- tenced to one month's hard labour. At.Sucderland Police Court, on Wednesday, the bearing of the cb trrs of embezzlement and falsification of accounts stgainA W. Ii Dixon, shipowner and secretary of the Steam Shipping Company, was resumed. Evidence was given showing that the prisoner had altered the bank passbook to cover a deficiency of £1.200, and had also made false state- ments in what purported to be balance sheets. He was com- mitted for. trial. Tbe Blackburn magistrates, on Wednesday morning, fined William Henry Whalley, weaver, of Damen, 20s and costa for bre.kitig the communicating glass in a railway carriage on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, between Blackburn and Lower Darwen, at eleven o'clock at night. The defendant said be was drunk, and broke the glass net knowing what it was for. Upon the breaking of the glass the vacuum brake was applied, and the train was delayti 16 minutes. div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TIIIIRSDAYu
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TIIIIRSDAYu

MILITARY EXAMINATIONS —The Marquis 61 SAL:9III7RX asked for an explanation of the fresh regulations in connec- tion with the ex oninations for admission to the Royal Military Collegts at Sandhurst, which would have the effect of discouraging the study of English literature and natural science.—The Earl of MORLEY said the object had been to encourage the taking up of subjects which could be taught in preference to those which could be crammed.—The Duke of CAMBRIDGE thought the principle laid down in the new regulations was a sound one, and he trusted that the great schools would give their assistance in preparing young men to go direct from them to the military college.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TwurtspaY, GENERAL GORDON AND THE ARAITS.—The Marquis Of HARTINOTON communicated to the House atranslation of the letter which General Gordon sent to the Arab chiefs be- fore the battle of Tub. It summoned them to disperse before daybreak on the following morning, and asked them instead of fighting the English te send delegates to General Gordon at Khartoum. The note stated that the English were not at war with the Arabs, but that they were determined to ois- perse the force before Strakim, and closed with a warning th tt if the tribes refused to dis- perse the consequences would be on their own heads. LONDON GOVERNMENT BILL —The HOME SECRETARY stated that the London Gioyerament Bill would be taken at the earliest possible time after the second reading of the Franchise Bill and the Budget bad been disposed of. THE VOLUNTEERS —ln reply to Colonel Walrond, Mr. BRAND s•ated that the Government could not undertake to issue 200 000 Martini-Henri rifles on loan to volunteers. There were at present 250000 of these rifles in store, and that was somewhat below the ordinary number.

OPERATIONS IN THE SOUDAN —The Marquis of HAIITINGF- TON read a telegram from Admiral Hewitt, dated two p.m. Thursday, to the effect that General Graham had driven the Arabs away from Tamanieb village, and got at water— much needed. It was added that there were no casualties on our side, and that the Arabs were dispersing.

TILE Fivormarsz BILL.—The debate on the second read- I ing or the Franchise Bell was resumed by Mr. Rmans.—ln the course of the debate Mr. CHAMBERLAIN spoke of the un- reality of the oppoAtion, which might be due either to the knowledge of the Conservatives that when the bill left that House it was going to a strange and inhospitable country from which it might never safely return, or from a feeling that the b'll was so urgently demanded by the country that it was useless to "kick against the pricks." The inference from the amendment was that the Conservative party did not admit that the extension of the franchise was either good or bad. The Government, however, held that it was a desirable thing to include the largest possible number of capable citizens within the limits of the constitution, whether or not that was followed up by a scheme of redistribution, or whatever might be the scheme of redistribution. The interests ef the agricultural !showers had been too long neglected, and as the result they had been robbed of their land. (Cries of "No, no," and in- terruptions.) They had been robbed of their rights in the r commons and open spaces and they were still being robbed, not only of lands, but of endowments that were left for the benefit of the poor. Both political parties were to blame for those wrongs, but they would never have been committed if the agricultural labourer had had a vote. Unless the re- presentation of Ireland was to be made a fraud, the Irish people should have the same electoral rights as those of England and Scotland. It would be difficult, if not im- possible, to taks Ireland out of the Bill. Hence the Govern- ment would stand on the bill, the whole bill, and nothing but the bill.—The debate was adjourned.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.

The Lords Committee on the Ship Canal Bill on Monday hear I further evidence from Mr. Marshall Steven, shipping agent, of Liverpool and Gersten. Afterwards Mr. Richard Hartley, a director, and for ten years the manager of the Old Si!Katona and Dodworth Colliery Company, near Barns- ley, was examined to show how the proposed canal would benefit his district. In the course of his statement he said it was estimated that the amount of coal in Yorkshire still to be worked was 23,000.000,000 tons, practically an inex- haustible snooty He thought that 3,000 000 tons of c eel per year might very shortly pass over the Ship Canal from the Yotkshire coalfield. Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer, was called to describe his scheme for the construction of tha Ship Canal, and he was under examination when the Com- tnitcee adjourned. Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer of the Ship Canal schema, was under examination throughout Tuesday. He I went fully into the question of plans, and explained in what respects the present proposals differed from those of last year. The examination of Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer, was continued on Wednesday. Being pressed by the chid.- man (the Duke of Richmond) te say whether he could guarantee that no injury would be done by the canal to the estuary of the Mersey, the witness said the best answer ha could give WAS that Manchester was prepared to spend such a large stun of money in making a canal which would be rendered useless if the bar or the estuary were injured in the way the opponents of the bill suggested. The Chair- man asked if the promoters were taking powers to carry out whatever works in the estuary should be ordered by the Mersey Ci.mmiesieners. r. Pember (counsel for the Bill) sold he believed that at some future time Admiral Spratt (the acting Conservator) would come to the conclusion that the appieheneion expressed by him in his report was un- founded, but the Commissioners had insisted that the works should be made obligatory on the promoters, and a clause to this eifoct had been agreed to. In mentioning that the committee would rise to-morrow week for the Easter re- cess, the Chairman said they had no wish to shorten the in- quiry, and they did not thirk that any time had been wasted so far. On Thursday Mr. Abrirnathy, Cs., Was examined on be- half of the promoters of the bill. He said he had gone carefully into the estimates and was satisfied that they were sufficient for the work. Tne witness was followed by Mr. Deas, engineer to the Clyde Navigation, and Mr. Fowler, engineer to the Tees Conservancy. The latter gentleman said he considered that the estuary of the Tees resembled to a great ex:ent that of the Mersey, and am iujurioas influence whatever had been exercised upon it by the execution of the works; indeed, the effect of the works uptm the bar at the mouth of the Tees had been to entirely carry away the southern part of it and to increase the depth of the water over the rest from 4ft. Bin. to lift. He saw no reason why the same result should not follow from the works in the es- tuary in the Mersey as had followed from the works oil the Tees.

The inquest on the body of the womin MAry Ann Yeats, who was murdered in a house in Burton Crescent, London, was concluded on WednesdAy. Evidence w,r.s given show- ing that the deceased was found in the streets at the age of five years and taken to a charitable institution. She was afterwards in service until three or four years ago, when she commenced leading an irregular life. Profceser Pepper sCki death was evidently c ward by strangulation with a to.r. I. The jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against somo person.anknown.

div.head: CONS ERVATITE MEETING AT WARRINGTON. – SOUTH-WEST WARD.
div.p: CONS ERVATITE MEETING AT WARRINGTON. - SOUTH-WEST WARD.

On Wednesday evening the annual meeting Of the Con- ervatives of the South,West Ward of Warrington was held in floly 'Trinity Church Schoolroom, Museum-street, under the presidency of Mr. Robert Pierpoinr, J.P. There were also present Sir G. Grethen, Bart., Captain Reynolds, J.P., Counciliors Wright, rierpoint, Sutton, Burgess, and Messrs. Taylor and Rebertsf&c., cfm. There was not a very large atrendance.—Councillor J. PIERPOIN7 moved the first resolution, which was to the effect that Mr. Robert Pier.' point be appointed chairman, Councillor Thomas Sutton vice-chairman, and Councillor Wright hon. see, of the Ward .Committee. The resolution also ,roposed the appointment of certain gentlemen as delegates to the Council of the Con- servative Associ-ition. kle was sure that the gentlemen named in the resolution would make a, good working com- mittee,. and ventured the assertion that when the time arrived when they should be upend doing—and they might expest almost weekly to hear some things- that would pat them on the qv vise—:hey wvold elect Sir Gilbert Grinnell again for the borough of War- ringtont -••.- Mr. GRICIS seconded, and the reao-• intim eras carried.—Mr. Surrox proposed "that the reivainder of the Ward Committee he the same as it was last year, with the additiocr of all Conservatives- of the ward who off 6. to • work voluntarily withou: payment at any election:" He thought that the signs of the time• pointed to au.marly dissslution,and when an election came,he thought, if ;he Conservatives worked with aan and in earnest, they would sucseed:—Mr. WRIGHT seconded the resolution, whleth was carriisd.—Mlr. TAyIiIR priiposed "That this meeting ivof 'opinion rrat the Franchise Bil:Mow be-

eee [fore the House of•Commensis- a mere parry tick whereby 'the Government teepee to gala-votes for its supportens at the ;twit election of county members, and considers that until the measure is aceompanied by an equitable redistribution of mate it ought to have the &song opposition of Conserva- tives." He denielthat the preemses made by the present Ceerernment had been- falfitled; and con;emned the action of England in Egypt. The peace policy with which the Government Came Moe office bad nct been carried out in any ' way, and as regarded the promises e 4 a reduction of the - national debt aud expenditure be claimed that they also had ' not been redueed, . and thee the acts of the Liberal Government weeild result. in an increased harden of tanattion. He pointed to what he mil. d the rebellious' state of Ireland as indicating what the reform of the Goverernent had been ace}, speaking to the resolution, said that thwPranehise seamed to him to be an attempt by the Liberal perty to manipulate the strings of political power for their own advantage, and to obtain a continuance of oftee, by swamping the votes- of the upper and middle classes and, respectable artisans. The trade of the ceuntry was depressed and in Warringtcu there were manyahrown out of work who were desirous of working. If any either Government had been in office the working people would have had a right to look to the Goverument for an inceeiry into the cause of the de- pression, but they had the mefertune te have a Government that would not take any intereet in the matter.—r. BUR- GESS, in B°C nding the resolution remarked that the present House of Commons was dead, and that ail the- wind of the Radice' bellows in England could but- nfuse life into its dry bones. Parliament was incapable and. the Government utterly discreditable. They were promised peace, and war had been chronic ever since Mr. Glad- stone took office. Workingmen were promised an improved condition of things, lied at the preeent moment the artisans of one of the most- imp mtant ingustries of Warrington were out of employment b -eauee they hesitated to accept a reductien of nearly 2f3 yer c 'or. in their wages.— Sir GILBERT GREVALL supported the reseiution, and stig- matised the Egyptian policy of the Liberal Government as one of bloodshed, saying that tlie history of recent occur- rences in Egypt, if recorded, woula be writteu in shameful and dreadfo? letters of blood! Ea/erring to the election to the House of Commons of Sir leeb.at Peel, he remarked that he had written his congratulations to that gentleman. who replied that he had a most kindly recollection of his - visit to Warrington, and that if -be came again into the neighbourhood he was sure that he would be received in the Baffle manner again. (Applauee.)— ll'he CHAIRMAN il!a0 • supported the resolution. He maintained that the country itself took no interest in the Franchise Bill, for, said he,- he heard mention of Egypt in every street, and of the Soudan at every corner, but be heard no mention of the Franchiee Bill. Few of them read the speeches on that subject, and and he was sure that none of tho-ei who did benefited by it. At a Liberal .meeting held at Penketh Egypt was oaly mentioned in passing, and he believed that the Soudan was not mentioned at all, but the meeting regaled itself with tea, breed-and-butter, and the County Franchise Bill. (Laughter.) That bill was merely a red- herring dragged acreise the trail. It was not that the Con- servatives talked about Egypt to take the attention of the country, but it was-the Liberal a...my who were continually talking of the Franchise Bill. When the country saw that ' the policy of blood of the Government was disgracing England in the East, they cared nothing about the Franchise Bill, but they wieued have right done, and they would not have blood-abed and- slaughter occasioned in order that the County Franchise Bill might poss. He con- cluded by urging the meeting to support the Conservative party strenuously in prefeeence to the Government that "dawned in a misty halo of lies-and deceptions, and whose - sun was now set in a sea of blood."—The resolution was then put and carried.—Captain DETITOLDS prepesed " that this meeting pledges itself to. do its utmost to return Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., to Parliament as member for the borough at the next general olection."— The Rev. E. C. E. Caner/met seconded, and referring to the Liberal meeting held the evening previous at the Co-opera- tive Hall, remerked.that the lecturer at that meeting was in the pay of the National Reform Union, and euch men were not open to conviction, for to admit themselves defeated would mean the loss of their situation. The heat discussions they could have were not at public exhibitions on any. platform, but were those where they could sit together round a table as committee men simply for the express par-. pose of enquiring into the question.—Prie reselution was carried, and A vote of thanks accorded to the chairman, on the motion of Councillor FaaNCOILB, seconded by Councillor Ilurcitiersow, concluded, the meeting.

div.head: ELOPEMENT OF A PUBLICAN'S WIFE IVITII A LODGER. THE RUNAWAY COUPLE AT ELBLESTOWN.
div.p: ELOPEMENT OF A PUBLICAN'S WIFE IVITII A LODGER. THE RUNAWAY COUPLE AT ELBLESTOWN.

The details of an elopement. tinged with the shade of the. romantic, have recently been disclosed in Earlestown, and, the affair has formed the chief topic of conversation among those resident in the immediate locality. On S..turdav night a middle-aged man, who said he hailed frton Ludden- denfoet, Yorkshire, applied to the Earlestown police offic.ers to assist him in tracing the whereabouts of his wife, who, he stated, had deserted him and run away with another man who lodged with him He had a photograph of the missing "fair one" in his possession, and on its being exhibited to P.C. Lloyd, that officer iinneediately recognised it as the portrait of a woman residing with a certain driver as his wife. Owing to the lateness of the hour, however, the con- stable advised the deserted husband" to s-ek lodgings in the town for the night, as no doubt on the following morn- ing he would be eb'e to let him have a proper view of bis missing wife. The man agreed, and on the following day be turned up at the time arranged. The constable Rotor- dingly led him to a certain cottage in a row not far from the Earlestown railway station, and knocked at the r'e r, while the Yorkshire- man stood a abort distancl away. - On the door being opened the officer was cordially invi-ed inside, but he beckoned the Yorkshireman, who accordingly advanced, and on reaching the door he found himself confronted with his long loot wire, who had in her arms a stepping infant daughter, whom the lierkshireman had not previously numbered among hie family. Whether the scene was. affecting and impressive, or whether it was of a violent and stormy character, it is not needfu to relate, but it may be. added that the affair will probably have a sequel in the Divorce Court. the " hipbaud " having exoreseed his deter- mination to seek a divorce. It appears that about two years. ago the husband kept a public-house in Yorkshire, and a nib driver Came to lodge thereat. In course of time an in- timacy sprang up between the publican's wife and lodger,. and the result. WAS that they elopeditogether. all trace of the missing couple was lost from that time up to the pre- sent, when the publicau on hie way to S.iureport on buai- ness matters happened to stop at Earlestown, and while there showed a photograph of his wife to the police, which led to the discovery of the runaway couple.

A young " rou-rh-," rimed Thomas Lawson, was on Wed- nesday committed to prison for two months by the Bootla magistrates for wounding a Russian sailor earned Koskalo. No the slightest provocation had been given, bat Lawson beat Koskalo with a belt which had a heavy buckle, and in- flicted two serious wounds upon his bead. Two youths in the prisoner's company were arrested. but were discharged for want of direct evidence At the Wednesbury Police Court, on Tuesday. THE Representation of the People Bill now before the House of Commons is evok- ing, as might be expected of it, a debate much more worthy of the iratli;ions of that august assembly than the sort of peddling attacks upon the Egyptian policy of the Government to which the nation is getting too much accustomed. The battle now be- ing fought is a Bate Royal, and, as has ever been the case during such encounters, it is being watched with the keenest interest by those whose fortunes are directly at stake, "To be or not to be "—teat is the question which is laid before Parliament in the matter of enfranchising Two Millions Of HER MAJESTY'S subjects who, to the discredit of our representative system, are as yet outside the pale of the Constitution. It is true that they can be taxed for the State; thy are good enough to fight for the State; but they ate not permitted to vote for the State. The Liberal partY, mindful of their pledges at the hustings in 188 q, propose to remedy this long-standing grievance, and hence the Franchise Bill, noW under consideration, which is to be followed next session by a R, distlibution Bill—the principles of which have already been laid before the House .of Commons by the PRIME MINISTER. Ihe proposal is straigh,t, and clear, and "the intelligent foreigner, whose intelligence is not, however, great enough to enable him to read between the lines, would be disposed to conclude that there would be no difficulty in getting the ' measure through the House of Commons. He would have seen how reties, as well es Liberals, claim t ) be the friend of the people," and, having been reminded again and again that the Tories were in power when the Household Suffrage Bill for Parlia- mentary boroughs was placed on the Statute Book, he would naTrally think that they, at any rate, would not seek to block the way. But how does the matter stand? What is the position of the To-y party on this County Franchise Question? Ju t this—they ate_ "willing to wound and yet afraid t°

div.p: faith, or rather lack Of faith. Indeed Mr. HOLYOAXE has a satirical eye to the whole situation when he quotes Lord SHERBOOOKE as having once said that "If we had an atheistic oath established in Parliament, there would be shoals of Chris- tian members who would find reasons for taking it as good as those they find now." So far as the House of Commons is con- cerned, the issue is one of law and not of conscience, and it is just because Mr. BRAD- LAUGH has the law on his side that, if he persevere, he will win in the end. Mr. PILCHER pleads "guilty to a large extent to the accusation" of not having "supported Mr BRADLAUGH," anxious as he is to "up- hold the right of constituencies to return to Parliament persons whom theythink proper." But if a constituency is being wronged in the violation of its right, how is it possible, consistent with adherence to Liberal prin- ciples, to refrain from supporting the in- dividual through whom the wrong is being done? The issue at stake is a principle— not a man. It is the Tory fashion to confuse' the two to secure their own ends ; but Liberals should be careful not to be led astray. by this red herring trailed across the scent. It is a small matter shouting for sound principles when they are popular and triumphant; the true courage is to stand by them and ight for them in adversity—to support them even when by an accident of the time they centre in a man as obnoxious as the member for North- ampton proves to be. The •Liberals of Northampton have gallantly done their duty in supporting the man of their choice.; their share of the burden is heavy compared with that of outsiders; but they appear to have seen the end from the beginning, and we commend them for their determination to terminate in the language of Mr. HOLY- OAICE "the scandal of imposing upon conscience a political penalty."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 29, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 29, 1884.

THE GENESIS OF HISTORY—Mr. T. Glover lectured on this subject on Thursday evening, before the trieinbrs of the Historical Class of the Runcirn Y.M.C.A. Mr. W. J. Shore presided. LICINSING MATTERS AT WIDNEF—At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday. the In taistratei granted the fol- lowing temporary translate :—A7 Parkes, from Railway Hotel, Waterloo-road, to Central Hotel, Victoria-road ; The nas Orrnesher. from the Vine Inn to the Railway Rotel ; Mr. William etanke, from the Grapes len, Halton- road, Runcorn, to the Vine too, Watet loc-road, Widnes. TEE MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT DlTTON.—Before Mr. F. Goesa.ge, at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, John Malley, labourer, Ditton, was brought up 00 remand charged with haying, on the 18th instant, unlawfully wounded Patrick Brophy by kicking hitn in the stomach. The prosecuted' and prisoner, it will be remembered, became engaged in a wordy altercation when the latter kicked the former in the stomach, inflicting serious internal injuries. Inspector Wood said the prisoner was unable to appear, bring confined to his bed, and asked for a remand until Tuesday next. The prisoner was remanded. Wrherse SCIOOL BOARD AT WORE —Mr. G. H. Danhy, the clerk to the School Beard, summoned the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. including costs, was im- posed in each case:—Thomas McNatnara, Elizabeth Delaney, ! William Webster, Abraham Burgess, John Bowyer, Patrick I Fits Simmons, John Hayes, James Kelly, James Lynch, John Taucey, Thomas Owen, William Fallon, and Walter Murphy. Jernes Peacock, nine years of age, a waif alto was found rambling about the street, was committed to an industrial school. MAINTENANCE OF A MOTHER AT RUNCORN.—WiIIimn Stanley, of Widnes, was summoned to Runcorn Pt tty Ses- sions, on Monday, by Mr. Houghton the collector to Run- corn Board of Guardians. who sought an order for the pay- ment of £lO 17e., due to the Guardians on acc tunt of the ! maintenance of the defendant's mother.—Mr. Houghton stated that on the 27th June, 1881, an order hid been made on the defendant for the payment of Is. per week towards the support of his mother. Ile had, however, made no pay- ments, and two distress warrants had been taken ont.—The Bench made an order for the payment of the amount ' claimed, with costs 10. s 6d., within 14 days. ALLEGED TRESPASS IN PURSUIT OF GAME AT DITTO/Q. I —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday Thos. Wright,' a young mac, was summoned on a charge of trespassing in pursuit of game en land in the occupation of Joseph DOD* ton, at Ditton.—Henry Pace, gamekeeper for Mr. Reynolds, at Wootton, deposed that on Monday morning, the 17th inetast, he saw the defendant walk over several fields, one of which was ploughed, belonging to Mr. Langton. The defendant had a "big stick "in one hand, and in the other a stone, which be saw him throw. The place where the defendant was was a likely one for hares.—ln answer to the Bench, witness said he did net see the defendant throw the! stone at anything.—The case was dismissed. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT RIINCORN.—John Roberts, an! engine driver on the London and North-Western Railway, I was injured at Runcorn railway station on Friday night. ! He was the driver of the $-15 p.m. goods train from Crewe, I and on allaying at Ruccorn the signal wi.s against him, and , he had to stop his train " Johnstone's Bridge." Alighting for the purpose of speaking to the signalman be stood in i the sixfoot, when the train from St. Helens ran up and knocked him down. His right leg was cat clear off below the knee, and his head was slightly injured. Dr. Mac- Dougall was se at for, and attended to the injured man, who ; was subsequently conveyed to Crewe in a special train, and ; taken to the infirmary. PRESENTATION TO StneDLY SCHOOL TEACHERS AT RUN. CORN.—The teachers of Bethesda Sunday School have re- cently presented their Pe-workers, Miss Morris and Miss , Edwards, with a testimonial of their regard and esteem, the ' former on the occasion of her marriage to Mr. J. D. Janes, ' and the latter On her departure from the town to commence business in Brighton with her brother. For two years the ladies have laboured as teachers at Bethelida Bclito9l. and their services have been highly appreciated by their c Ales- goes, who on Sunday afternoon appointed a deputation, con- sisting of Messrs. Fairhurst, Tunna, Epck, and Wiley, to wait upon them, and present each lady with a handsome inkstand and the poems of Wordsworth and Mrs. Hernans in beautiful volumes. FOUND DEAD IN BED AT WIDNES.—At the Alexandria hotel, Widnes, in Monday, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy-coroner, held an inquiry touching the death of Sea. Harper, 75 years of age, who lodged with Mrs. Elizabeth Harper, his niece, in Witt-road, Widnes. At Christmas, the deceased paid a visit to his daughter, Mary Tickle, wife of William Tickle, engineer, Eccleeton Hill. He was then ailing froni various complaints, and consulted a broker at I Prescet. The doctor informed the daughter that he WAS suffering from old age and heart disease, and was worn out. 1 The deceased was employed as a weigher at Memel, Het. I chinson's chemical works, and worked until Saturday at I noon. At night he retired to bed, and next morning he was found dead. A verdict that deatk was the result of "Natural causes" was recorded. "Coca OW THE YARD" AT RUNCORN.--At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, James Owen was summoned for assaulting Martha Worthington, and the latter was I charged under a cross-summons with assaulting Jane Owen. —Mrs. Owen said she lived in a court off King-street, and on Saturday night, the 15th instant, as she was going down the yard Mrs. Worthington and the man she lived with were quarrelling. Mrs. Worthington seized her by the hair of the head, knocked her down, and kicked her.—Mrs. Wore thington alleged that Mrs. Owen came down the yard drunk—bouncing, as usual, for she was supposed to be the "cock of the yard" and a champion fighter. (Laughter.) Mrs. Owen seized her by the hair and dragged her to the ground.—The Bench did not believe Mrs. Worthington's story. and bound her over te keep the peace for six months, herself in £lO and one surety in £5; the other summons was dismissed. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN AT RUNCORN.--In the schoolroom of the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen Bolton Locks, on Monday evening, a free en- tertainment was given to a crowded audience, composed of seamen, fiatmen, and ethers. Mr. W. Shaw presided. Songs, readings, recitations, &c., were given by Miss Howard, the pupils from Miss Gentles' school, Miss Davies, and Messrs. G. [inward, W. Pownall, F. Mack, and A. Par- sons. The piano was kindly lent by Miss Gentles. On Wednesday evening, about 50 members of the "class meet- ing" sat down to an excellent tea in the Mission-room, Mrs. Allen and Mrs, WalmsleY presiding at the tables. The class meetinrs were inaugurated in May last, when Mrs. Allen was appointed leader, and that lady! has filled the posit tion with great:credit to herself and much benefit to the members of the class. After tea a meeting, presided over by Mr. Shelf, was held, and addresses were delivered by the Chairman, Mrs. Allen, Mrs. Walmeloy, Mr. and Mrs. Holmes, ligessrs. Mort, Howard, Wilson, and several others. During the evening one of the members, who had received benefit from attending the meetings, resented a handsome Bible for the use of the class.

RESCUED FROM BROWNING AT WIDNES. ALLANT CONDUCT OF A, PUPIL TEACHER. On Monday afternoon a 133 y named Lightfoot, who lives at TAS, Warrington-read, Widnes, went with another boy into a field known as the Riddings, near Halton View, where Orel, engaged in various games. In the field is a large pit of considerable depth, and whilistthe boys were playing with , each other Lightfoot fell into the water. His playmate ran I home and told his mother, who informed Mrs. Lightfoot of ,what had taken place, and they proceeded to the pit. They Ifound Lightfoot waS clinging to the rushes, which grow 'thickly on the elite of the pond, and was thus keeping him- self from sinking. Mrs. lighcfoot, who was labouring under the greatest excitement, with the aid of two other women attempted to reach the boy, but without success. Other persons arrived en the scene, but none dire venture into the water to rescue the little fellow from his perilous position. , For nearly half .an hour he clung to the rushes, but be- coming exhausted, he relaxed his hold, and sank beneath the surface of the water, amid the cries of the byestandere. At this moment Mr. Thomas Phillips, pupil teacher at the Warrington-road schools, who is the son of • Mr. Phillips, builder, having heard of the occurrence, appeared at the edge of the pond. The -spot where the boy had sunk was pointed out I. him, and without a moment's hesitation he dived into the water. in descending his head came in con- tact with the root of ad old tree and he becoming entangled at the bottom 4f the pond, a short time elapsed before he again appeared in sight. The greatest excitement pre- vailed amongst those who had watched the brave action, but with a cry of venal they saw him rise to the surface. At this time Ligktfoot's head also appeared out of the water., and Mr. Phillips at once seized the lad, and a rope being thrown to hitx, the rescued and the rescuer were drawn from the pond in an exhausted state and partially unconscioue. Lightfoot was carried home and attended to, and is now doing very well:; whilst we are glad to say Mr. Phillips feels no ill effects from his submersion. There is not the slightest doubt that had it not been for the bravery of Mr. Phillips the lad must have found a watery grave.
dinner invitation from the Speaker is, in its way, equal to a "command "to one of those uncomfortable and happily • rare state banquets that take place at Windsor.

Memb,rs uncover when they meet the Speaker in the park or tt:e street. I have heard one or two speak of the strangeness of this neeerwity in the c *9B of Mr. Peel. But yesterday he wss a retiring end inconsiderable member of the House, whom one iright elap on the back and ask whether he wanted to pair. To-day he is bpe:..lier, and from the Plime Minister down to the newest member courtesy demands that the hat should be raised in saluting, as it la in the case of the Prince ef Wales.

By the way, there is a good deal of curiosity as to what passed between the speaker and Sir Robert Peel when two brothers met on Monday in strange circumstances. The Speaker was observed to be shaking his brother's hand for an unusually long time, and addressing words to him evi- dently beyond the customary formal welcome. Sir Robert Peel makes no secret of the purport of the conversation. "Oh, he made a nice little speech," Sir Robert says. "He welcomed me in two capacities, one as a new member and the ether as a dear brother. Well old fellow,' I said, 'I am glad to see you, anyhow.'" The notion of addressing the Speaker in the chair as "old fellow" takes one's breath away.

Procrastinatierz is the thief of time, and some artists that I know of have this week been severely testing the truth of that obi adage, and exerting all their might to get in the iniehing strokes for Sunday. Not every peint!r is gifted with the same rapidity of execution as a certain contributor to the present exhibition of the "Nineteenth Century Art Society," one of whose canvasses, sketched with a vague suggestion of something further to come, was hung on the wall to await "varnishing day," when he dexterously painted the picture with a fairly creditable result in the spice of five hours. This is rather suggestive of Mr. Elwin 1 Ellis. Some, , artists earn fame easily. For- cible rapid works, where effects are produced with one sweep of the brush, certainly have a charm of their own, and some people much prefer them to the result of earnest labour and thought. But it is difficult to feel the same respect for things thus easily gained as for details of nature seen with the eve of an artist who discerns more beauties in looking for five minutes at a bit of rock or sea than an ordinary observer would detect in as many years. It is said of Mr. Brett. that "too conscientious was he daring his studies at the Academy Schools, that he even re-produced the dust on the statues." Acil that is not by any means the worst reputathm a man can have in these days of "Impressionist" methods of painting. The "Sandwich Supper" of Mr. Woodall, member for Stoke, is growing to be one of the social incidents of the season. It took place latt night, and was an itumense success. Everyone was there including three of the ministers,wko drove over from the Speaker's dinner. They were in ministerial uni- form, with a difference that excited some curiosity. The Lord-Advocate wore a handsome suit of velvet with cambric ruffles at his wrist and frilled shirt front, the Under- Secretary for India and Mr. Herbert Gladstone wearing the richly gold-braided semi-military suit, which is known as the Windsor uniform, The d'fference is established by the old usage which precludes the legal members of the ministry from wearing anything but velvet' as Court dress. The Attorney-General and Solicitor- General at the Speaker's dinner were dressed as the Lord-Advocate, and certainly had the advantage over the stiffer and more common-place Windsor uniform. The gathering at Mr. Woodall's was a most remarkable one, testifying to the retnarhable popularity and wide acquain- tance of the host. There were, I suppose, over three hun- dred present at one time or other, members of parliament, painters, poets, journalists, authors, actors, singers, and the most remarkable card-trickster I ever saw. The way be transferred eleven cards, via his sleeve, from his extended left hand to his breast pocket was a marvel which was crowned by thetiscovery of the last three cards between the shirt and waistcoat of Dr. Jope, who was silent for the rust of the evening wondering hew it had been done.

EVERTON.—Much public interest cmtres in the mach between Earlestown and Ever ton in the final tie of the competition for the Liverpool and District Football Association Challenge Cdp, which will ba played at Bootle to-morrow (Saturday). The Earlestown players have this week undergone a special training, and Along everyone in .Earleetown heartily spiehes them suc- cess in the contest.

div.head: SCALDED TO DEATH AT WIDNES:
div.p: SCALDED TO DEATH AT WIDNES:

Michael Slowey, a labourer, 2tt years of age, who lived in Eleanor-street, Widnes, died on Thursday evening in the Widnes Accident Hospital. Slowey was employed at the British Alkali Works, Moss Bank, and on Wednesday at noon he was assisting a fitter named Richard Bean to repair a steam cylinder. Whilst so engaged a five-inch p;pe burst, and the escaping steam scalded both men very severely about the face, Neck, and breast. The internal organs of the deceased were also injured. They were conveyed to the Accident Hospital, where Mr. R'chards, the assistant to Dr. McDonnell, attended to the injured men, and did everything possible to alleviate their sufferings, Little hope was how- ever, held out cf blowey's recovery, and he died at the time stated. Bean is progressing satisfactorily.

div.head: HANGMAN AT 'LUTON.
div.p: THE HANGMAN AT 'LUTON.

BINS BRINGS TROUBLE. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. W. Banks and Mr. A. Thomas, Edwin Field, landlord of the Norton Arms Inn, Halton, was summoned for having his house open for the sale of liquors on Sunday, the 16th inst. Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, defended. The witnesses were ordered to leave the court during the hearing of the case.—P.S. Lowndes said that at 2-45 pm. on Sunday, the 16th inst., he visited the defendant's house. He found four persons in the front parlour, three e whom stated they C4lllO from Weston Point, and the fourth came from Man- chester. There were glasses containing liquor on the table. He told the defendant to be very careful who he allowed in his house during closing time. LONDON, Thursday. Mr. Gladstone is still absent, shut up in his room at Coombe, fretting at his loss of exerciae, and the chiefest question of the day for him lieing " Which way does the ' wind blow 1" It so happens that it has been blowing Eist or North-East for the past few days, a circumstance which of itself is sufficient to account for the fremier's slow recovery. If we had had a continuance of the mild spring weather which a fortnight ago sent the leaves and buds out by leaps and bounds, he would probably before this have shaken off his cold, and been back at his post. It is a coincidence, not without melancholy im- port, that this was the very time of the year when Lord Beaconsfield lay between life and death. In those early April days of 1;51, it. chanced that there came a nip of cold weather, like that under ihich Landon is shivering '.just now. It was, an remains the belief of Lord Beaconsfield's medical attendant that but for the turn of the wiad he would Lave lived, for the worst seemed passed. He was daily gaining strength when the east wind fell like a blight upon , young life and old age, and Lord Beaconsfield died. Mr. Gladstone is not broken dovvn ar Lord Beaconetleld wee when this last enemy attacked him. Stitl, the Sother the ; wind changes the lees cause there will be for anxiety.

He has wonderfully improved since now nearly ten years age, he was called upon after tho famous meeting in the smoking-room of the Reform Club. to accept the leadership of the Liberal party in the House of Commons. He is not any less modest now than then, but he has acquired greater confidence in his own powers, and has considerably improved as a par- liamentary speaker. His principal failing is an excess of courteous deference to obtrusivo obstructionists. Mr. Dodson has a comical way of regarding anyone who questions him, as if he wore a criminal. Lord Hareington errs on the side of too-generously interpreting the right of members of the House of Commons to interrogate ministers. A little snubbing, if not of permanent benefit, would be of temporary use in the case of such persons as Mr. Ashmead- Bartlett, Lord Randolph Churchill, and Mr. Warton. Lord Hartington ataders them as laboriously and With as much fulness as if tkey really were in search of useful informa- tion.
