The debate on the Franchisel, mauled to-night, has not yet come anywhere near khe level of former debates on the same subj:ct. The sufficient reason for this is the hol- lowness and artificiality of the proceedings. There is no fight in the Conservative party, and in the House of Com- mons, as elsewhere, a sham battle is not a very inspiritieg affair. The Conservatives, with the conspicuous exception of Mr. James Lowther, are playing a part with a mask on that deceives no one, least of all themselves. They hate Parliamentary reform now as they hated it in 1832; but they dare not fight it after the Caine manner. They have, in- deed, to make believe to love it, and their complaint against the Ministry is not that that they propose too much, but that their scheme is incomplete. The Conservatives sot only watt to see two million new voters added to the register, but they desire te see swept away all those anomalies which make Dungarvon half as powerful in the senate as Sheffield, and leave Leicester with only twice the voting power of Caine. This little game impeses upon them the necessity ot talking a great deal &bent the redistribution of seats which is not before the House, and very little about the extension of the franchise which is. All ttris conspires to mat s the pro- ceedings sickeningly artificial— Members even on the Con- servative side will not aseist by their pretence, the conse- quence being that for hour after hour the most momentous political.cuestion of the eny is talked over in the presence of half-a-doaen members.

The two events of personal interest in the Parliamentary I , history of the week me Sir R. Cross's escapade of Friday night, and Mr. BrighrUs speech on Menday. As for Sir Richard perhaps enough has been said on a subject which, though excessively comical in some of its aspects, was really a painful affair, discreditable to the House of Com- mons. The latest stou is that Sir Richard is in daily receipt of bits of blue ribbon such as members of the Blue Ribbon Army wear in their button holes. It is remembered that though, owing to a concatinationof circumstances, this affair attracted an unusual exeasure of attention, it is not the first time Sir Richard has been -" out to dinner.:' One night early in last session he presented himself at the table and in 1 his impressive atanner madri a few remarks on the subject , under discussion, which were absolutely unintelligible, though they had about them that curious semblance of ' senrie which speeches made under similar circumstances by persons of grave and magisterial disposition sometimes have. The House did not laugh then, being simply puzzled, and sat listening and listening, painfully endeavou.ing to get the clue of the speech. At the end of live minutes Sir Richard resumed his seat with that air of supreme self- satisfaction he always wears, and with the evident convic- tion that he had settled that point. As for Mr. Bright's speech it was the first distinct indica- tion he has given of failing oratorical power. Since his re- turn to public life I have beard nearly everyone of his great speeches, whether delivered in the House or in the country, and though there was that tendency to dwell upon his own achievements in the past, which is the privilege of our elders, I never noted a falling off either in vigour of thought or grace of rFetien. Bath were painfully manifest in the speech of Monday. This was the more striking because it was evident that Mr. Bright, recognising the personal in- terest of the occasion, had devoted unusual care to the pre- paration of his speech. Ile. had, in truth, almost written it out, and instead of the two scraps of paper, habitual accompaniment of his greatest speeches, he had a sheaf of notes to which front time to time he turned aad undisguisedly read whole sentences. Perhaps it was the over-preparation that spoiled him. He was much nearer his old form in the brief encounter he had later in the evening with Mr. James Lowther, and to which he, of course, rose on the spur of the moment. Town is crowded now, and dinner parties are in full swing. As of old, Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday nights are the great political dinner nights; hut Tuesdays and Fridays have now been impressed into the service of dinner givers. On these nights business in the House is not likely to be exciting, and it seems to be coming about as a regular thing that on Tuesday there should be a count out. Last night the new Speaker gave his first dinner, the guests being chiefly confined to liar Majesty's Ministers. Mr. Chamberlain, who had previously issued invitations to diaXer the same night, was obliged to put it off. •A.
LIBERAL LECTURE AT RUNCORN.
MR. B. ENIVE.TON ON REFORM.

The last of the series of lectures on political subjects pro- moted by the Runcorn Liberal Association for the winter mouths, was given in Bethesda Schoolroom, on Tuesday eveniog. The lecturer was Mr. B. Kniveton, an enthu- siastic local Liberal, who had chosen for his subject " Past acte of reform and their beneficial effect on the nation." There was a good attendance. Mr. T. Norman presided, and on the platform were Slessrs. James Handley, J.P., W. Handley, F. J. Norman, G. Bellamy, J. Beveridge, and 0. Leak (local agent). Tne CHAIRMAN said they were met there that night to listen 10 a lecture by one of their townsmen. (Applause.) He thought this fact sp lee well for Runcorn. He did not see why they should always go abroad for talent—(A Voice: "No need to do.")—when they had men amongst them who could undertake to speak on the question of re- form. (Hear, hear.) He had no doubt Mr. Kniveton would be aisle to deal with this matter as fully as any man they could send for. (Hear, hear.) At the coaclusion of the lecture he had no doubt the audience would be delighted to nave heard Mr. Rniveton and be thankful that they had .such a man in the town. (Applause.) Before calling upon him, he would just say that the Liberal Association in the town was desirous of extending its powers by increasing the number of members. All Liberals could become mem- bers for twelve months by purchasing a ticket for a shiliing. These lectures were not organised without cost, and they , should like as many young men as possible, and the friends of Liberalism generally, to take up their position amongst them, and take a share of the responsibility. Unity was strength, and if they all pulled together nothing could defeat them. There was no mistake that the town of Run- corn wee Liberal in feeling. Let them keep up their posi- tion as Liberals and unite together. (Applause.) Mr. linivaros, who had a cordial reception, then Asa to deliver his lecture, their subject, he said, carried them back to the beginning of the present century, and the question arose what were the circumstances and causes which led to the passing of the Reform Bill of 1832 The reply was the deplorable condition of the people physically, and intellectually. When the century was opening, events were transpiring in Europe pregnant with the most momentous consequences to society. Men had been taught to believe in the divine right of kings, the acknowledgment of which bad been one of the chief causes of the wars that had scourged mankind. (Hear, hear.) Acting under the influence of this pernicious principle, the sovereigns of Europe, supported by many of the aristocracy, had pursued a career of aggrandisement, at the expense of their subjects' welfare, and the life and treasure of the nations were wasted with a profusion, fearful to contem- plate. Amongst the offenders France, under Louis XV., occupied the kid pre-eminence. Under his terrible reign every species of oppression and insult was resorted to. Mean, selfish, licentious and powerful, his one care was to find fuel to feed his base and ignoble nature, and under his blighting reign liberty and justice withered and died. At his imperial , feet, new and heavy taxes were laid upon the people, and ; by the adoption of stern, cruel, and cold-blooded measures, , the discontent of the people was repressed. But they might as well hope to stifle out the fires in Mount Etna by closing up the crater as hope to quench feelings of discontent berm of oppression, injustice, and wrong. (Applause.) Yet, this was what Louis X.V. tried to do. He consigned large num- bers to prison without trial, and kept them there until they died, and the grim and glaring towers and prisons of the , Butt: le were feted with those Who knew not why they had I been doomed to such a dreadful late. In his presumption I and folly he fl ittered himself that his measures of repression had convinced those of his subjects wile denied his right to dispose at his will of the lives and property of the people, that they were only deceiving themselves. But the startling suddenness and terrible scenes and desolations of the Revolution revealed, to his dismay and ram, thit the fires of just indignation and discontent bad been fanned into an intense heat by the measures he had adopted to extin- guish them. (Applause.) The despot who had robbed his subjects of their birthright " Liberty," sad who for long years had had his foot on the necks of his subjects was overthrown and men hoped that a new era had dawned, and that the welfare of society was assured. Such, alas ! was not the case. Men who had been goaded to desperation by centuries of misrule became intoxicated with the new power they had acquired, and such was the spirit of vindic- tiveness they meuitested towards those who had ruled them with a rod of iron, that Europe stood aghast at their deeds, and declared that the remedy they had applied to the evils of society was tenfold worse than the disease. After a brief respite of peace, another dial arber came on the scene in the person of Napoleon Bonaparte. Inflamed with a mad am- bition for universe! empire, this scourge of mankind went through Europe and Asia overturning thrones and upsetting kingdoms, and his career of havoc and desolation was not arreeted until a large part of the wealth and blood of Europe had been poured out. (Hear, hear.) Into this sanguinary conflict England had to take a foremost part, and it wss mainly due to her efforts that the insatiable ambition of Napoleon Bonaparte was first curbed, and his power ulti- mately broken. (Applause.) But the victory, complete as it was, had been purchased at a fearful price. We had been compelled to double our fleet, and equip and maintain a naval force such as the world had never seen. Oar fighting strength on land had to be raised from 80,000 to 500,000 men, and our national debt rose from 2M millions to 484 millions. For over 20 years Europe had not known rest, ant when the Jesuits of this reign ef carnage and blood came to be tabulated it was found that millions of lives had \ been sacrificed, qutold wealth wasted, and a frightful in. ' cubits of debt bequeathed to the nation, makiug a heavy tax on future generations, and subtracting from the sum of their enjoyment. Still something had been gained in the terrible political upheavals and earthquakes. Old despotisms had received a shock, the effects of which were to endure. The people began to speak with bated breath of their rights to justice and to power, and the unbridled despotism of tyrants contributed to the dissemination and final triumph of Liberal principles. (Applause.) During this lengthened period of war the social condition of the English people was fairly tolerable. So large a proportion of the adult male population being engaged in fighting, work was more plenti- ful for those who remained at home, and this, combined with a good demand in the various markets, tended to improve somewhat the wages of the toiler. After the war was over, however, the increased demand for the products of the working classes fell off. The army of producers was in- greased by the large numbers who retuimd from the battle- field to the peaceful pursuits of commerce. Taxation stood at an oppressively high figure, and the industries of the cenntry, agricultural and commercial, were crippled by un- just and oppressive restrictions. The common labourer received about 108 or lie a week, and the skilled artisan 13s to 15a per week. Labour became scarce; food excassively dear. Ira the early part of the century and during the war the price of wheat usually ranged from 80s to 100 s per quarter, and in the year 1801 the 4th loaf sold for Is I.od. With the return of peace and the operation of natural laws, this state of things must soon have improved, for millions who for years had been wholly employed with the sword were now handling the plough, and other implee mente of husbandry, and a good and cheap supply of food could have been had in foreign countries. But our legisla- tors, who at that time were Tories and landowners, in order to keep up the;r rents, passed a law in 1815 that no foreign grain was to be imported until wheat in the home markets had been for six months at or over 803 per quarter, which meant to the consumers dear bread. And etrange to say this iniquitous law was not repealed until 1845. The plain English of the enactment was this: " We must have our high rents. In order to pry these the farmer must have high prices, and if the people cannot purchase at these paces they 'mist do without." (Applause.) It was the Tory principle—legislation lot the privileged few; the mass must shift for themselves. (Applause.) The result of this legislation was that famines were of frequent occurrence, ani bread riots were not unknown. The people were poorly and insufficiently led, and being doomed to 15 or 16 hours labour a day, became emaciited and weak, the ready vic- tims of- disease. Children of the tender years of six and seven, weak in constitution through poor and insufficient food, were compelled to work for long weary hours. and a very large percentage of these grew into pale, sickly, and deformed men and women, and the fouudation of a popula- tion feeble, short-lived, and debised were being rapidly laid. These things went on until the rectuiting sergeants declared th it in the manufacturing districts they could not find men with stamina in tbem sufficient to fit them for military service. The intellectual condi- tion of the masses was on a par with this social condition, as it ever must be. (Applause ) The people had neither the means nor the opportunity to acquire knowledge. Schools were almost unknown, books were exceedingly dear, and the newspaper, that natural enemy of despotic govern- ments—(applause)—and the noble defence of popular rights, was taxed to the extent of about 4d a copy. This was about 1515. Fifty per cent, of the population were unable to write their own Dames. Public political meetings were either forbidden, or if permitted, conditions were at- tached that rendered them useless for purposes of agitation for reform. Unjust laws and stern measures to repress manifestations of discontent were the order or the day. Stiil ' what the people dared not proclaim in public they whis- pered in private, and the cause of this misery and degrada- tion began to be largely discussed in private, with the result of a deep conviction that an improvement was hopeless until a reform in the representation of the people had been brought about. (Applause ) The discovery was made that the privileged class held nearly every seat in the House of Commons—that laws were enacted to promote their interests and theirs alone. The people had little influence and no authority over their Government. The representative sys- tem under which they lived was a mockery. Nearly every great nobleman had a number of seats at his disposal. The Duke of Norfolk "owned "eleven members, Lord Lonedale, nine, Duke of Rutland, six. Seventy members were re- turned by thirty-five places, where there were scarcely any ' voters at all. Old Sarum had two members and not one i nhabitant—(laughter)—Gratton had two members and seven electors, and seats were publicly sold. At last this state of affairs became intoler- able, and a few bold spirits with William Cobnett— (applause)—at their head, translated the people's thoughts into words, and reform became the burning question of the day. (Applause.) From 1816 to 1330 the agitation pro- ceeded and gathered strength, and the Whig party lent a little of their favour. In the year 1830, an event happened in France which had a marvellous influence for good in the cause of popular rights in England. The rule of the House of Bourbon, which had been restored, after the overthrow of Napoleon, bad become intolerable on account of its despot- ism. The French nation, stung to desperation by the exactions and tyranny to which they we re subjected under their ralere, roes in arms against .authority, and in three days overthrew the King and his Government, and vindica-
tllSe,

ted their right to be geverned as they pleased. (Appian. This event produced a profound impression upon the Eng- lish people. Popular excitement became unboundrd—eveets march quickly. The privileged class became alarmed, and announced their readiness to make concessions to the popu- lar demand. A Reform Bill was introduced into the fieuee of Commons and passed by a great majority. (Applause.) Of course, it was thrown out by the Rouse of Lords, under the leadership of the Duke of Wellington. The , People, exasperated and insulted, seemed bent on imitating the French people. Ultimately, however, a way out of the difficulty was found by creating a number of new peers suffi- ment to quell the resistance of the obstructive., and tl-.- - "Iron Duke " had to bend before the irresistible logic of events. (Applause.) Amid rejoicing each as was never witnessed before in England, the Government of the people by the people for the people was settled for ever. (Ap- plause.) The passing of the Reform Bill of 1932 stood eat as one of the land marks in English history. Tie newly - elected members realised the situation at ones, felt tla • pressure of public- opinion behind them, and set to work to, remove the heavy burdens and let the oppressed go free.- (applause.) One of their first acts was to strike the man- acles from the wriEts If several million slayee, and at art [immense cost •f treasure enfranchised tbern in the brother- hood of mei" (Applause.) Was it not fitting that the. newly-emancipated should become emancipators? and that through their representatives they should wipe from Eng- land's escutcheon the foul blot of slavery, reassert the prin- ciple of the brotherhood of men, and thus ley the foundation. of those grand and far-reaching reforms of which the abo- lition of slavery Was the herald. (Applause.) Another reform specially calculated to benefit the working classes was posed into law. By an old Act of Parliament work. men were forbidden to combine for the purpose of obtaining better wages. This Act made the position of the labourer one of servitude to his employer. Public opinion demanded the repeal of this unjust law, and this WAS done, and the era of trades unions flawned. (Applause.) The homes of labour for women and children were curtailed. The employment of young children under nice years was forbidden. Women were forbidden to work in coal mines, and Government in- spectors were appointed to see that these beneficial reforms were carried out. By the Test Act Rmien Catholics and Nonconformist were debarred from holding office in the State, but tbe reformed House of Cominoas cleared this law from the statute book, and consigned it to the limbo of Tory curiosities. (Laughter and applause.) Another reform to which they put their hands was that of educating th 3 people. Tire upper classes had a profound distrust of the people, and knowing that knowledge was power, feared that the edueation of the poor would be attended with lament- able results and that the. newly-enfranchised, intoxiceted with their newly-acquired rights, would be playing lat skittles with crowns and thrones. The grant for &fact- tlon was merle, sctioels were opened, and increased eduei- Lion had brought increased stability to the throne and con- stitution. (Applause.) Then came the repeal of the News- paper Tax. The fetters on the Pre.e were removed, and it went forth on its beneficient mission, ?mattering intelligence a. nd.biessings aim:mast the nations exposing eiror, falsehood, injustice, and giving voice to the boundless aspirations of the people. (Applause.) These reforms, however, valuable as they were, would have been incomplete se long as the iniquitous corn laws passed in the intereste of landlords In 1815 remained in force, for after all the fooe question holds , a foremost position in the affairs of this life. Public at- , tentio,n Was called to this important matter by Richard Cob- den,—(applause)—John Bright,—(applause)—end others; and under their instruction and guidance the nevi° soon learned that their bread was heavily taxed in order that the rich man might grow richer. .Smarting under an intolerable grievance, and conscious of the justness of their cause, the people banded together for the removal of this law, and the House of Commons, under the leadership of Sir R. Peel,—(applause)—abolished the corn laws by a triumphant majority. (Applause.) The Duke of Welling- ton advised the Rouse of Lords, anxioua as usual to throw out the bill, to accept the inevitable. “You cannot "he said "dislike the bill more than I do, but we must all vote for it." They would again hear language like that in the Rouse of Lords before long. (Applause.) In the year 1842, about 1,200 articles were taxed at British ports. New there were less than 20. (Hear, hear.) The restrietionq which existed on our commerce had been removed one after another. These measures, which had netrly all been opposed by the Tories, had had the effect of cheapening the necessaries of life, placing within the reach of the people luxuries to which our forefathers were al- together strangers, and instead of national decoy and ruin we had national vigour, and security, and prosperity such' as the most sanguine of our ancestors never dreamt of. (Ap- plause.) Our foreign commerce in 1846—imports and ex- ports—amounted to £134,000,000, now it was near £800,000,000. (Applause.) Sash were a few of the bene- fits arising out of the Reform Bill of 1832. Whilst these legislative enactments were in agitation, the moral and in- tellectual improvement of the people was grawing apace. The energies ef the Press were being largely increased, cheep ant wholesome literature was being scattered broadcast on the land, habits of thrift and frugality were being formed; savings banks, co-operative societies, and building socsocietiesties were multiptied, and the science of politics and of political economy were being studied; mechanics inatitations, public libraries, and other educational institutions were on the in- crease, and amid the c anges of party government the people steadily pursued the path of advancement and pro- gress. Mr. Disraeli brought in a Reform Bill in 1859, bat the concessions made were se miserably small that the Rouse of Commons rejected it with contempt, and a dui- solution took place. Mr. Gladstone—(applause) next in- troduced a Reform Bill, in which lue proposed lowering the II franchise to £l4 rental in the counties and £7 in the I boroughs. The natural enemies of reform, the Tories, were I up in arms again, and the wolf cry was raised once more. IThe Bill was violently opposed by Mr. Disraeli, who de- scribed it as revolutionary. Mr. Gladstone was defeated and resigned, and then the man who had described the 4114 and £7 franchise as revolutionary brought in ik bill giving a £l2 franchise to the counties and household suffrage to the boroughs. The bll passed, and another great victory on behalf of the cause of popular rights was registered on the statute book. What a marvellous revolu- tion, and hew peacefully effected! (Applause ) In 1830 : tbe people powerless; to-day all powerful. The eyes of the members of the Howse of Commons no Longer tnrued tett , catch the nod of the great landowner, but their ears were open to catch the whispers of the public, whose intlaenca ware felt in every division in the House of Commons. (Ap- plause.) The lecturer then referred to the Ed ucation.Act, , the dieestablishinent of the Irish Church, and the abolui.tra i of purchase in the army by Mr. Gladstoriee Government, arid observed that the list of reforms he had given by o 0 1 means exhausted the long catalogue of beneficent reform inaugurated and carried by the great Liberal party. The Bankruptcy Act, the Employers' Liability Act, and the Corrupt Practices Act all aimed at consolidating and extend- lug England's greatness and promoting the welfare of het, people. (Applause.) But great as had been the triumphs' of the Liberal party their work was not yet finished. In the- sphere of law of commerce, and of agriculture there- were wrongs to be righted, grievances and anomalies to be swept away; and above all, and preparatory to the accom- -1 plishment of these, there was the enfranchisement of mil- lions who were unrepresented and without a veice in the country's government. But the hour of their enfranchise- ment drew near—nay it had come, and with the hour the man. (Applause.) The tree of privilege WAS doomed to fall. Already the axe was laid to the root of the tree, and under the stalwart blows of the woodman it quivers to the fall. As of yore ihe the privileged class. alarmed and filled with forebodinge of coming evils, cried," Woodman, spare that tree. It's lumens 1 fruit has often regaled our appetite, and under it's shelter fwe have been screened from a thousand ills that have scourged our fellows. Oh spare that tree." But he heeded them not. Stroke after stroke fell at its root, and between 1 the woodman's blows, there came borne on every breeze, the Mandate of the people "Cut it down. Cut it down." (Ap- plause.) That mandate would be obeyed, and when it fell the air would resound with the jubilant exclamations of a free, virtuous, intelligent, and loyal people. God speed the day ! (Loud applause) Mr. Amigo:omen Moved a beady vote of thanks to Mr. kniveton for his eloquent address. Mr. F. .1. NORMAN seconded the motion in a lengthy speech, and it was carried with acclamation. Mr. IC:morrow replied, and proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman for presiding. It was seconded by Mr. G. BELLAMY, and carried. meeting then terminated.

_ THE LIBERAL*, DEMONSTRLTION AT SABLES ['OWN. • 81r,—In your report of the speech made by me at the Liberal demonstration, at Earlagoiro, minim 19th last., I am represented as having stated "that it was p ,ssible to increase the food supply of this country by £3000,000 per annum—between 50 and 100 per cent." vr hat I did say was, "that the annual produce from agriculture in this country was estimated at £300,000,000,and that according to the best authorities this could be increased by 50 to 100 per cent. I farther contended that this incre &se would be rea- lised if the c.indition of the ovrnerehip and tenure of land were so altered as to give security to all concerned for a full return on improvements eff,cted." I should not have troubled you with this correction, bat holding, as I do, the somewhat representative position of hon, secretary of the National Reform Ullik,l7, I am bound hi consider that organ- isation. By insertinz, this in your next issue you will much oblige, yours faithfully, R. C. RICHARDS. Ellershe, Huyton, March 24th, 1884.

PERAMBULATORS We THE FOOTPATH. Sir,—Tbere appears to be considerable indignation amongst many of our townspeople (and I think rightly so) owing to the great activity displayed by our policemen in compelling people to wneel their perambulators in the Street, instead of on the foothpath. Ido not in any way blame the" gentlemen in blue" for carrying out waat are no doubt their histinctione, but I certainly think the law (whoever may have instituted it) a very unwise one, and One that cannot fail," if strictly carried out," to end in dis- aster. Warrington of all places,' considering its streets are so narrow," ought to be one of the last to carry out a law of this description. I should not have troubled you with a letter upon this subject had it not been that the matter was brought forcibly bet or use this morning. A lady who was evidently desirous of obeying the powers that be, was wheeling her perambulator up Bridge-street, and was only within a trifle of laving run olio., barely being able to draw the machine on to the footpath. when a carriage drawn by a spirited horse rushed past. When a serious accident hap- pens it will be too late to take the matter up, and I feel sure there are many who share the opinion that the lives and limbs of both children and parents are too valuable to be risked in dodging about amongst the carts and carriages which, espieially on market days, crowd our narrow stree,s. —Yours, G. J. B.

CHURCH NISTORV: A. SKETCH. Dear Sir,—A One) wider the above heading appeared in the Examiner of Saturday last, and the object of the writer seems to be to prove that those that preached the Gospel in Britain in the 2uei and 3rd centwies were not sent by the power of the Roman See. And be also says that the Church of England of to-day is a continuation of the churches of *the earliest ages. lie peaks about the Gospel being preached in those times, but he does not say who preached the Gos- pel. He mentioned the wife Aulus Plantias, and also Pudens and his wife, who was a British convert. But he has not a word to say about their son St. Timothens, who had been ordained a priest by Pope Pins the let, and sent to teach the faith in Britain. St. Marcellus, a Britain by birth, and after- wards bishop of Treves, had also preached the Gospel to his countrymen. King Lucius, who was the first Christian king in Britain, deputed two of his subjects, named Eluan and Meduan, to St Eleutherius (who bad lately succeeded .Si. Suter in St. Peter's chair) entreating him that he and his subjects might be instructed in the Christian religion. Upon this the Pope immediately despatched certain holy men thither, viz, Fogatius and Damianua, with letters which are yet extant. Fugatius and Damianus returned with the British envoys, akdrian and Elnan, and they in- structed and baptised the king and queen. Many theueands of the people flocked round in crowds to follow their sove- reign's example. This happened in the year 183 Tnree years after their arrival the holy prelates. Fugatius and Darnianue, went back to Rome, as Matthew of Westminster relates, and reported to Eleutherins the success of their ralesion. Eleutherius approved of all they bad done, and sent them back, with many °there, whose names and acts are recorded by St. Glides, a British historian, in his book of the victory of Aurelius Ambrosias. Great Britain had thus the honour of being governed by the first Christian king. This faith, as the venerable Bede and all ancient writers unanimously affirm, she received from the Roman See, and preserved in- violate till the Saxon conquest. When St. Austin came to Britain be was sent by Pope Gregory to spread the faith of Christ a second lime over the idolatrous land of Britain. The writer of this ketch, after damning St. Austin with faint praise, has the presumption to say that tits mission was not a nieces,- With candour Mr. Collier writes of St. Austin, that he avos engaged in a glorious undertaking, and was blessed with wonderful success; that he converted the kingdom of Kent by the strength of his own conduct and miracles. The genuine works of the fathers who lived in the fourth age faithfully unfold the self-same doctrines which the Catholic Church has invariably believed and taught through every subsequent age to the present—viz., the unity and trinity of God, the incarnation and divinity of the co-eternal Son of God, the divinity of the Holy Ghost, the pure oblation of the Mass, the real presence, auricular confession, the invocation of the tiainta, prayers for the faithful departed, the merit of fasting, and practise of the three religious vows of voluntary poverty, chastity, and obedience. Now, I want to know if the Protestant Church of to-day teach these doctrines, if not, how can she I be called a continuation of the Church of the early ages? The writer of this aketch seems to have followed in the font- , steps of the centuriators of Madgeburgh, four devoted enemies of Rome. They have asserted on their own credit that groat Britain never received her faith from Route, but from J.rueatem or from Greece, or from some oriental teachers independent of and unconnected with the Roman See. The assertion, though destitute of proof, has been loudly echoed by their anti-Catholic brethren of England, by Matthew Parker, by the Apostee Bale, Francis Good- win, John Speed, and other cisalpioe favourers of schism. To establish a fact of such importance, and at such a dis- tance of time, when all the world was preposeessed with a contrary opinion, it was incumbent on them (and the writer of this sketch of Church history) to adduce positive and undeniable evidence for its support. Title they have not done, whence we may fairly conclude they could ma. On no authentic record and in no ancient writer does it appear. nor dare they determine from what particular country these pretended oriental teachers came, at what time they came, by what name they were known, and by whom they were sent.—Yonra respectfully, JOHN MANNISON. Warrington, March 25th.

side-issues whilst leaving the central questions untouched." ' I am astonished that Mr. Peers above anyone should have made each an accusition considering the way in which he " peddled around" my request that he should give us the Act or Acts of Parliameutby which the Church of England was established. Mr. Peers also implies that the aforesaid correspondents lack boldness, and, "to enable some bolder spirit to step forward" he says he again asks an answer to his three questions, two of whicb, at least, I may say were sufaciently answered by the short sketch of church history sent you last week. Mr. Peers, I euppose, by striking us out of the list for want of boldness and retaining his position claims some amount of that virtue. To my mind, sir, when boldness assumes the character which Mr. Peers has displayed in making statements in support of which be ham no proof it should be called " im- prudence." For a email amount of knowledge of the sub- ject upoe which he has had tha "boldness" to address you would have shown him that the Church of England was not established by Henry VIII, or any other such exquisite person. Therefore, so far as lam concerned, Mr. Peers is quite welcome to claim this particular kind of boldne.as all. to himself. Just a word as to his queries, and I have done. The first two, as I have before stated, have been answered. The third I will now deal with. It is this:—" 3. Could not a secular Parliament be better employed than attemp- ting to regelate the internal affairs of the Church ?" In the first place I say emphatically, no. I believe with a great writer upon this subject that "no Christian statesman can fail to regard, as the true and lasting object of society, the promotion of man's present and future happiness, and in so doing the glory of his Maker. Our rulers should regard the State as re- ligion regards an individual, as having temporal,' subordinate to eternal interests, with corresponding duties, motives, and objects." "In a Christian commonwealth," says Edmund Burke, "the Church and the State are one and the same thing, being different integral parts of the same whole. Religion is so far from being out of the pro- vince, or duty of a Christian magistrate, that it is, and it ought to be, not only his c ire, but the principal thing in his care; because it is one of the great bonds of human society, and its object the supreme good,—the ultimate end and object of man himself." Agate, as to Parliament regu- lating the internal affairs of the Church of England, does she not regulate tha internal affairs of any other religious body? Decidedly:; if a minister of a Nonconformist chapel preach a doctrine at variance with the trust deeds, and those connected with the chapel chose to raise the question I do not say they always do, because it was rather the boast of the president a while ago, at the annual meeting of the Con- gregational Union in Yorkshire, that half the ministers of that denomination were preaching doctrines at variance with the trust deeds of their chapels, and that if they must require conformation to the trust deeds they would empty their pulpits of half their best men; but still we have even seen within the last year or two where divisions had arisen amongst them upon questions of doctrine—that the law had been appealed to just as it would be in the case of a clergy- man of the Church of Eogland. Dissenting commnnities are just as much State-governed as the Church of England is, and they hive just as mach St de protection. I hope that this rather lengthy answer may be sufficient for Mr. Peers.—Yours, (E.

CHURCH HISTORY: A SKETCH. (Continued.) Having, as I conceive, adduced sufficient evidence to show as nearly as possible the early establishment of the Church of England in this country, circurn•tances will not permit me to examine the doctrinal development of the corruption of the Church of Rome which had been going on apace4uring several centuries preceding Henry VIII.'s accession. With the exception of till dogma of the Im- maculate Conception, promulgated in 1854, we may say generally, without being far from the truth, that the modern , errors of the Church of Home reached their final form about ' the year 1500, or, to be a little more precise, that the Church of Rome acquired Its final and most finished state of cwruption in the year 1563, the date of the end of the Council of Trent. One by one errors of doctrine and prac- tice had been cmcoctd by men and adopted by Popes as articles of faith. Musheim thus deals with this notorious fact : Nearly all the Roman Pontiffs likewise added simething new to the ancient ceremonies. as if they had supposed thst no one could teach Christianity with success unless he could de- light a Christian assembly with strange shows and mummery. Thme rites and usages were. In the time of 'Charlemagne, pro- pagated from Rome among the other Lain Churches, for the arrtgance of the Pontiffs would not suffer any of them [the Churches] to deviate from the Roman usage. (Institutes of Eccl Hist. cent. vii. pt. 2, ch. lv.§ 1, trans Murdock, Lond. 1859.)

Mani, of these errors had been grafted into the Church of England. What happened under Henry VIII. was, that firat one and then another of these errors was got rid of. That the king, when he began his anti-papal agitation, ex- pected, or intended, or even desired, the nation and Church to be purged of these errors, I do not b 3 any means assert ; all that came about step by step, and accidentally, as some might say—but, as I prefer to put it, by the overruling Pro- vidence of God. To bring in here what belongs to this Dart of my story would be simply to transcribe half-a-dozen pages from any moderately good history of England. I will, therefore, he very brief in reminding you that the Re- formation, so far as Henry VIII. was concerned, was simply, as the word literally states, a re-formation." You know that we talk of a corneany of soldiers " forming " and " reforming " their • ranks. It is simply a matter of change of position ; the same sol- diers are present after the process is over, as before it began. So with the Church : the Church after the Reformation is one with the Church before the Reformation. "But what is the meaning of the word Reformation,' it surely implies the previous existence of the thing reformed, not the creation of something new; as, for intrance, when the Reform Act of 1832 is spoken of, it is implied that Par- liament existed before'in an unreformed state, not that it was then first introduced as a factor into English politics. No Acts of Parliament can be cited which (1) established at any time the Church of England; or (2) transferred the buildings and emoluments from Roman Catholics to Pro- testants; as, for example, such Acts as those of 1560 and 1690, with respect to Scotland, whereby the Presbyterian Kirk obtaired is status and endowments "—(Elore, Eigh- teenth Centuries, p. 603.) The learned Dissenting writer, Toulmin Smith, a lawyer of great experience in ecclesias- tical matters, illustrated very forcibly the points I have just been advancing. in his evidence before the Lords Committee on Church Rates, in 1859.

[Q 510.] 'Do you oonsider the pre6ent Church and the Chu oh before the Reformation as• identical ?"—" Undoubted- i7 ..—{Q. 5.5 t ] "Are you aware that the Chnrch, at what ii os.lled the Retort...a:don, professed and believed itarlf to be the same Church with that of the preceding age, only laying aside cer sin mrdizval aecretiens?"—"So I have always under- ' stood."—[Q. 555 ] " So,ln point of tact Re pr.-V-6'6ton was not to be a new Chu. ch. but to be the old receiver of the old en- dowments ?"—" That I understood "—(Q 555] And that they hold the doctrines of the orig Thai receivers ?"—" That I understand to be the case; but on such topics I must ep eak wth great diffidence."—(Q. 557.] "Are you, therefore, aware that the Roman Cathoqc body is not con,iderei by the mem- bers of the t hurch of England the sap ments of the old Onurch of England. but is a branch of a foreign Church which has settled in this cauntry ?'—" So I understand, and the records I have qu attd go far to prove it " Another able writer puts the matter in this form . _

We might as well say that Israel was not the same people after being delivered from Egyptian bon.-age--that Beaman the Syrian was not the same person after e was cleanse t from his lesrose—or that the Jewish Church was nut the saute after she was delivered from liabylonlsh eeptivity—as to sae that the Chn.cl of England lost her identity at the ite'ormatlon as the ancieat Churlh of this 'ant, because. Indeed, she nur fled her- self from e tor, a,serted her freedom from all forego ju iedic- diction and threw ..ff the gal log fe-ters nf 11.mleh hondage.— (The Church of England in her Fourfold ATpec% .4nd ed. p. 59.) - • - • • - - -

This will bring my short eketch to a close. I hope I have shown therein that the Church of England was not estab- lished by Act or Acts of ParliArnent either "in the reign of Henry Vlll.,when that monarch was constituted its head," to use Mr. Peers' words, or in the reign of any other monarch. Bat that the Church of England was established and endowed by its own inherent growth centuries before Parliament existed in England. Does Mr. Peers know that the "royal supremicy " was not a new claim set up by Henry VIII.. for it is abundantly clear in history that" the princlples wbich nourished it were firmly planted in the roots of the English constitution, which, itself slowly built up, was but a reflex of the character and genius of the people" (Brooke)? In the words of Mr. Gladstone, and of the poet! will cenclude:—" Take the Church of England out of the History of England, and the History of England becomes a chaos without order, without life, and without meaning." Therefore .• Let no rude hand sever 7 he link.; that corns between Our dear old courch of England, The altar, and our Q teen."

Aw OLD OIFFENDER.—Richard McCormick, a young man who is a fuquent occupant of the prisoner's box, was on Tuesday char.4ed at the St. Helene Police Court with having been drunk and disorderly and also with having aseaulred P.C. STRUGGLE WITH A FOWL STRALBR.—ThOMSB GOTDAT and Michael McGarry, apparently tramps, were on Monday charged at the Sr. Helens Pollee Court with having stolen four towls, the property of James Ranson, farmer, Windle, on Saturday last.—P.S. Smith said that about one o'clock on Saturday morning he was on duty near Mr. Ranson' farm when he heard some fowls cackling. He went in the direction of the farm, and on getting there met the two prisoners coming away from the premises, Cromer carrying something in his hand. Gorner at (ince got hold of witness and cried out to his companion, " Come on, Jim, there is only one." Witness blew his whistle, and McGarry then ran away. Garner, however, continued to struggle for about 20 minutes before witness succeeded in handcuffing him. —Garner (interrupting): "I would have struggled thou, too, if I bad net been drunk."-:-McGarry was afterwards ap- prehended at a lodging-house on Greenbank by P.C. Cottam. Oct the way to the station he said, "If I had not acted the coward and ran away you would not have got off so easy.— Both prisoners were committed far trial.—The same pri- soners were charged with having stolen three ducks, the pro- perty of Mr. Bold, farmer, Windle. After Gorner's arrest by P.S. Smith he pointed out a ditch where he said there were some ducks which he had stolen c.mcealed. The ducks were found covered with some hey.—The prisoners were also committed on this charge. THE STORING OF EXPLOSIVES : A S. HELENS ALDER- MAN FlNED.—Alderman James Hadley. colliery proprieto,, at St. Helens, was on Monday charged at the St. Helens Polio I Court, before Messrs. T. Pilkington and C. Gamble, with fear offences under the Explosives Act —Superinten- dent Johnston said that on the 12th init. he accompanied Colonel Ford, one of Her Majesty's inspectors, on a visit te the powder store kept hy Mr. Radtey for his works at But- ton Hew b, and the inspector directed him to lay four in- formations against Mr. Ridley. The first information was on the ground Out the interior of the store was not lined; the second for not having a lightning conductor; the third for not having a notice posted outside the store; and, another for keeping gunpowder in an'anthorised place. The gunpowder was kept in a room at the end of the stores in, the colliery yard. There were in it two casks of 1001b5..niis opened; one cok of 100Ibs. that had been opened; and another cask, out of which there had been a good deal need, only about 15Ms. being left. Those quantities combined made 3151b5. of powder kept where only 3011,5. WAS legally allowed to b! kept, an excess of 2851h5. The shed was not a good one to have powder in at all.-Mr. J. 0. Swift,who ap- peared on behalf of the defendant, said that everything had been done in connection with the store that the defendant knew to be necessary. The store had been visited by In- spector Wood, and all the suggestions be made bad been cirried out —The Bench considered that in regard to each of the first three informations a nominal fine of 103 and costs would meet the case, but with regard to the fourth charge, that of keePing a large quantity of powder in an irepropee place, they thought that more serious, and would inflict a fine of £5 and costs.—The Roughdales Fire Clay having ti Comp,o tha an ty t hLei fm. tut rett, w chargee r e si mi ni 1 at rhl iys case h aer gweda swf oi trh ntohte excep- fiprocs,poerf Ist: esanadn dc costs tost hini each in a ch go wchasicebwton iinipnotsoetdh.e store.—A.

STEALING Bluer AT ASIITON.—James Stoop, Bryn Cross, Park-lane, WAS charged at the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, with stealing 19Iba of beef, on the 22nd inst., the property of Thomas Booth.—Ellen Booth said the beef and handkerchief produced belonged to her husband and the beef was worth 108. 3d. The meat was bought on Saturday night, and she went to the Red Lion public-house to meet her husband. She put the beef on the table. She had occasion to go out about ten o'clock, and when she left the prisoner was in the house. She returned a short time afterwards, and missed the bundle coutaining the beef. She told P.C. Barber, and he brought the prisoner back to the inn with the beef in his possession.—Catharine Hughes, wife of William Hughes, Park-lane, said she saw the defen- dent take the bundle oat of the Red Lion Inn, and she told the last witness what she had seen.—P.C. Barber, stationed at Park-lane, said the prisoner passed him near the Red Liou and he had the bundle produced with him. The defendant went towards his own home.- The first witness made a com- plaint to him, and he followed the defendant and asked what be had got in the bundle.• lie said it was beef which be- longed to him, and he was taking it borne. He took him back to the public-house, and the first witness said the bundle %las hers. He then charged him with stealing the beef, and the prisoner seid, "Nonsense. I did not steal it."— Prisoner said he was taking the beef to Booth's house.— Police-constable Barber raid the defendant was going in the (Weal m of his own home when be saw him.—etoop was fined 20s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. • CADISEEAD. I ADDRESS ON Theteer.—The Wesleyan minister of Cadis- . head on Monday last from half-past twelve to one o'clock addressed a large gathering of workpeople in the cutting shop of Mr. P. Johnson, on ' Thrift." The meeting was well attended and the address proved deeply interesting. Such addresses are calculated to be of great benefit to the people. Tux SUNDAY CLOSING MOVEMENT. The Wesleyan quarterly meeting el the Cadishead circuit on Monday week adopted a petition to the House of Commons praying for the closing of public-houses on Sundays. The Chairman of the meeting forwarded the same to the Marquis of Hartington, requesting him t 3 present it to the House. The chairman has received an answer through his lordship's secretary, , stating "that his lordship will present the petition forwarded to the House of Commons respecting the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday." Sr. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION AT HOT, DORMS.— rho branch of the St. John Ambulance Associa- tion, established at Golborne some time ago, is still pro- gressing. There are a goodly number of both lady and gentleman students, who are taught by Dr. Mapei. Con- sidering that the association is established to educate the people in the rendering of aid in accidents of almost daily occurrence, it is one well worthy the support of all. Dr. Mapei gives th,o lectures and andresees free of charge, and he is deserving of every support for his kindness. The classes, which are also free, meet every Tuesday evening in St. Thomas's School, those for ladies and gentlemen meet. lug on alternate Tuesdays. SAD ACCIDENT AT HOLBORN'S COLLI ART .—On Tuesday morning, a see accident occurred to a young man named PAW Brown, residing In Churchestreet, Golborne, and em- ployed as a drawer at the premises of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. Brown was engaged in pushing a loaded waggon along one of the brows when he slipped and fell. The wazgon ran back a little and severely injured Brown on ' the back and legs. Several pereons immediately went to his aesistance,and he was conveyed to the pit mouth and carried home on a stretcher. Among the persons who rendered help were Messrs. S. Collier, P. Yates, Walmsley, and Bate, members of the St. John Ambulance Association. The poor fellow has since been attended by Dr. Mapei, and he istradually recovering from the effect of his accident. HAYDOCK. SERVICE OF SONG AT HARDOCE.—Under the auspices of the Hayduck Wesleyan Band of Hope Society., a service of sacred song, entitled "The Lord's Lilies," was rendered in the Weeleyan schoolroom by the choir of the Earleetown ' Gospel Mis.iion. There was a pretty large attendadce, and the efforts of the choir gave every satisfaction. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Fairhurst, who in opening the meeting expressed the great pleasure it gave him to see his Earlestown friends, and said he hoped all present would spend a very pleasant and enjoyable night. The service of song was then proceeded with, Mr. John Clarke, of Eerles- town, officiating as reader. The choir gave the musical selections in an exc dlent manner; Mr. T. Birks accompanied , on the harmonium, whilst the Eartestown Gospel Mission string bend creditably fulfilled their parts under the leader- ,1 ship of Mr. G. Birke. Mr. J Biltinge afterwards moved a hearty vote of thanks to the E itlestown choir and friends; observing that he hid enjoyed the service very Much, and he thought every one to that room had also enjoyed it. The motion was seconded by Mr. G. Raxendale, who re- marked that they were greatly indebted to the visitors for the able manner in which they had rendered the service of song. The motion Was heartily carried, and Mr. John Clarke suitably acknowledged the compliment, after which the proceedings concluded. HOUGHTON GREEN. PRESENTATION AT HITYTON QUARRY.—An interesting gathering took place on Tuesday evening, in the Iron Church Mission School, for the purpose of presenting Mr. J. L. Medea with a Bible and an address. Mr. By. Kilshaw occupiod the chair, and the room was well filled. Miss Lea presided at the harmonium. The Chairman said he felt it a privilege to preside on the occasion, met as they were to give honour whero honour was due, namel-y, to John L. , Morice, who for nearly nine years had been their superin- tendent. Mr. Thomas Rimmer ni4cle the presentation and read the address. He explained that the 'presmtation was made by the teachers, scholars, and friends to Mr. Minion on his retirement from the superintendency of their Misiion Schools. Be referred in eulogistic terms to the services rendered lty Mr. Morice, and said it was mainly owing to his efforts that the iron church was erected. He wished him long life to work still amongst them. The Bible and ad- dress were then beaded to Mr. Morice, who feelisgly re- sponded to the kind remirks, and thanked there for the handsome present made to him. He said that thou4h he was retiring from the position he had held he was not leaving them, and he intended to work still in the neigh- bourhood. The Bible was one of Bagster's comprehensive, largest edition, and contained the fcliowing inscription, illuminated Presented to John L. Morice upon his re- signation of the office of superintendent of the Huyton Quarry Iron Mission Church Sunday School, by the teachers, scholars, and friends, as a token of their high esteem and love for his faithful and zealous labours for a period of nearly nine years." (Numbers vi., 24, 25, 26.) Miss Cassanave presented Mr. Morice with a list of the sub- scribers, and the meeting closed with votes of thanks to the chairman, ladies, and gentlemen concerned.

LYNNE (MID-CHESIIIRE) LIBERAL ASSOCIATION The following resolutions were unanimously adop,ed at a full meeting of she General Committee of the above association, held on Tuesday evening:—" That the members of this as- sociation desire to express : (1) 'Their unabated confidence in Her Majesty's Government, and in the main principles of the policy they are pursuing, whether at home or Abroad.' (2) The strong and rismg indignation with which they view the purely obstructive tactics resorted to mauy members of the Opposition, whereby not only the best in- terests of the people are set at naught, but the credit of the House of Commons as an institution is eudangered." the members of this association desire to express their hearty admiration of Mr. Chamberlain's efforts to lessen the risks to which many of their sea-going follow-countrymen are so wantonly exposed, and their hope that he may so triumph over interested obstruction as to see the Merchant Shipping Bill become law in the course of the present session."

RATBPAyEne MESTING.:=A—n-ie—e-ting of the ratepayers of the township of Penketh was held on Monday evening, at the Red Lion Inn, Mr. B. Hobson being elected chairman. There were present Messrs. C. E. Randall, W. Green, &t.—The accounts were audited, and a report presented, which was accepted. A rate of Is 3d in the £ was made for the next half year; an incidental rate of id in the £ was also hid. The followiag were nominated as overseers :—Messrs. Henry Hughes, James Turner, Jonas Foster. B. Hobson, W. Hankinson, R. Boardman, P. Board- man, A. Bennett, E. Cross, and J. Jackson, Mather, Deintith, Ashley, and Brime- low (assistant overseer).—On the motion of Mr. Houghton, seconded by Mr. Mather, Mr. Jenkins Was voted to the chair. The Chairman read the notice convening the meeting, and the minutes of the previous meeting, and afterwards a statement of the accounts of the overseers for the past year, which was approved and unanimously passed, on the motion of Mr. Jackson, seconded by Mr. Mather.— Mr. Jackson moved, and Mr. Daintith seconded, that Mr. Houghton and Mr. Mstber be appointed overseers for the ensuing year, and the motion was cirried unanimously.— Mr. Houghton moved, and Mr. Mather seconded, that Mr. William Royston be re-elected waywarden for the ensuing year. which was also carried unanimously.—Mr. Thomas Ashley and Mr. John Lythgoe were unanimously appointed burley-men for the ensuing year, on the motion of Mr. Houghton, seconded by Mr. Daintith.—Mr. Jackson moved, and Mr. Daintith seconded, that Mr. Britnelow be re-ap- pointed assistant overseer for the ensuing year at a salary of £2B per annum, which was carried, only one voting against the motion.—The Chairman having read the minutes of the meeting, and ignited them, Mr. Houghton moved, and Mr. Daintith secionded.that a hearty vote of thanks be given to the chairman, which was unanimously carried, and the proceedings terminated. RAINFORD. ALLSCHED CRTAILTY TO A CAT.—M*ry Lydiatt, of Rain. ford, was, en Monday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court, with having cruelly ill-treated a cat belonging te a neighbour named Margaret Fletcher.—Mr. Thomas pro- secuted, and Mr. Swift defended.—Mrs. Fletcher stated that on the 3rd inst. she Was in her backyard and saw the defen- dant with a large stink in her hand going up and down her yard striking something. She watched defendant a nhort time, and SAW the latter lift up the cat and put it on a wall. The cat could not get off the wall and defendant con- sequently knocked it off. Mrs. Fletcher caupd it to be carried into her house, but it died the next day.—Bernard Lockwood, an officer of the R S P.C.A., from Liverpool, said ha bad exhumed the cat after it Was buried, and found bruises upon its body which might have been caused by a stick, and would probably cause its death.—ln defence it was denied that the defendant had ill-used the cat, and it was mentioned that there had several Cats died in a similar manner at Rtinford recently.—The Bench considered that there was not sufficient evidence to justify a conviction.— The case was accordingly dismissed.

RAINIIILL ASYLUM, According to the report of the County Lunatic Asylums, only 159 patients have b.-ten ad- mitted during the past year, the average num er of daily residents being 694. Fewer patients had been admitted, and the average number resident had been less than in previous years, the explanation being that there had been more ac- commodation is the other asylums in the county. There had been 72 patients discharged as "recovered '-" one of those "recovered" had since been admitted, and 18 had been discharged to the care of friends, to other asylums, or to workhouses; 78> patients had died, and one coroner's in- quest had been held. The balance-sheet for the year showed the total receipts £75,86.4 lie 2.1, and there WAS a balance of £I,IM Os sd. RIXTON. WESLEYAN SCHOOL Exeraisa:rtort.—The Government examination of the Wesleyan day school of Rixton was held on Tu.sday. The children were thoroughly and effi- ciently examined in the different branches required by the code by Mr. Keyes, one of the sub-inspectors of the district. The children presented a very creditable appearance, and some of them did exceedingly well in some of the more ad- vancot branches. Up,n the whole the sewing of the girls was excet duigly neat and accurate. Tile inspector appeared to he gratified with the progress of the school daring the year. A good report is expected. THE CHURCH DISPUTE AT EARLES- TOWN., ANOTEIEIt tIikREHITABLE SCENE. The dispute at St. John's Church, Earlestown, betweeii the vicar (the Rev. F. R. Matthews) and the organist (Mr. H. J. Carman), gave rise to another discreditable scene on Sunday last. The morning service was well attended, and the choir were also in their usual places. Mr. Duman oc- cupied a seat amongst the choir. Orring to the absence of the curate (the Rev. H. E. Smith), who was officiating ' elsewhere, the only clergyman present was the vicar. As soon as the service commenced it was evident that a recon- I dilation had not been effected, for the choir did not take the least part in the service. lhe majority of the congrega- tion, too, appeared indisposed to join in the responses, but a few did so. As the service proceeded the responses became 1 more audible. No hymns were given out by the vicar, and constqa;ntly there was not the least attempt at singing, nor was the organ p'ayed. When Mr. Matthews entered the pulpit to preach many persons left the church, including several members of the choir. When the com- motion had subsided the vicar, before proceeding with his sermon, said : Perhaps I ought to say one or two words before I proceed with the sermon— and they shall be very few as I never like to ape tk any- thing unless it is part of the sermon. But what I have to say is simply this, that it is not my fault that we have no singing bete to day. The rev, gentleman then selected as his text the words "What must Ido to be saved," (Acts XVI., 30th verse), from which he preached. The offertory was afterwards made as usual, but few persons seemed in- clined to give anything. In the evening there was a large congregation. The service partook of the same character as that of the forenoon; but the responses on the part of the congregation were somewhat more audible. The choir did not take any part in the service, and consequently there was no singing, nor were any hymns announced. The Rev. T. R. Matthews (vicar) was again the only clergyman in attendance, and as he entered the pulpit to preach several persons again left the church. No other noteworthy in- cident.oocurred in connection with the service.

On Tu.sday last several of the parties who have been connected with the dispute at St. John's Church, Eartestewn, journeyed to Liverpool in order to have an interview with the Bishop of Liverpool and his solicitors. Among those who proceeded thither were the vicar (the Bev. T. R. Matthews), the Rev. H. E. Smith (curate), Mr. H. J. Dorman (organist), and Mr. B. Corlett and Mr. Slinn (churchwardens). We understand that the Bishop expreseed regret at the sad state of affairs which at present existed in the parish. After hearing Mr. Corlett's statement about the dispute, we believe that gentleman was informed by the Bishop's splicitore that the vicar had sole control over the organ and organist, choir and chancel. and that he (the vicar). bad only acted within his rights in the course of the action he had pursued. Mr. Corlett, however, opposed the contention, and asked for the laws to be read which gave the Vicar that power. The ap- plication was refused, and apparently no definite decision aff.icting the dispute was mime to, neither side surrendering even one portion of their contentions. From some cause or other there was no service held in the Church on Thursday evening. Considerable doubt and uncertainty appears to pill exist among the parishioners as to what the upshot of the regrettable disagreement will be; white many persons are becoming thoroughly disgusted with the matter from beginning to end. Everyone would like to see the dispute settled, but as neither of the contending parties will giv4 way in the least, this much-to-be desired end is apparently as far off as ever..

CHESHIRE FARMERS AND MILK —A meeting of the mem- pEARS' (Signed) LILLLE LANGTRY. leers of the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association took place at Naotwich on Saturday afternoon, and was very largely Seed Everywhere in Tablets and attended. Captain Cotton presided. The secretary of the DEARS' Fails Is. each. association (Mr. George Willis, of Banbury), read a paper "I- on the production of milk. Cheshire farmers, he said, live Larger sizes, lie and 2,6. by the proauction of milk, and yet, he feared, that to be pEARS' honest in the matter be must confess that their knowledge, ' either of the product itself or the conditions affecting its I production, preservation, and management, was not such as ! they had any reason to be proud of. There were, he thought, I many farms in Cheshire on which unprofitable cows are kept, and if farmers would only weed out the unprofitable ones, they would find themselves receiving RS much from 30 good cows as they now realise from 50. In the course of a discussion which followed, the Chairman said he thought the condition of the pasture land upon which their cows fed mast materially affect the production of milk, and he hoped that one result of their turning attention to this subject would be that the landlords of the country would turn their attention more to the draining and manuring of the laud. (Applause )—Mr. Parton expressed doubts as to the capa- bilities of cows to give sena Illy milk sufficient for 7ewt. of cheese, saying it was as mach as farmers could do to get 4cwt.—Mr. Dutton said that a neighbour of his was making 7iewt. of cheese. per year per cow; and Mr. Willis gave an instance where 7cwt. had been made. He did not mean to sty that that was the average for every cow in a large dairy, but since there was such a material difference, great pains should be taken to secure a good breed of milk-pro- ducing animals, for these were the most profitable* to the farmer—Votes of thanks to Mr. Willis and the chairman closed the proceedings.

It seems that on Stturdav afternoon last the child had been sent out on an , errand, and lost half a sovereign belonging to her parents. She was in consmquence afraid to go home herself, but sent her shawl by another little girl. Nothing has since been heard of her,.and although pits of water round the localitf have been Searotied, her body has not been found. On Thursday. we understand, a telegram was received from the Warrington police stating that the girl had been found to be in service at that town. ANNUAL
CONCERT.

Under the auspices of Earlestown— Association Foot- ball Club, a very succaseful and enjoyable concert WAS held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, Eirlestown, on '1 Monday evening. The hall was crowded with an enthusi- astic audience. The vocalists were—Miss Bothwell (New- ton), Miss Burton (Golborne), Miss Rose (Newton), Mr. P. Hastie (Earlestown), Mr. S. Swann (Earlestown), Mr. J. . Owen (Earlestown), and Mr. J. Butcher (Laverppol), ; while humournus selections were given by Mr. J. W. ' Williams (Earlestown) and Mr. Jackson (Galbarne). The'programme opened with a pianoforte solo by Mr. M. Atherton, of Liverpool, which was fairly executed. Mr. S. ! Swans, of Earlestown received a hearty welcome, and a well-earned recall for his song, "Harbour Lights at Sea" (Piusuti). In response he gave "Under the old flag." The song, "Kathleen Mavourneen," was sweetly and impres- sively rendered by Miss Burton, of Golborne, whose efforts were rewarded with an outburst of hearty applause. On being recalled she gave equally well "Sweet dreamland , fame." -After Mr. Butcher, of Liverpsol, had given " The Little Hero" (Barn), Miss Rose, of Newton, was warmly encored for her song, The Bells of London." Ou making her reappearance she gave "The old Lock." Mr. J. Owen ! effectively sang," The Arab's farewell to his Steed" (Block- ley), and was heartily applauded, but did not respond to the eucore. Mr. Jackson, of Golborne, by his humourous selec- tions, created, much enthusiasm. His first song, "The Wooden Leg Brigade," was rendered in an effective manner, , sad in response te the recall he gave " Braunigan's Band." The song "Only an ivy leaf" (G. Wood) was sung by. Miss Bothwell, of Newton, who merited the hearty and enthusiastic commendation. ,of the audience. When recalled the gave " Ebren on the Rhino." Another humorous selection followed, and was given by Mr. J. W. Williams, of Earlestown, who WIS warmly received. He was recalled after singing " Hilde- brand Montrose," and responded with 'Poor Mr. Wright." The second part of the programme was opmed by Mr. Peter Hastie, who met with a mmit sothusiastic reception. T bough suffering from a throat affection, he splendidly rendered Molloy's popular song "Polly," and the applause with which it was greeted was long continued. On appearing a second time, hegave "The Irish emigrant" in an equally effective manner. Mies Burton next gave "The miller and the maid " (Marxials), and was deservedly recalled, where upon she repeated the last verse. Mr. Swann was well re- ceived, and was again encored for the capital style in which he sang Pinsati's " Trusty as steel." A second , warm reception was accorded to Miss Hothwell, who effec- , lively rendered the Scotch piece " thro' the rye," and she was called upon to repeat the Ltat verso as an encore. "The runaway musketeer," a humorous selection ;by Mr. Jackson was given in an amusing manner; WAS also" Why did'i marry Martha Box ?" with which he re- !Tended to the encore. Mr. Butcher was heartily corn. mended for his song "The old brigade " (S. Adams); awl Miss Rose was also warmly applauded for her interpreta- fion Of Summer showers." A song by Mr. J. Owen was most excellently rendered, and he received the commenda- tion of the audience. The programme was then brought to A (nose by Mr. J. W. Williams, who evoked loud outbursts of laughter by hie humorous selections, including a van. trilcquial exhibition.
