.kNEARLESTOWN DOMESTIC SERVANT ATTACKED BY A DOG. AMON FOR DAMAGES. At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before l'r• W. W. Pfoutkes, judge, and a jury, Mary Merrick, •emeatic servant, single woman, residing with her mother at Peel-street, Earlestown, sued to recover damages set down la, 450 for injuries sustained by plaintiff in consequence r4,ber being bitten on January 11th and 23rd by a fierce and 1111I9ohiev008 dog, belonging to and kept by defendant, i .ehard Walton, and for loss and expense thereby occa- atoned, and for medical and other charges and exp tnses 'aid by her."—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Taylor, barrister, Liverpool, for the defendant. , Mr. Swift, in opening the case, said that his client was a li!agle woman and a domestic servant, and was at present t IL,'ving with her mother at Peel-street. Earlestown, cud the ~,,T.endant, Richard Walton, was a ilin4 glass manufacturer, t u 0 resided and carried on business it Crow-lane, Earles- ijw; and it appeared that in January—about New Year's the present year, the plaintiff entered the defend- Service as a general servant. At that time the de- tendant keeping a large dog—either a mastiff, New- leant:Rand, St. Bernard, or some equally large dog—but, Ilafortunately, as it turned out, it was a dog of a very rage disposition. The plaintiff stayed in the house com- tablv until the 11th January. On the evening of that 'layMrs. Walton, wife of the defendant, brought the dog Va the kitchen, and told the plaintiff to give it its supper. 151 dog apparently wanted to go out into the yard, ,nd the th'till let it do so. She let the dog iuto kitchen again, and as she was going about her work it flew at her, and caught and her by. by.the nose, and then bit her under the left eye, N /1 upon the temple. She screamed, and the defendant and tik Walton came into the kitchen, and soothed the plain- end TbeY were good enough to get her upstairs to bed, had eoathe her with water and vinegar, Mr. Walton, who had Well xperience in previous bites, saying that he could do as ,as a doctor. lie told her that he knew what to do, and administered externally whisky and vinegar, and internally whisky and water. However, plaintiff afterwards fainted, and, 43 a matter of fact, Mrs. Walton slept with her that did and the defendant stayed up by her bedside, and they what they could for her. They told her that she bad nothing to be afraid of, and that they would take care that the dog should not injure her any more. They rettinaded her not to let her friends know about the affair, and to remain with them. All went Pretty smoothly until the 23rd of January. On that day the - dog was at home, and the plaintiff was going about her Work in the usual way, when Mrs. Walton told her that she did not feel very well, and that she would go to bed. The Plaintiff assisted Mrs. Walton to bed, and flaw her into bed. Mrs. Walton seemed to have a strong liking for the dog, and to have acquired considerable control over it, and the dog seemed to have taken a strong affection for her. On this occasion Mrs. Walton had the dog upstairs with her, and it was lying dawn on the bed. Mrs. Walton seemed so Proud of this achievement that she called the plaintiff up- Stairs to look at the dog and see hew quietly it was lying on the bed. Plaintiff went downstairs again, and Immediately afterwards Mrs. Walton again rang the bell lor her. Once or twice Mrs. Walton told the dog to bring the plaintiff to her, and it did so quietly by pulling at her dress. Plaintiff did not like this, and went Outside the room „"fi to the landing, and Mrs. Walton sent ""e dog after her. The dog, however, had aParently had enough of it, and made another attack on ile Plaintiff, flew at her, and bit her upon the lip and under weentaw' to consecl wilco of which she bled terribly. She away the next day. On the night when the affair :urred she was attended by Mr. Walton's own doctor, and leer leaving she was attended for nearly a month by Dr. thrdriide at Earlestown, and by his assistant. Those were .injuries for which the plaintiff sued the defendant. She her alined from him damages far the injuries inflicted upon ' by the dog. She would not be able to recover any 11.,Tages unlest he could prove that the defendant knew, or S übstantial reason to know, that the dog was a savage ;ring mischievous one, and therefore he should produce evi- tleioneti to show that the defendant had that knowledge. Ile calf have no &Meaty in showing that, becer se he should the •ive or Rix witnesses who woad say that either they peoniteel•es had been bitten, or that they had seen other 4tor e worried or bitten by this dog. He was satisfied that clute e. hearing the evide,nce the jury would come to the coo- tloolon that the dug was of a vicious and savage dispoei- .othj and whatever control Mrs. Waltonmight have over it, r People had not tke same control. Lie should now e,„B,derice in support of his statement, and the question PlrY to consider wan as to what damages the plaintiff 9 entitled to. Re th en called ties plaintiff, who said that she was now he lig with her mother at Peel-street, E', stown. In the detrie.ll,l x ,og of January of the present year she went as 111,37" e servant to the house of the defendant. eeVer,4 k!i3t a very large dog, which she fed t,tt , &1W0.% On Friday, the 11th of J.nu Ary, between ' :;elev:u o'clock at night, Mrs. Walton brought the I.lt. the kitchen, an I asked witness to It.-ep it there anii • `e Its supper. The dog went into the yard and com-

mewed barking. She went out into the yard, and said, "Pluto, what are you barking at, there's no one there," but she had no sooner got the words out of her mouth than the dog flew at her, put his paws on her shoulder, and bit her across the nose, under the left eye, and on the temple. Wit- ness screamed, and Mr. and Mrs. Walton came to her. She was then bleeding very much from all three bites. Mr. Welton said if she sent for a doctor be would mark bet for life, and that he (Mr. Walton) could do as well for her as the doctor. Defendant said that he was soi ry, and asked her if she was engaged to be married. She replied that she was not, and he said that if she was not, he and Mrs. Wal- ton would try to make her comfortable, aid would give her five guineas at the end of the quarter. She agreed to re- main. On Wednesday, the 23rd, she was ironing in the kitchen, when Mrs. Walton called her upstairs. Mrs. Wal- ton sent the dog. to her when she was upstairs, and it took hold of her dress and pulled her to its mistress. Paving been bitten once, witness told Mrs. Walton that she was frightened, and asked her to call the dog away. Witness went downstairs, and in a few moments she went upstairs again to answer Mrs. VValton's bell. 'The dog was then on the bed, and Mrs. Walton told it to fetch witness to her. Witness went out of the room and closed the door. Mrs. Walton opened the door and let the dog out, and it hither upon the lower lip. Mrs. Walton said, "Oh, the dog has not bit you ?" Witness said, "Oh yes, he has; I can feel and ran downstairs screaming. Wken the defendant came hems in the evening he said that he would poison the dog; he had had enough bother about it and would have no more. Mrs. Walton moaned and cried and said, "Oh, don't poison the dog." Witness felt severe pain from the bites even yet, and she often dreamt that the dog was going to fly at her, in consequence of which she suffered from nervousness and was liable to being suddenly startled. She had since ap- plied far three different situations at Warrington. She should have got one but the application that was made to Mre. Walton for her character was not answered. At the other places where she applied inquiries were made as to the bites, and as to hew she received the marks on her face. She had been under the doctor for some time, had been out of a situation, and had had to have extra nourlshment.—Ms. Taylor thought witness had better allow thejary a closer inspection of the marks on her face. —Mr. Swift: She looks as though she had been erruck with a bottle in a public-house brawl. By Mr. Taylor: I did not put my arms round the dog and try to drag hies from the bed. I was not fond of him,and did not touch him at all. Elizabeth Merrick, widow; mother of the plaintiff, was called to speak to the expense incurred by the plaintiff through being bitten. Plaintiff went to the doctor every day for a fortnight, and every other day for another fort- night. She had to have wine, fresh eggs and milk, and other nourishing food. Before she was bit the plaintiff was very brave, but now she was startled and frightened sud- denly. Jane Banks, domestic servant at 3, Stanley street, Earles- town, said that she was formerly in service at the house of the defendant. The dog was as big *as a donkey. (Laughter.) That was its reputation in Earlestown. People called the dog Jumbo, so they might guess his size. (Laughter.) It used to fly at people some times when they came to the door. She was with the de.

fendant ten months, and came back to his service tempor- arily last August, and in September the dog flew at her and bit her. "Pluto" was supposed in Earlestown to be a very savage dog. Eliza Mulhers, married woman. Gas-street, Newton-le- Willows, said that on one occasion she saw the dog in a public-house in Earlestown and patted it. Young Mr. Walton was with the deg, and said to her "Don't mess with him," She said, "Pluto would not bite me ;" and Mr. Walton said "Lit him alfme." The dog then jumped up ad caught her in the face. She did not %Wok that the dog would have touched her if she had not touched !! firSt, JI was her own fault.

George Adams, nightsoil-man, Crow•lane, Earlestown, said that he was at a farm opposi e Mr. Walton's about six months ago, when he heard screams and cries of murder. He then saw Mrs. Walton's servant girl and another girl on the footpath, and saw also a large dog. Some persons who were near went up, one with a pitchfork, another I with a billhook and a third with a spade. Mrs. Walton got the dog away. It was a fine, bonny dog as regarded its loeks—(laughter)—but witness did not like to go near it.— Mr. Taylor: What you saw was an army of pitchforks go- ing to meet the invader? (Laughter.) Then you sum- moned the clotactuneut 111 the rear? (InCtilaSed !aughter.) —Witness: I stood on guard; you would stand on guard if you were there.—Mr. Taylor: I should climb up a tree. How far off were you? I was walking on the footpath, and when I saw the dog I stuck to the road.—Had you any offensive armour? No, sir.—You had not a pitchfork or a spade? No.—Nothing but honesty and courage? Nothing bat a lamp. (Laughter.)—You say you knew the dog? Yes —Did you think it better to keep away? I did; I wanted it to keep off me. Edward Connor, farm labourer, Newton, said that on the 21st November last he was going down Evana's railway line when he met the defendant with his dog. It had a strap round its neck and the defendant was beating it back with a stick. The dog sprang at witness and knocked him down; 14e received a cut by the fall. The dog caught him by the arm and tore his coat. Witness showed the jury td e rents in his coat. (His Honour: Have you never had your coat mended yet since last November? No, sir.) Mr. Walton commenced "laying on the dog and witness jumped over a fence and got away.—Mr. Taylor: Had you that coat on at the time ? Yes, it is my best coat (laughter.)—Mr. Swift: Would it have bitten you if it had not been beaten away ? I was too poor, it could not, I was too thin. (Laughter.) P.C. Charles Fraser, Earlestown, said that he had been stationed at Earlestown 15 months, and had known the dog I all that time.. It was as Isig as a cilf. In coosequence of

„ information given him by witness Conner he went to see Mr. Walton, and cautioned him that he must keep the dog fastened up, and that if it was seen loose about the town he would be reported. Mr. E. J. Foulston, assistant to Dr. Handyside, &ales- town, deposed to the injuries received by the plaintiff. He said that it was quite possible that she might suffer from dreams, lass of sleep, and sudden fright in consequence of having received those injuries. In fact, be had noticed her to be startled at sudden noises during the time she had been

in his surgery. The dog flew at witness cue night. The amount of Dr. Handyside's bill against the plaintiff was its. 6d. The marks on the cheek of the plaintiff would be permanent. This concluded the case for the prosecution, and wit- nesses were then called for the defence. Dr., John Davis, assistant to Dr. Watkins, Newton, said that he had been called in to attend the plaintiff for the wounds that she received on the second occasion. They . _
;were sa-perficial wounds, and not such as would be described as severe. He ri.” of opinion thlt the marks would be per-
manent.
Sarah Elizabeth Walton, wife of the defendant, was also called, and said that she never, on the 23rd of January, when she was in bed,..crdered the dog to take hold of the
plaintiff's dress to pull her into the room. On the contrary, she alleged that the plaintiff bent down to the dog and put her hands on it. She admitted that it bit the plaintiff then.
The dog was quiet, but did not like teasing, and the plain- tiff had often been told not to pet and make a fuss of him:
The dog had ntiver touched anyone who had not touched it first. . . . .

Thomas Tew, foreman in the employ of the defendant, deposed that he had known the animal ever since it was six weeks old, and that it had been ander his care ever since, about two years and a half. During that time it had always behaved well to him. He h-. 1 taaen it amongst large _ . .

~ crowds not only in Earlestown and the neighbourhood, Cut in Liverpool, and its conduct had always been good. By Mr. Swift: We are good friends; I wish everyone were as good friends as we are. He would not bite me; I have trusted him.

Eether Neal, domestic servant, now in the employ of the defendant, said that the dog ran loose about the house, and would take anything from her hand. She always gave it its supper, and thought that it was right enough so long as it was not touched.

Mr. Taylor then addressed the jury for the defence. It was quite clear, he said, that the dog bit the plaintiff on two occasion, and that was not denied. It was also quite clear that if anyoae were bit they must suffer. There were only two questions upon which he should trouble them. The first was as to whether the defendant was liable to pay for thos:‘ bites which the dog inflicted, and the second was as to how much he was, in the estimation of the jury, deemed necessary to pay. According to the law of England anyone might keep a dog, and if that dog chose to bite anyone they were not ;labia to pay for it unless they know that the dog was of a vicious nature, which, as they would see tor themselves. was only common sense. It was not enough for him to kn. w that if a dog was provoked too much it would snap at its provokers, for such a one need not be a vicious dog when usprevoked. On this point there was a considerable amount of evidence, and it was not all on one side. Which . . . .

was right it was a matter fo;. the iury to decide. - Several witnesses testified that the dog was quiet and only - flew at anyone when it was provoked to it, and on the other band they had evidence given by the plaintiff and her witnesses that on several occasions the dog had attacked various people when it was not provoked. It was not for the defence to piove that the dog was quiet, but it was for the other side to prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that it was vicious and ferocious. He then reviewed the evidence. His Honour having summed up at length, the Jury retired, and on their return announced that they had found in favour of the plaintiff, damages £l5. His Honour allowed costs upon the amount sued for.

THREATENING A. SIGNALMAN.—On Monday, at the St. Helens Police Court, a young man named Dennis Rattigan was charged with having threatened Jam, s Bradbury, a signalman, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company.—Bradbury was employed at the Fleet- lane signal Lox. About five minutes to two o'clock on the morning of the 15th inst. the defendant wanted the crossing gates at Fleet-lane opened, but as Bradbury, seeing that there was no conveyance, would not open them, the defen- dafat commenced to threaten him in a most violent manner, and tried to force his way into the signal box.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months. ' ALLEGED TRESPASS AT ECOLEST N.—William Houghton was, on Monday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having trespassed upon land belonging to Edward Houghton, at Eccleston. Mr. Thomas prosecuted, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended.—A min named Critchley said that on the 11th March, about 6,50 p.m., he saw the defendant get over the fence from a field belonging to Mr. Middlehurst, farmer, int) one belonging to the complainant. A hare then started up, and the defendant fired and wounded it. When accused of this the defendant said he had fired at a cat.— The defence was that the defendant had leave from Mr. Middlehurst to shoot over his land, and on the night in question he was out with his gun shooting vermin. He did shoot at a hare, but that was on Mr. Middlehurst's ground.—A fine of 205 and costs was imposed.—Notice of appeal WAS given. Bench, Namely: Alderman Kean, and Messrs. John Harrison, Thomas Jolley, Richard Roberts, Thomas Hirtle, R. W. Francomb, William Burn, , David Hooley, John Halton, John Hall, Samuel Lees, and John Pierpoint. He (Dr. Mackie) supposed that it was pretty generally understood that the first four names were always accepted by the magistrates unless there were some lspecial reason for the contrary. These four names included Alderman Kean, who had well and faithfully served the ratepayers for sixteen years, Mr. Harrison, who had filled twiny public offices, Mr. Jolley and Mr. Richard Roberts, the latter of ahem had been in many-public offices and the former of whom was at present in public office. Assuming that the justices accepted them, they were running no risk in taking untried men, but the other gentlemen who fol- lowed on the list were all perfectly suitable for the office, so that they might safely leave the matter in the hands of the justices, if they carried the whole list as it had been read. Ha then referred in eulogistic terms to the services and character of the late assistant overseer, Mr. Pilling, and proceeded to say that he was sorry as a retiring officer to say, that whilst the rates were announced to be lighter than the , year before, there was very little hope held out that they would be lighter in the future. When he took office three years ago be was in the hope that something considerable might be done in the way of reducing the rates, but he was sorry to say that his hopes had been very largely disap- pointed. In fact, be thought that they were utterly help- less as overseers to do anything that would materially lemon the rates, and, what was worse, the Guardians of the Poor seemed in pretty much the same position. He also referred to the influence of the county magistrates on the question, and said that the magistrates merely administered the money placed in their power, and he moet earnestly looked forward to the thne when the present or eons other Government wcmkzl give them a representative County Board, and that tlTry would be able to enter fully into the question of rates and reductions, instead of merely receiving from Preston a fiat ordering them to ply such and such a SUM. and the Guardiaas having to pay it whether firmly con- vinced of its correctness or not.-Mr. S. DUNBOBBIN seconded the resolution.—Mr. H. ROBERTS, in supporting it, said he believed that on the v. tpde the townspeople were very fairly and equitably rated, that was to say, between one owner of property and another there was very little digerence. He thoueht that the gentlemen now proposed as overseers were competent and suitable, and he wis glad to support their nomination.—The resolution was then put and carried. This was all the bueineas. and the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman. MEETING AT PADGATE. Last evening a meeting or the inhabitants contributing to the highway rates of the highway parish of Warrington was held at the King and Queen Inn, Padgate-lane, for the pur- pose of receiving and considering the accounts of the way- warden, applintin a wayererden for the ensuing year, and fixing the remuneration of the collector of highway rates. Mr. Grounds was voted to the chair, and there were also present Messrs. Samuel Clare, Isaac Ashcroft, Win. Smith, John Thompson, and J. L. Taastall (collect or). THE ACCOrNTS. Mr. TUESTALL road the statement of acconnfs as follows: —Receipts: Balance from previous year, £203 193 ; received from rates, £463 108 3d; received from Govern- ment bounty, .£23 18s 64 ; received from costs repaid, 10464 total, £704 As 11d. Expenditure: To the treasurer of the *Highway Board, £525 19e 84; stationery and stamps, £4 Is 10d ,• costs of recovery of rates, 13s 6d; collector's salary, £2O; balance in hand, £153 33 lid; total, £704 183 11d. The rate made amounted to £5OO 04 2d. there was collt cted therefrom the sum of £466 15s 10d, allowed ter compeeaation £3O 3e31, legally excused £1 is 94, unoc cupied property £1 19s 44, total £5OO Os 2d.—The accounts were approved and adopted, on the motion of Mr. CLARE, seconded by Mr. Tnomrsos. APPOINT:SEM' or WATWARDEN. On the proposition of Mr. CLARE, seconded by Mr. Asacrtorr, Mr. Grounds was re-appointed waywardeo for the ensuing year.

TOWNSHIP MEETINGS WESTON The annual meeting of the ratepayers of Halton was held in the Church Schoolroom. on Tuesday evening. The Rev. Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and there were present the Rev. J. J. Bryant, Messrs. F. J. Clandet, E. Aaron, T. India 3,, T. Ford, J. W. Kirkham, W. Norman, Jas. Ford, J. Tudor, W. Johnson, ,te The following list of candidates for the office of Overseer, to be submitted to the I 'magistrates, was approved :—Messrs. E. Aaron, hos. Ford, J: W. Kirkhern, and W. Armstrong. Messrs, E. Aaron wed 3. Collier were appointed assessors of income and aesessed taxes. Mr. Thomas Handley was appointed waywarden. The Overseers were autkorised to purchase an ordence map a .the township ler their use. A vote of thanks to the Chairman for presiding, concluded the meeting. 111./NCORN. IRTBRRSTING S2RECR BY MR. RANDLEY. The annual township meeting of Runcorn was held in etheada Schoolroom, on Thursday. There was a felt at- tendance. Mr. W. Handley was voted to the chair, and Amongst those present were Messrs. W. Whittaker, H.:Cole- man T. Handley, F. Fairhurst, J. Poole, T. Riley, W. J elen- Son, ,J. K. Diggs, W. Hankinson, and W, Sutton (assistant overseer:) The first business was the appontment of a member to serve on the Burial Board in place of Mr. Geo. Rhodes, elec,eaared, and the CRAIRISSAN said he need not add anything to what had already been said as to the value a Mr. Rhodes' Services In any mehlic office that he filled. Everybody sung Lie praises. The 'ratepayers knew that he was a man .whom sveryone could place confidence in, and they all regretted Lis removal by death; but having been removed it was their duty to appoint a member to fill his place on the Burial Board. Mr. FAIRRCRST also referred to the loss sustained by the town in the death of Mr. Rhodes, and moved that Mr. W. IL Rogerson be appointed a member of the Burial Board, Mr. J. K. MORES seconded the motion, which was carried

•staaninnualy. Mr. F. Fairhurst and Mr. John Poole were appointed hi audit the accounts of the Burial Board. The CRAIRIUN said Wore the election of overseers took place it might interest the ratepayers to know what money they had contributed during the past year, and how that money had been spent. On the 26th March, 1883, the Overseers heti a balance in hand of £7BO 0324. During the year the overseers had levied rates amounting to Is 6,1 in the £, made up as follows :—Poore' rate 71a, county rates ed, Burial Bard id, School Board 2, registration and Office expenses lid. These rates levied 94 each half year produced £3 583 Sc, and they had received from the bank interest amounting to £6 181 111, making a total cipital of £4,370 4s 1.4. The expenditure had b 'en as follows : Paid Geardians Runcorn Union £2,978, Burial Board £2OO, and School Board £350 Then they had paid an item which Vary fortunately—perhaps some would say unfortunately— they were not called upon to pay very frequently. That,was £42 12s 8t for the prosecution of Mrs. Abbott for keeping a _Louse of ill fame. The overseers hid p 0.4 this SIMI under et law passed 150 years ago, and he thought it We 3 time it lshould be repealed, because at that time there Was no county Constabulary. Now they had to maintain the constabulary. and in his opinion the prosecution a such persons should be included in the police duties. (Hear, hear.) The parliamentary regi• atration and office expenses amounted to £268 12s 104, and there was a balance in hand on ths previous day of £530 181 Id. There was a table which he had been at some tremble to prepare that perhaps might impart a little information to the ratepayers. A " flitting " very often caused a lot of rubbish to be disturbed, and in preparing to remove to Waterloo House the old rate books of the town had turned up, and they had them almost continuously from 1820 to the present day. He believed the earliest rate book made Out for the township WAS in 1520, and it would be interest- log to trace the progress of the town from the year 1821, taking each decade. In 1821 the rateable valae of the whole C 1 Runcorn was £6,631, there were 563 assessments, 542 dwelling-houses, and a population of 2500. In 1831 the rateable value was £3,594, the assessments numbered 1,020, there were 985 dwelling-houses, and a population a/ 4.500. In 1841 the rateable value had risen to £14,443, the number of assessments was 1.358. and the population would be 5,600. In 1881, the year before the formation of the Board of Commissioners, the rateable value had increased to £22,742, the assessments numbered 1,867, and the census gave the population at 8,688. In 1861 the rateable valae had increased to £25,993, the assessments to 2,287, and the population according to the census returns was 9,513. la 1871 the rateable value was £36,277, the aesesements 2,858, and the population, including Halton Within Runcorn, 12,444. In 1881 the rateable value was £47,537, the assessments 3,559, dwelling-houses 3,253, and the population 15,133. They would thus see that the town Lad made considerable progress. The rate in 1821 was 3s in the £, and in 1881 was 3s 6d, and seeing that in recent years so much had been thrown upon local authorities, the rate in 1881 was lower than the rate in 1821 in proportion. The rateahle value of the town now stood at something like £52 000 or £53,900. There WAS another table he had taken teat pleasure and interest in working out, and that was to discover how the town had progressed commercially. The tatcable value of the works in 1821 Alas £2,956, and the assessable value of the Bridgewater Trustees was something Like £2,650 In 1831 the assessable value of the works was £3,365; in 1841, £5,376; in 1851, £7,912; in 1561, £7,916 ; --ts 1871, £10,198; in 1881, £14,947. They would notice that &Jai 1851 to 1861 Runcorn stood absolutely still as regarded the rateable value of the works' only an increase 0.1£4 taking place. Although the town had gone on pro- greseiog from 1821 to the present time, both as regarded welling-houses, population, or works, the rate was really less now than it was GO years ago. (Applause.) Messrs. W. Fisher, W. Whitaker, and W. Handley were then nominated for the office of overseer. In complimentary terms Mr. Coramonst moved, and Mr. diansmost seconded the appointment of Mr. Sutton as the collector of assessed taxes, and on the motion of Mr. Warr. reran, seconded by Mr. T. HANDLEY, Mr. John Simpson was appointed aesessor of taxes. A Vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Handley for pre- adding, and the meeting terminated. HALTON. - -- .

Four of the above candidates are nominated by the Owners aed Occupiers' Association and' boar by the Ratepayers' Association while the other three are totem! 'indepen- dent" candidates. It will be seen that elec- , bons are probable only in the townships of Runcorn and Weston. div.p: TIE EX AAIINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 29, 1884.

THE WIREDRAWERS' STRIKE AT WARRINGTON- The position Of affairs in connection with the strike of Warrington wiredrawers remains unaltered. No arrange- I merit has been effected, and so far as can be seen neither of the contending parties is prepared to yield. On Tuesday afternoon, at a meeting of the Iron, and Steel Wire Manufacturers' Association, held at Manchester, a resolu- tion was unanimously- carried, to the effect that the lock- out should continue until the wiredrawers of Warrington re- sumed work on the reduced list, and reports were presented showing the working of the new list in various districts. The following letter has been forwarded to us for publi- cation by Mr. C. J. Morris, secretary of tha Iron and Steel Wire Manufacturers' Association :—Sir,—As there appears to be some little misapprehension in the public mind as to the present existing la.neatable strike in the wire trade, I should be obliged if you would allow me to state a few facts on the subject. First, as to the reduced list of prices for wire drawing agreed upon 'by the employers. This, it Is said, will not give a fair wage for a week's work. A suf- ficient answer to such a statement is the fact that a great many wiredrawe s are today working at much lower maces than those in the employers new reduced list. But further, I the wiredrawere in Birmingham, Halisax, and Manchester t have been working at the reduction for three weeks, and I am in possession of copies of lists of wages actually paid at various works in these districts for work done at this re- • ducad list. The sums actually paid to journeymen at the works referred to for a week's work under ordin- ary conditions have run from 303. to 130 s. The average is 403. to 453. per, week. that is to I say that hundreds of men are thrown out of work and great loss indicted upon many persons because some wiredrawers in Warrington will not accept a list which, on an average, will give 40s to 453 for a week's work. Next as to the cause for the action of the employers. Let it be clearly understood that the question before the employers is not a question of a little more or a little less profit, but the question as to whether the wire trade is to remain in this country or not. , In spite of the enormous development of the use of wire in all quarters of the globe, during recent years the amount of wire actually produced in F.ntland has fallen off considaraby, an.l so have the shipments of Eng- lish wire to foreign countries. This is caused by the fact that other countries Can produce wire cheaper than we have hitherto been able to do in England. The English wire manufacturer is endeavouring to reduce the cost of production by putting capital into improved machinery, and he asks the wiredrawer to do his share to enable him to conserve to England an important trade which gives empfoyment to many hundreds of people. That the reduction in wages asked for by the manufacturer is not too great is proved by the fact already referred to, that many wiredrawers are to-day working attower prices than those proposed, and also by the fact that wiredrawers in nearly all the districts outside Warrington are not only willing to work at the reduction, but have been working at it, with the result of average weekly wages of 40e to 45s per week.—Yeurs faithfully, CLAUDE J. MORRIS, Hon. Secretary Iron and Steel Wire Manufacturers' Association. Warrington, 27th March, 1884.

PRESENTATION TO THE REV. IL C. STUBBS, WARRINGTON. Ou Tuesday ;afternoon the presentation of a watch and a pure of gold, which had been subscribed by a number of friends, was made in the News Room, Market-gate, by the Mayor (Joseph liatrison, Esq.), to the Rev. H. C. Stubbs, who for 33 years has been Clerical Principal at St. Elphin's Institution, Warrington, and who has now left to undertake pastoral duties at Ashton-Heyes. near Chester. Amongst those present were Miss Bebbington, Miss :Hallett, Major Hamilton, Mr. J. P. Baker, Mr. William Dutton, Mr. John Hatton, and Mr. Powleon, In requesting the Mayor to make the presentation, Mr. Powhson said that for his long period of 33 years Mr. Stubbs had held a semi-public position in the towel, sod although be bad occupied ne municipal office, and bad very commendably been undistinguished by any strong poli- tical partizanship, he had not failed to render assistance on general occasions of public interest, when the presence of the more thoughtful and usually retiring was essential te :he successful prosecution of a desired object. While from him there had been no multitudinous platform utterances, there had been in private the offering of judicious counsel, of discriminating suggestion, and of acute criticism; and all so tempered with the sweet reasonableness ef Christian judgment as te afford charm and vitae, Interest and instruction, to what had been urged. Mr. Stubbs, as an officiating clergyman, was also probably one of the best known and most highly esteemed in the neighbourhood. From the circumstances that he had al- ways been of remarkably, activebabits, and nnfettered by parochial claims, his pastoral ministrations in local and district churches had been exceptionally numerous. And while his earnestness and zeal when thus engaged had com- mended hie work, his doctrine had been orthodox, his con- duct of Divine worship free from puerilities, innovations and contemdtible but mischievoae assumptions; and he bad acquitted himself like a man in his great Master's work; and not played the fool in divers articles of millinery, in posturising, or in any other form of self-glorification. The natural tendency of his laboura had been to instruct and to spiritualise, rather than to mystify and materialise. And in doing all that he had both deserved and commanded the respect of his hearers and fellow-worshippers. His views of Church discipline had always been Anglican, and not Raman; while his strong English common-sense, and innate sensitiveness to the feelings of his neighbours had always lent a charm te private interchange of views; and' he had shown himself sapible of respecting independence, and eminently tolerant of difference in opinion. Bat it bad been particularly in conaection with his. pastoral- and scholastic work at the noble and most important Collegiate institutions at St. Elphia's that Mr. Stubbs ha* lived his life, exercised his Influence, and proved his worth. Sonia years ago Mr. Stubbs nearly sank beneath bin inceeerant trial, but the Com- mittee of the lustitutiens very naturally highly appreciated his services, and regarded the probability of fieding an equally effective substitute then afra very dubious question; and the devoted Clerical Principal was induced to recon- sider hit determination. But the time for complete change had at last unmistakably arrived; hia work in Warrington aype ired to he breaght to a close; and he would carry with him the earnest assurance of their bark wishes for a long, a happy, and a useful future in the service if the Redeemer. (Applause.) The M &TOR said he had known Mr.. Rtubbe for a very great number of years, and he never knew anything of him but go d. He had been long associated) with one of the leading educational and religious institutions of Warring- ton, and his active Christian devotion to his duties had in many instarices4 borne rich fruit. He was sore that Mr. Stubbs would cot accept those presents became of their in- ; trinale worth only, but rather from the motive of esteem and regard that had prompted the subscribers to offer them to him. They were simply expressive of good will and kindly feeling towards him, which he had 'inetly merited, after being connected with them so long, and which should find a fitting oat-let in a presentation of that kind. There were some lives so quiet, so unostentatoues and so on- presuming that it almost seemed cruelty to drag them forth within the clamour of public recognition. The life of Mr. Stubbs had been one of that kind; it had been, a life that many persons might emulate with great advantage to them- selves and to the community amongst which they lived. (Applause.) The following letter was read to the meeting : Rectory, March 25th.—Dear Mr. Powlson.—E have this morning received your letter requesting my attendance at the presentation of a testimonial to the Rev 11. O. Stubbs. I re- gret to Bay that L have been confined to my bed stews Satur- day. lam glad that Mr. Stubbe has found to many kind friends in Warrington. who, with yourself, knew Is Av to ap- preciate his long past useful services. lam sure it will gratify film and his family, and I join my best wishes to. him, with those of the assembled partv.—Be !eve me to be. yours faith- fully, W QUECIENTI, ruwlson. Hon. t4ec. Mr. Durrou endorsed all that the Mayor and. Mr. rowl- son had said. He had known Mr. Stubbs for more than twenty years, and he had always found him a very straight- forward gentleman indeed. As a clergyman of the Church of England, he was beloved and respected by all the inhabi- tants of Warrington. (Applause.) The Rev. H. C. STUBBS, in receiving the preeents, said he felt deeply grateful for the gift—which is valuable in itself—because of thekindly feeling it showed. Luring the time he had been in. Warrington he bad bran' most kindly treated by all. For the substantial and exceedingly valuable testimonials he hadreceived from the committee with which he had worked,. and his beloved pupils, he should never cease to feel grateful. fie was also greatly gratified by that kind mark of esteem from his fellow.townstnen,and no one,he thought, had less mixed himself up with them than he had done. But he looked upon their kind gift as one ta a man who had tried to do his best. He hoped he bad done well, though he took no praise to himself.' As far as Warrington was concerned, he had never had any- thing but kind welcome in it. He felt greatly attached to the town; in fact he (night almost say that he loved every stone in the streets. At first sight, Warrington was not a place to attract much, but he was permitted to do his work quietly. He certainly worked hard, and both himself and wife met with the greatest possible kindness. Often at a distance they can hear of the good old town of Warrington; it was indeed a good old town. There was ever a readiness displayed to appreciate one's efforts, and that, after all, was the best thing a man could wish for. From the bottom of hie heart he thanked them all for that substantial expres- sion of their kindness. (applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded to the Mayor for pre- siding.

The first meeting of creditors was to be on the Br& April. and he (Mr. Gittins) mufti not examine the statement, which contained a great amount of detail, before that date. The examination was then adjourned to tbelth I April at twelve o'clock, no °petitions being asked by any of I the creditors eeesent. A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednesday, Patrick Brennan, last from Northwich, a labourer, was charged he- fore Mr. John Faircloueh with being a person of suspicious character, mai with being fbund on the premises of the Corporation Gas Works the same morning.—Prisoner ad- mitted being on the premises, but denied that he had any intention of stealing.—Evidenoe was given showing that at 1-15 on Wednesday morning bhe prisoner was observed no the roof of a building at the Mersey-street Gas Works by a person who was working there. Ile endeavoural to get , through the yard, but was secured and given into custody. • When arrested the prisoner said that he was looking for work.—Mr. Feirclough : Whet, on the top of the coon, (Laughter.)—Prisoner, who admitted being a deserter and ' having been in gaol, said that the roof was not much die. fence from the ground, and he went over it to get onto a , footpath. Hundreds of people. judging by the marks, MUSS have passed over it before him—lie was discharged on pro- mising to leave the town stance. , SINGULAR DEATH AT WARRINGTON: CHOKED RD A BUTT oti.—On Monday afternoon a lad of nine years of age, named Henry Williamson, the son of Samuel Williamson, a wiredrawer, living in Liverpool-road, met his death in: a , very singular manner. It appears that he was playing with a button, which he put into his mouth. It slipped into his throat, dhere it stuck, and, the poor fellow died before it amid be removed. He was at once taken to the Infirmary I on the accident occurring, but all efforts to save his life proved unavailiog, and he died at six o'clock in the evening. An incedry into the circumstances of the death was held at the white Hart Hotel on Wednesday mottling, before Mr. Hwband, deputy coroner, when a boy named Henry Prince deposed that he was playing with the de- ceased when the latter put a button into his mouth. DireCtiv afterwards, and as they sv:re running, the deceased suddenly fell backwards. A woman who was near at the titne a, tended to him, and he was taken to the Inerrnery, where he died. The tiny returned a verdict of " Accidental death." SILVER STREET WESLEY HALL GOSPEL TEMPERANCE WARRINOTON.—On Monday "wain, the mem- bers of the above society held a Gospel. Tem- perance mission in the Wesleyan Chapel, Lymm. The party were conveyed to Lymm in one of Mr. Maesey's wagonettes, which left the Temperance Hotel, Sankeer-street, ab 6-45 p.m. On their arrival at Lvmm the members proceeded to the chapel,. singing as they went alenz,. In the chapel a platform was erected for the occasion. The chair was taken by Mr. J. Shaw Green, of Werriegton. Messrs. Thosaas, Richards, Wellett, Howell, Gough, inlet others spoke of the blessingeof temperance, earnestly inviting those present to sign the *dee, which many did at the close. Mrs. Rifle)+, of Warrington, gave a short and touching eddrese, inviting the women to become abetainers for their children's sake. Mr. Bailey read por- tiere.; of Scripture. Miss Dickenson sung "Brightly beams our Feather's mercy" (Sankey ) in a very pleasing manner, whilst Miss Wood s cog " Mvaer, the tempest is raging" kSankey) which also was much appreciated. The7membees jeined in the choruses. The meeting was brought to a close by Mr. Brown, of Lyearn, proposing a vote of thanks tc.the Chairman and to the members of the mission, which was seconded arid carried unanimously. After sin *lle the hymn, "We s'ne of the realms of the blest," the inedie- lion was pronounced by Mr. Green. Afterwards the mem- lbers of the Mission Band were regaled in the school-gown, supper being provided for them by their Lymm friends. A vote of thanks was moved and seconded thanking the people of Lymm for the kind manner in which they had been re- ceived, and promising another visit. The Mitilioll band drove to the Warrington Temperance Hotel, and there separated.

Taxartosr.—Mr. Pate called the attention of the House to the subject of local taxation, and moved that the House, while ready to entertain any necessary reforms in local administration, deprecated the postponement of further measures of relief acknowledged to be due to ratepayers in counties and boroughs in respect of local charges imposes on them for national services. He insisted, in face of ex- travagant expenditure of the Local Government Board, it was absolutely necessary, that relief Should be given to the focal ratepayers, and to defer that until some grand scheme of local government was framed, was on their part simply a subterfuge, arerpeactically refused to deal with the subject. I DOUGLAS supported the motion.—Mr. RATHBON'II objected to the resolution passing at the moment. EDIFT SITTING.]

div.head: DEATH OF H.R.IT. THE DUKE OF ALBANY.
div.p: DEATH OF H.R.IT. THE DUKE OF ALBANY.

The intelligence of the death of the Duke of Albany, which arrived from Cannes yesterday, will cause genuine sorrow throughout the country. There lad been no previous intimation of any serious indisposition, an& the regret ex- perienced at the end bereavement sustained by Her Majesty the Queen and the Royal Family will be intensified by the suddenness of the loss. His Royal Highness Leopold Gorge Duncan Albert, Duke of Albany, was the eighth child and youngest son of Her Majesty. He was born on the 7th of April, 1953, and consequently would have com- pleted his 31.4 year nine days hence. On the 27th of April, 1882. he was married to the Princess Helen, daughter of the Prince of Vitald•ck, born on the 17. th February, Iggi, He leaves an only daughter, Alice Mary Victoria Augusta Paulins, borne on the 25th of February, 1883. The. Prince oi Wales, who was attouding Liverpocl Races, was tslegraped for. At Aintree, Spectrum and Cal!ander were weighed for the Crosby Plate, but on the report of the death of the Duke of Alrany Sir Co. Chetwynd and the Duke of Montrose declined to. run. The Duke went a few days age to the Contiwilt.

div.head: ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT WARRINGTON.

This week's Truth says :—Why is it considered BO venial. an offence to belabour one's wile? At Warrington Balite G6urt, last week, Mr. Cborley, "a tradesman of good posi- tion in the town." was charged with assaulting his wife. .113 had come home mad drunk on Sunday morning, and &led to turn her out of the house. She locked herself in her room, but he smashed the door open, swore he would :have her life, threw her down, knelt on her chest, and *throttled her till she became insensible. Three months before be had given her two black eyes and driven cove, al , hairpins into her head. Toe sympathising magistrates said "it was a painful case, and they thought that Mr. Charley, :with whom they were both well accEsainvd, °ma .of the last men to be brought up on such a charge." The defendant was fined 410, and a separation order granted to his wife, under, which he was to allow her the magnificent slim of 16s a week. But it seems to ins that Chorley ought either to have been Bet to gaol for a few months' hard labour orislee incarceratedju lunatic asylum. The facts that he occupied a good posi- tion and was an educated man aggravate the offewm enor- mously, and it magistrates will not make an example in a case like this cannot see where they are likely to begin. John Colvaill, "a stalwart young boatman," was a little less fortunate than Mr. Chorley, but he also may fairly con- gratulate himself on having got off cheaply. lie kicked his wife all over the body because she asked him for food, and then dealt her two tremendous blows in the face, drenching her with blood. The Ilfracoin'oe magistrabes sent him co prison for seven days, expressing the exceedingly sanguine bone that this punishment would "tame him." Cases like tkasi are simply a public scandal.
